review_clean: A chilling narrative about the incompetency of the policing standard in the 80s, Memories of Murder delves into the investigation of the rapes and murders of several women in an urban district of South Korea. Great performances from the cast and Bong Joon-Ho creates an eerie and stressful atmosphere with his cinematography. The ending leaves you empty yet satisfied, leaving you to fill in the gaps in the case as if you were one of the protagonists.

Dead Poets Society is a heartfelt, tear-jerking story of a group of boys learning how to express themselves through poetry and art. The chemistry between the cast is exceptional and it feels like a real group of friends. Robin Williams was just fantastic in any role he played, and Dead Poets Society is no different. He plays the emphatic English teacher that inspires the group to pursue what was true to themselves.

A heavily underrated crime boss movie that twists every expectation of the sub-genre, boasting a solid performance from Ray Winstone and an absolutely timeless one from Ben Kingsley. Glazer has one of the coolest filmographies out there.

A minor improvement on the shambles that was the second film, The King's Man is an okay addition to the Kingsman franchise but fails when it takes itself too seriously. A predictable plot twist that wasn't really necessary. More Rasputin would have been appreciated, and I strongly believe he would have served as a better antagonist.

A lot slower paced than Tarantino's other films, but I didn't mind at all. The direction and production is very good as always with a cast that's perfectly suited to providing an engaging atmosphere across overlapping storylines.
This is Wes Anderson's best film. It delivers on all fronts from being funny and wholesome, while also being deep and emotional.

The premise of this film of it being told as the journey progresses along the train is brilliant and by far the best part about this film. The scenery and atmosphere are beautiful but I feel like it could have been taken a bit further with a deeper dive into the relationships between the characters to make it even more poignant.
Anthony Hopkins is perfect in every scene he's in and steals the show in the little over 16 minutes he's on screen.
Ok, I get the hype.
Jack Nicholson and Shelley Duvall are utter perfection in this.

Racing Stripes is a vacuous mix of Cars and Babe and manages to be worse than both. The CGI on the mouths of the talking animals is so distractingly bad that it almost makes me forget about the horrible dialogue coming of them- they somehow manage to stuff every clichéd line you could possibly think of and get 102 minutes out of it. All that dragged out time to reach a conclusion that I could have told you by reading the title or looking at the poster. The film exhausts every possible way of saying that Stripes doesn't fit in and that he's the underdog that you become tired with the number of times it's said, as if we didn't understand that the first time or from the fact that he's a zebra racing amongst horses. I really don't know why I watched this. The 1 1/2 stars is for imagining what it looked like watching David Spade delivering lines about eating horse shit. Also Wendie Malick playing Beatrice Horseman in human form.

Legend doesn't offer much more than it's stunning looks. The story is an incoherent attempt at a fairy tale version of Blade Runner - the characters are one-dimensional, the dialogue is pretty poor and the story doesn't really go anywhere interesting. I think it may have fell victim to Ridley Scott's aim to make this a dark adventure story, but it doesn't really stick to either direction of tone. It should have either been a light, heartfelt film with a vividly impactful style or a darker fantasy tale. Ridley Scott doesn't really make that distinction with Legend , but yeah, it really does look phenomenal, and Tim Curry's devil is just superb.

Hail, Caesar! is the Coen brothers' love letter to cinema by being a comedy, mystery, historical drama all at once while not being that good at any of them. I feel like it was just a barrage of niche references or homages that I didn't get, along with an overstuffed format, which made the whole experience pretty boring. There are definitely moments I enjoyed, notably Josh Brolin and Alden Ehrenreich's performances as well as Channing Tatum's dance routine, but they're not enough to redeem this into being more than just an average film.

film_key: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964)
review_clean: Probably the weakest of the Kubrick films I've seen, but mainly because I feel the humour doesn't really translate over as well over time. There were definitely moments were I laughed, like when Ripper blamed his decline in the bedroom on a conspiracy theory that the Russian's were poisoning the water, but in general I felt I couldn't really connect with any of the characters. This disconnect as well as the dark comedy combined with superficial characterisation do make for a pretty brilliant political satire which pokes fun at the poor decision making in government institutions (particularly during the Cold War).
I'm glad I'm not the only one who does the awkward hand wave to dry my hands after using hand sanitiser.

A sign of a great film is not being able to stop thinking about it once the credits roll. That's exactly what Satoshi Kon has achieved with his debut feature Perfect Blue . A story of expectations, of both oneself and from others, and whether these bars that are set for us are too high to reach. It would be hard to write a review about Perfect Blue and not talk about the prominent film that it inspired, Darren Aronofsky's Black Swan . While Black Swan tackles the theme of obsession as the incessant practice to master one's craft, Perfect Blue flips that on it's head, and looks at obsession in the way in which it is directed to someone in the limelight. It sees fame as an outlet to which young women are often exploited, with their decisions being made without their consent. As a result, a rift is formed in Mima's very being, splitting herself into 3 distinct parts: one which conforms to the patriarchal view of what she should be, one which remains as a pop star that blindly follows the path that others have set out for her, and the other which exists outside these two paths, but deems herself to be a victim of her own shortcomings and failures and so succumbs to a murderous instinct. But more than that, this third persona is deemed unworthy by an industry she has given up everything for, just to be replaced by someone younger without a second thought. Perfect Blue expertly creates a blur between reality and dream- Mima's final words of "No. I'm the real thing" offer hopefulness, in that she is living proof that it is possible to leave this box of expectations. And while I am a sucker for an ambiguous ending, this one seems fitting enough.

While The Godfather was a grandiose, flashy introduction into the Corleone family as part of larger mafia empire, The Godfather: Part II treats this as the norm, as a way of life. Don Michael Corleone is a leader who keeps his cards close to his chest; who doesn't need ostentatious displays of his power to make the others in the room feel it. In fact, we don't see Michael directly impact anything throughout the film, and instead his direction is fed through his chain of command, with instructions delivered through something as simple as a glare. That's the genius of this film- Michael stares deep within the souls of those around him, while he slowly loses his own. In the final shot, we see a close up of Michael, covering his mouth with his hand, but with his eyes in full view, as he calmly sits, contemplating all that he has lost.
There's not much else I can say other than that this is a masterpiece. It's been said a million times but how on Earth do you put this and Jurassic Park out in the same year?

Spectre had all the ingredients to become a great Bond film: Christoph Waltz as the villain, Léa Seydoux as a Bond girl, and Sam Mendes returning to direct after bringing us the brilliance that was Skyfall . But unfortunately it just falls flat. For starters, the title sequence was horrible, and the song doesn't really do it for me. Also, by no means am I saying Waltz was a bad villain, in fact, his presence was menacing, but I found his introduction and his very existence to be pretty lazily written. To just say that he was behind everything that Bond has endured comes out of nowhere, and it just feels all a bit too coincidental. Overall, Spectre is visually impressive (although not quite as impressive as Roger Deakins' work on Skyfall ), but undeniably dull.
The dream sequence was my favourite part, but I think it may take some time for me to fully appreciate this for what it is.

John Carpenter's The Thing goes perfectly hand in hand with Ridley Scott's Alien in that they are both pinnacles of their genre that make use of some grotesque yet impressive practical effects. Carpenter instills a chilling sense of fear and paranoia; the type that causes friends to turn on each other in an instant, bringing forth a layer of harsh unpredictability. The score only further adds to this chilling atmosphere, if the unforgiving Antarctic blizzards weren't enough. All these aspects combined with Kurt Russells iconic performance cement The Thing as an absolute classic and a staple in the horror genre.
There's a point in this film where they mimicked the saxophone in the score with the cat's meowing and I feel like that really resonated with me on a spiritual level.
Yet another stellar performance from Al Pacino that he didn't win an Oscar for. Devastating.
This was so cute. I just couldn't stop smiling throughout. There's something about Studio Ghibli films that make me so inexplicably happy. I think I preferred this to Spirited Away .

One of the things I like most about Hayao Miyazaki's films is that there's no need for an antagonist. The only battle is the overcoming of one's struggles, which makes them all the more personal and wholesome. In Kiki's Delivery Service , this struggle is both responsibility and self confidence. I loved the little detail at the end how Jiji meowed instead of talked, signifying that Kiki doesn't quite have everything under control, and she still has some improvement left to do if she wants to make it back to her best.
That shot with the medium was so cool.

Chungking Express has this ethereal dreaminess to it, a similar feeling captured in Sofia Coppola's Lost in Translation . While visually striking and poetically written, I do think it missed out on not having a more substantial bridge between the storylines in its two halves, rather than just a thematic one.

"If there was no God, would it really make a difference" One thing shared between Schrader's First Reformed and Bergman's Winter Light is their unequivocal bleakness. Bergman makes use of a painful silence, to push the feeling of cynicism and hopelessness towards humanity even further than Schrader did. Though First Reformed captured the theme of sin and vice better than Winter Light did, Bergman's film shows the loss of the comfort of faith through skepticism of God's existence in a more poignant manner, and his exploration into the inner turmoil of a man who sees himself as a living contradiction is deeply powerful. While I do prefer Schrader's more extensive study into the sinful actions of humanity as well as the secularism of religion, Bergman achieves most of this in only 80 minutes, which is undeniably impressive.
A twisted amalgam of surrealist body-horror and the metamorphosis of technology to create an otherworldly atmosphere.

Hitchcock's direction and camerawork is obviously incredibly good, but what makes Psycho work for me is Anthony Perkins' outrageously brilliant performance, bringing to life one of the most iconic villains in all of film.

Close-Up is an introspective character study of an impoverished man posing as famed director Mohsen Makhmalbaf in order to gain respect from others. Kiarostami allows the people from the real-life case play as themselves, adding a whole new layer of depth to people otherwise fairly unknown. This makes the film feels even more natural and human, complemented thoroughly by the editing and direction. Kiarostami provides a platform for Hossain Sabzian to explain his actions, as to why he'd rather represent himself as another, more accomplished man than himself. The film is not only a deconstruction of the influence of cinema on people, but an investigation, not dissimilar to Farazmand's journalistic process, into those same people, and their dreams, desires and motivations.
"A pig's gotta fly"

Pulse makes use of sepulchral, brutalist Japanese architecture and a masterful use of light, or lack thereof, to enforce an air of terror. I appreciate the fact that Kurosawa's trusts the audience's intelligence enough as to not spell everything out for them. Keeping things vague and mysterious only adds to the horror further. There are some scenes in this film that are honestly so petrifying that they will be etched into my mind forever. Apparitions hide as shadows which bleed into the darkness. Ghosts are the embodiments of the loneliness we feel in life, which are forced to continue to walk the Earth, cursed to live with this eternal solitude into death. As the usage of technology rises, meaningful connections collapse, and we lose those closest to us to the darkness. One of the brilliant ways Kurosawa decides to convey this loneliness is by making the film very empty. Not only is it mostly devoid of colour, but it's also devoid of crowds of people: the public transport has nobody on it, and neither do the streets. Even the sound design flippantly goes between a harsh, screeching score to completely nothing in the following scene. He uses the internet as a system- a means of connection between people that slowly collapses, causing more and more people to succumb to the emptiness, and causing the flashing and jarring glitches of footage to become more frequent. This results in the enigmatic finale, where all collapses around our protagonists, as they attempt to escape amidst the chaos. Kiyoshi Kurosawa knows exactly how to make his films feel as haunting as possible, and Pulse is no exception to that, with every scene as terrifying as the last.

Just when I thought the Alien franchise couldn't get much worse after Alien³ , Alien Resurrection comes around to prove me wrong. It's riddled with awful filmmaking decisions and terrible, misogynistic dialogue, of course a symptom of Joss Whedon's pathetic writing. Sigourney Weaver and Winona Ryder do their best to try and rescue what little they can of this dreadful film, but it's simply not enough. They should have just left Ripley to die and let her escape this franchise. The special effects were half decent at least, which made parts of the film a little entertaining. On the bright side, at least I get to watch Prometheus next, hopefully Ridley Scott can offer some redemption.
At least Paris, Texas has the added bonus of not having any French people there.

The Noah Baumbach and Greta Gerwig combo remains undefeated in this 84 minute theatrical manifestation of the millennial experience in a big city. Brooke and Tracy are both young, ambitious women aiming to fulfil their ambitions while also trying to figure themselves out. Baumbach uses his quintessential fast paced dialogue to make us feel like these relationships have been going on for much longer than they appear, which proves to be both a positive and a negative in Mistress America, as while it feels in tune with a present day conversational experience with an abundance of cross talking and redundant verbiage, it ultimately makes some of the less recurrent characters such as Brooke feel slightly underwritten. As a result, the ending sequence feels a bit rushed, which another 15 to 20 minutes would have fit nicely. In spite of this, the dialogue and the characters make Mistress America one of Baumbach's most enjoyable films, with sharp-witted comedic moments well balanced with the more hard-hitting ones. While it may come across a little cheesy or pretentious at times, I feel this fits in well with the characters and makes sense for the kind of vibe the film is going for. Lola Kirke does well in her role, and the chemistry in the scenes with Gerwig's character is where she really shines.

Visually, The Face of Another is unbelievably well done, with Hiroshi Teshigahara leaving me mind-boggled at times with how he pulled off some of these complex shots. As for the films themes, it pulls off its ideas about identity and self well, but without a whole lot of nuance. With most of the dialogue being solely about the mask, it's hard to focus on much else. It doesn't take much of a break from it's nihilistic sentiment either, which can lead to the film dragging at times, especially in the second half. While I do very much appreciate Teshigahara's intention and craftsmanship, as well as Segawa's beautiful cinematography, The Face of Another just feels a little empty to me, and goes on for a bit too long.

Federico Fellini's 8 1/2 is perhaps one of the most self-referential, meta films I've seen, as it is itself a film about an artist's inability to create, told by an artist who is unable to create. A filmmaker whose lack of inspiration becomes his inspiration. A cinematic personification of procrastination. 8 1/2 is so self-referential in fact, that its very title is a reference to the number of films Fellini had created up until that point. Marcello Mastroianni plays Fellini's alter ego, Guido Anselmi, an artist strained by his shortcomings as a man and as a filmmaker. He continues to be troubled by the ghosts of his past, fading in and out of dreams until his motivations in those become indistinguishable from those of his current reality. Both cinematographer Gianni Di Venanzo and composer Nino Rota work in unison to create an illusive atmosphere, with the popping bright white canvases and symphonies of classical music painting the background of the film. While the first half didn't grab me entirely, the second half blew me away, and there's no doubt in my mind that there's something in everyone that can relate to parts of 8 1/2 , and on repeat viewings, I can only see that feeling growing.

City of God feels way longer than its 130 minute runtime, but this in no way is a criticism of its pacing or excitement. In fact, it is a testament to how much it accomplishes in that time. Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund paint a perfect portrait of the lives of these impoverished Brazilian kids living in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro. Children living in a godless hell where every action is shrouded in the ulterior motives of revenge or climbing up the ladder of power. "Why return to the City of God, where God forgets about you?"

Edward Yang's Yi Yi is no doubt a momentous film, much more than the familial drama it appears to be. Sean Baker described the film as almost being a period piece, despite it being released only just over 20 years ago. I agree with this sentiment wholeheartedly; Yang elegantly depicts Taipei's modernistic development for the time as the 20th century turned to the 21st. As a result, this development has changed so incredibly rapidly since then, leaving Yi Yi feeling like a foregone relic. Yet, in a time of accelerated growth and connections, it's themes are more pertinent than ever. In the film, the Grandmother slips into a coma after suffering a stroke. Each family member comes to her in their own time and confesses their truths, knowing full well they won't receive an answer. This exchange represents the matriarchal values of a past time, and showing us, the viewer, the afflictions these individuals are experiencing throughout different stages of life. These individuals are connected not only by familial relation, but by the choices that they have or haven't made. The older generation reflect on their choices from what feels like a previous life, seeing whether the things they left behind were worth it. Meanwhile, the children are making all these decisions for the first time, following in the footsteps of the adults they believe to have all the answers. Yi Yi 's narrative spans generations, holding focus on the little, fleeting moments we may forget as a kid, and contrasting these with the big decisions we have to face as an adult. To tie these stories together, Yang begins Yi Yi at a wedding, and ends it at a funeral. As I said before, Yi Yi is a momentous film, and I could write pages upon pages analysing it's complex characters and brilliant narrative, but I think it's best to just experience it for yourself.

Yojimbo was actually pretty goofy and funny, not quite what I expected of a Kurosawa film but it was a welcome surprise. Contrast this with the violence spouted from the gang war, and you get a excellent blending of themes that isn't easy to accomplish. It's clear to see Yojimbo 's influence on the westerns that followed, even though I haven't seen many (besides Star Wars of course), as well as Kurosawa's influence on film in general. Excited to see what Sanjuro brings, because I really enjoyed Toshirō Mifune's performance in this.
