There was a time in my life where I wouldn't have given a romantic comedy a chance, half expecting to be run down by a bombardment of clichés and kitschy melodrama, but I'm glad I've taken a turn since then, otherwise I wouldn't be able to appreciate the brilliance of films like Broadcast News . With a charming ensemble cast, and a superb screenplay by James L. Brooks, Broadcast News manages to expertly achieve the classic romantic love triangle trope without it feeling banal. As well as this, it manages to serve as a unique story of ambition over desire; trying to balance what you want with what will get you the furthest. It does this brilliantly through the medium of media, contrasting the way someone portrays themselves behind a camera to how they are in front of one. What truly makes Broadcast News work, however, is the cast. Holly Hunter, Albert Brooks and William Hurt are all phenomenal and give all timer performances that I won't soon forget. Hunter in particular was just wonderful every time she was on screen, delivering the exceptional dialogue with a charisma that is ever so delightful to see.

Much like the other Terrence Malick films I've seen, Knight of Cups is undeniably gorgeous. Lubezki's cinematography is second to none, and truly adds a whole new layer of introspection to the film. The camera wanders endlessly as a silent observer. Much the same, Rick has felt like an outside observer to his own life, watching the years tick away with wealth, power and mangled relationships. You definitely need to be in the right sort of headspace to watch a Malick flick. They are so deeply rooted in allowing the viewer to join the characters on their journey, empathising with their experience. Depending on how you're feeling, Knight of Cups could feel like a glorified perfume commercial, or it could feel like a deep deconstruction of self, with glorious cinematography and a beguiling sense of contemplation.
PCW simply does not miss.

It's so easy to find something to relate to in Ghibli films, no matter what stage of life you're at, which is, I assume, part of the reason they're so beloved. It's difficult trying to figure out how to balance what you have to do with what you want to do. Finding the time for both is no easy task, and Whisper of The Heart demonstrates that perfectly. As for the animation, it's almost like they're showing off here because it's just that good. From the sun rising amidst the city skyline to simply the train moving along the tracks, there's a meticulous level of detail in every frame, which just shows the love and care that goes into making these films. For now, Whisper of The Heart is my favourite Ghibli.
Probably the most convenient heart attack of all time.

I can't really put into words how much I loved Petite Maman. It's a film where emotions can only be explained by experiencing them. It's weird how much time we spend with our parents without ever really getting to know them. Whether things are better left unsaid or not, we only ever really obtain these small snippets of their lives through stories. Céline Sciamma has such a skill for bringing these stories to life through her films, and I adored every second of this one.

High and Low is a film as deceptively simple as its title. Toshirō Mifune nails his portrayal of a more modern man, and Kurosawa's stab at noir is everything I could have hoped for and more. We start the film in the house, which sits on the hill above the rest of the city, of business magnate Kingo Gondo, as he argues with his fellow shareholders about a potential takeover of the company. Later on, he gets a phone call saying his son has been kidnapped. Kurosawa uses scene framing perfectly here to make us feel suffocated, crowding people together in small spaces to create tension. Once it becomes apparent that the kidnapper took the wrong child, a conflict arises, presenting Gondo with the moral dilemma of whether he would do the same for the chauffeur's son that he would do for his own. This decision creates a sense of high and low in terms of status: whether the chauffeur's son's life is worth as much as a wealthy businessman's. We spend the first half of the film almost exclusively in Gondo's house, never seeing things from the kidnapper's perspective, until a point where the film becomes a police procedural, with the entire force gathered trying to figure out ways to catch the kidnapper. We see the city from a lower point, amidst the poorer folk, while Gondo's house is visible from above it all, much in the same way as Mount Fuji is seen as this constant presence. Slowly, we begin to see more from the kidnapper's perspective, instead of him just being a voice behind the phone. Alongside the police investigation, we as the viewer also feel like we're learning more about the kidnapper's identity, until the very end of the film, where he reveals all in an outburst of frustrated emotion and he's taken away by authorities, until we're left with Gondo's reflection, heralded for his actions by the public but nevertheless reduced to the lowly shoemaker he once was.

There are many facets of the mumblecore subgenre that I love; part of that is the sense of realism it brings to the film that you don't really get from other dramas. I mean, who else would think to open a film with an awkward kerfuffle of removing clothes before sex? The reason films from directors like Noah Baumbach or Greta Gerwig gel so well with me is the combination of this naturalistic style with excellent directing and a more-often-than-not first-rate script to boot. Perhaps I can forgive some of Nights and Weekends due to it being a directorial debut (for Gerwig that is, Swanberg not so much), but on the whole, it just felt like it lacked purpose. There are definitely moments that feel reminiscent of the more polished Baumbach features like Frances Ha , but others feel like they're trying to evoke particular feelings for no reason as they lead to nowhere, especially with that weak ending.

There's really so much I could say about A Brighter Summer Day . It's no doubt the biggest Yang film I've seen, and that's not even in reference to the runtime. In many ways, the film feels like a novel- an epic familial saga with an underlying story of crime, feeling like equal parts Yi Yi and City of God . Edward Yang has this incredible ability to make this particular event on which the film is based feel both substantial and personal, with each small moment having significant implications. The choreography of Yang's design is awe-inspiring, and I don't think I can think of a single director who does it better; the immaculate use of negative space and blocking is just bewildering as to how well it's executed. I don't think there's any uncertainty in me calling Yang one of my favourite directors now, an impressive feat considering I've only now seen three of his films.

Going into Stalker as my first Tarkovsky film, I was under the impression from others that his films are very slow burns and the word "boredom" often appears. For the first hour or so, I felt the same way. Then, we, alongside The Writer, Professor, and Stalker, embark on a journey to find a room inside a forbidden zone that can grant you your deepest desire. The film at this point takes a turn for the metaphysical, with long takes of symbolic imagery and philosophical dialogue. Upon the revelation of this room, we as the viewer think we would enter it without a second thought, but Tarkovsky employs us to consider the cost of this decision. The camera follows our ensemble like a weary watcher, or silent witness, staring from afar through these eerie passageways. Upon their arrival at the room, the professor and the writer question whether they even want to go inside, doubting its legitimacy while also wondering whether it would be worth the cost even if it were real. They say that even if they did enter this room and achieve their desires, they would have a moral responsibility to make sure nobody else could do the same, as just because they are deemed to be good doesn't mean other people will be. This demonstrates a key principle of the film: wouldn't they be evil if they don't allow others the hope of salvation? This in turn becomes a hypocrisy in itself as the room is supposed to only allow in those with pure intentions. Going into the room forces you to confront your deepest desire, and whether it is what you expect it to be is the biggest challenge. We are transported to this otherworldly plane inside 'The Zone', where the normal rules of left and right do not apply. The Professor and The Writer, being both men of logic and reason, reject this notion and refuse to accept that the room exists solely in faith, a quality The Stalker has in abundance. While he is not lacking in belief, The Stalker is sparse in willpower and guides others to their desires while he cannot fulfil his own. Of course, Stalker can be seen as an allegory of faith and the tests that one must overcome along the way, but Tarkovsky allows the film to be much more open than that, and it could be seen as a search for the meaning of life from the perspective of doubters. Coming back to the cost that must be paid in order to achieve one's desires, it seemed fitting that my first experience of Tarkovsky's work was what caused him so early to make his last, and ultimately the film that ended up taking his life, as well as the lives of his wife and Anatoly Solonitsyn, caused by the contamination from a chemical plant near where they shot the film. It's hauntingly beautiful in a way that this selfish decision from Tarkovsky was the very thing that led to the tragic deaths of these people. It's this context that elevates Stalker to masterpiece status for some, and I wouldn't blame them. For a man who believed that man's purpose on Earth was to create profound works of art, he sure sacrificed everything in order to fulfil it.

So this is officially the oldest film I've seen, and wow, was I impressed. Not only was it wildly creative and impressive technically for the time, but it was also pretty funny too. I may have to watch more James Whale films.

film_key: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders (1970)
review_clean: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders presents itself as a series of disjointed segments, where nothing really follows on from the last event. Whether this is just a means to obscure its pretty clearly exploitative plot, I'm unsure, but there's no doubt that the film is visually stunning. It's certainly a mastery of surrealism from Jireš, but despite this, I can't say I can overlook its downright disturbing qualities. I assume it was the intent for these scenes to be uncomfortable, but knowing that doesn't really take away from how uncomfortable they are. On the other hand, you can really feel what Jireš is going for here, controversial or not. The themes of naïveté, passion and sexuality all become apparent in this psychosexual fairytale of colliding imagery. Nevertheless, I just can't get past the earlier sentiments.

We walk past strangers every day of our lives. They only really exist to us in those fleeting moments we interact with them, be that a simple glance or a conversation. It seems trivial to say, but of course, behind this interaction there's a whole different person-one with emotions, dreams, and troubles just the same as anyone else. For those few intimate moments, we are bonded by this commonality. Vive L'amour follows the intersecting lives of three strangers, all of whom are struggling to find their place in the world. Much like in Yang's Taipei Story , Tsai Ming-liang explores the search for connection in the rapidly evolving urban culture of Taipei, which so often feels indifferent and hostile. This feeling is only amplified by Tsai's camerawork and carefully crafted mise-en-scène, which allow the surroundings to feel cold and impersonal while the connections are real and tangible. There's a distinct contrast between the relationship, or lack thereof, between both May Lin and Hsaio-kang and Ah-jung. May Lin is struggling to find meaning in her work, so she seeks to fulfil her desires through her relationships with men. Upon meeting Ah-jung, she finally feels that she may be able to fill the hole she feels she has. Hsaio-kang attempts suicide in an apartment that isn't even his, showing his lack of attachment to anything in his life. By the end of the film, we see May Lin having sex with Ah-jung while Hsaio-kang masturbates under the bed. May Lin leaves, and Hsaio-kang then shares a deeply personal yet unreciprocated moment of intimacy with a sleeping Ah-jung before pulling away. May Lin is next seen weeping on a bench while the sounds of city traffic pass by. This scene lasts for almost 5 minutes. Both May Lin and Hsaio-kang end up alone, despite their shared moments of intimacy, just as if they were strangers on the street passing each other by. The city continues as it was, as if nothing had ever happened at all.

"Some of the old tales of Japan have come down to us in curiously unfinished form. Why were they left unfinished? Perhaps the writer was lazy. Perhaps he had a quarrel with his publisher. Perhaps he was suddenly called away from his little desk and never returned. Perhaps Death stopped his writing brush in the middle of a sentence." A guilty conscience. A broken promise. A lost tale. A swallowed soul. These four stories tie together the saga of Kwaidan . Based on traditional Japanese ghost stories and folklore, Kwaidan is nothing short of a work of art, with stunning set design and boasting some of the best visuals I've ever seen in film. Its anthological style allows the 3 hour runtime to breeze by, and the use of colour and lighting is simply masterful, immersing the viewer in its eerie atmosphere almost instantly. While it may not exactly be horrifying, it certainly carries an otherworldly sense of mystery behind it, a feeling especially prominent in my favourite of the four stories, "The Woman in the Snow", for which I could have watched a whole film on its own.

The first time I watched Snowpiercer, I can't say I was well versed in the world of cinema, let alone familiar with any of the works of South Korean auteur Bong Joon-ho. At that time, I thought it was a fine movie, certainly captivating in its premise, but somewhat limited by it at the same time. I mean, there's only so much you can explore within the confines of a moving train. Despite this restriction, Bong Joon-ho does manage to create a discourse on political structures, as well as societal classes and even environmental concerns. Albeit, it seems to try and tackle too much and winds up accomplishing too little, leading me to feel more or less the same about Snowpiercer as I did back then. Go figure.

Retribution may not be as scary as Cure or Pulse , but one thing it does incredibly well is slowly peel back the layers of its meaning. It feels the most personal of the Kiyoshi Kurosawa films I've seen thus far, unravelling itself as a haunting love story, a substantial step away from the police procedural it begins as. This shift is more than tonal though; you can physically feel the atmosphere change throughout the film, and it's one of the things I admire most about Kurosawa as a filmmaker. From the precise set design to the practical effects to the manipulation of the sound, every aspect of a scene feels purposeful, and while it may seem simple, it's a level of mastery that most filmmakers wish they could achieve.

"If you place an object in a museum, does that make this object a piece of art?" After watching Triangle of Sadness , I said I was excited to explore the rest of Östlund's oeuvre, and I'm so glad I finally did. The Square , much like Peele's Nope from last year, is a story about spectacle. But instead of being about our desperation to capture a spectacle, The Square explores our aversion to one. It questions the classification of art: what qualifies and what doesn't, and more importantly, who decides? Is it up to the cultural elite or the common man? I must say that I feel like Östlund has mastered the ability to create uncomfortable situations without there ever being an outburst or shouting match that results from it. These moments perfectly encapsulate the characters he's trying to portray while often being hilarious at the same time. But again, who am I to decide what's uncomfortable and what isn't, and why does one moment of insincerity make me more uncomfortable than another? These are all questions that Östlund begs of the viewer throughout The Square , and Claes Bang in the leading role does excellently to tie them all together. All the themes of power, masculinity, and class imbalance coalesce through his characterisation, and they come together brilliantly throughout the film. A first of two Palme d'Or wins for Östlund, and it would be hard to argue that it wasn't deserved.
Can I get some French fries with that French fish?
I can't tell whether this comforts or terrifies me considering I'm graduating this year. Oh god, I'm graduating this year.

Ivan's Childhood is so impeccably shot and crafted by Tarkovsky- the camerawork and usage of blocking are just phenomenal. It follows the story of a boy so burdened by the experience of war that he knows nothing else besides it; his innocence stripped away just as quickly as his family was. Tarkovsky manages to depict the severity of the war-torn landscapes while also allowing the film to feel deeply human, with the connections between this boy and the soldiers, but that feeling is annulled by the film's overwhelming bleakness. So much so that at times it felt like a horror film, and at the end it gives us a glimpse of what Ivan's life could have been.

There's no doubt Black Girl is effective in its messaging on colonialism, which acts as a sort of prison that stops someone like Diouana from living her life to the fullest- a notion that her employers, or more aptly, slavers, take for granted. On a technical level, the film is most certainly lacking, but at times it almost adds to the humble charm of Sembène's debut. It's absolutely an important film on imperialism and social divide, as well as being the first feature film ever released by a sub-Saharan African director, but it definitely lacks depth in parts, and I just wish it held the same level of complexity that the epilogue had throughout.

A little too slow moving for me, and it probably should have been a little shorter, but when Eyes Without a Face hits, it hits hard. The combination of the impressive practical effects and some really cool visuals elevate this to being a horror must-watch- it would be a good film today, but it would have been quite something to witness in the 60s I'm sure. All the scenes around the surgery were so fascinating to watch, and those alongside the great ending are probably the reasons why I slightly prefer this to a similar film like Teshigahara's The Face of Another , which is probably a hot take. But in that same thought, both films are so eerily poetic that it's so interesting to watch them unfold, especially with the sprinkled lines of philosophical dialogue throughout each.

I've always preferred the more subdued coming-of-age films to the more overt ones, and Céline Sciamma's debut Water Lillies is a great example of the former. Most of the time, it's much more effective to allow the audience to feel the impact of a small moment so we experience it at the same time as the characters, rather than to beat the audience over the head with its message. While something like Eighth Grade captures the zeitgeist of that era of teens growing up, Water Lillies is able to become much more than that, exploring themes like femininity, sexuality, and friendship that can pertain to any time, much like how Marie and Floriane are at different stages in their lives.

The 400 Blows essentially sums up what I miss and don't miss about being a kid. The freedom of being able to just do something on a whim without thinking of the consequences, or the feeling of being in the back of your parents' car after a day out and just feeling content. Conversely, it shows Antoine being constantly neglected and not being taken seriously for anything he tries to do. I wanted to delve more into French New Wave cinema this year, and I thought there wasn't a much better place to start than with one of the pioneers of the era, François Truffaut, and one of the films that is said to have garnered more international acclaim towards the movement. It's safe to say I'm enthusiastic to see more from this period.

I'm really torn with this one. On the one hand, A Hidden Life might just be one of the best looking films I've ever seen, with an outstanding score and an incredibly personal narrative. On the other, the characters feel as cold and inane as the landscape that surrounds them, but at other times I would well up as if the story they were telling was my own, with gems of dialogue scattered few and far between. Malick's films are always more difficult to connect to simply because they really aren't like any others, with their spiritualistic style often taking precedence over any deep-cut storytelling- sometimes this is more effective, but sometimes it can feel preachy without any substance behind the words being said. Nevertheless, I just couldn't bring myself to fully dislike this. Terrence Malick's vision and camerawork are inspired as usual, and the story of Franz Jägerstätter is tragically beautiful.
Would've been better if Luis came at the end to recount the events of the film.

I'm actually bewildered at how good this soundtrack was- every time it played in the background, I couldn't help but have a massive grin on my face, no matter what violence or gore was ensuing on screen. But I'm so glad I loved Deep Red , because I didn't really connect with Suspiria when I watched it, beyond the lighting and colours at least, but it definitely felt like Deep Red had more depth to it. The mystery feels really gripping, and the camerawork is astounding, but what's more, the film is oddly progressive for its time, which only furthers my enjoyment. The dynamic between Marc and Gianna is electric, which Argento achieves simply by writing them well, and it makes the dialogue flow much smoother between them in spite of it being a little rough around the edges. The film brings forth unexpected romance and comedy elements as well, which was a welcome surprise. All this, and I haven't even touched on the horror yet, which is absolutely sublime, of course. It's so creatively audacious, and Argento does so well to build tension with the mystery here while simultaneously creating a spooky atmosphere; it felt so reminiscent of classic Hollywood slashers like Halloween and Scream with its music and body horror, and yet it came out before both- it really felt like something unique and special. I hope this can be my gateway into more of Argento's filmography.

"You must never forget this is only a play" I really wasn't expecting to love this as much as I did, with it being my first Cassavetes film and all, but it really blew me away. The layers of improvisation and subtext behind each stage performance were so incredible, and Gena Rowlands was just phenomenal- her performance instantly shot up to one of my favourites of all time. Cassavetes is brilliant both in front of and behind the camera. I haven't seen many films from actor-directors, but you can absolutely tell from his filmmaking here that he truly understands what it's like to be in front of the camera too. I mean, his scene blocking alone is sublime, but combined with some stupendous camera movement and I was totally floored. The way Opening Night flips back and forth so easily from being a play within a film to a film about a play is masterful, with the character's struggling to differentiate between the two adding this sense of meta self-awareness that was so interesting to see unfold. It reminded me of Kiarostami's Taste of Cherry in a way, because, through this Brechtian distancing, it's like Cassavetes is reminding us that this is just a film, but how easily this distinction can be lost in the mind of an actor trying so hard to enter the psyche of their character. Gena Rowlands does so well to capture this uncertainty too, with a nuanced vulnerability that feels utterly mesmeric right the way through.

Force Majeure was probably my most anticipated of Ruben Östlund's films, and boy, did it deliver. I could very easily upgrade this to a 5/5 in future, as it's probably one of the best shot and framed films I've seen in recent memory, and of course the idyllic scenery has a lot to do with that, but the use of subtle cinematography in every single shot is outstanding. I said this in my review for The Square , but I'll reiterate it here: Östlund's ability to capture the awkwardness of a confrontation is unmatched and arguably reaches its zenith in Force Majeure , with each marital spat gradually building to a powerful crescendo. I debated with myself about whether the penultimate scene was a little on the nose, thinking that Ebba would surely hold to the notion of protecting her kids first and foremost when put in a position such as the one she was in, as well as recognising the hypocrisy of her actions. However, Östlund argues that when put in a situation like that, one is reduced to their instincts, and regardless of what societal gender roles would assume of them, we can never know how we'd act in the moment. Naturally, this is a reflection of Tomas' actions at the start of the film, but it's also perfectly mirrored in the final scene, where Tomas initially rejects his inhibition but then changes his mind. It's brilliantly prophetic.

Takeshi Kitano's debut, Violent Cop is as decadently violent as its title suggests, contrasting moments of visceral brutality with a smooth jazz backdrop. It's clear to see Kitano's style straight away, especially his comedic background, as not many people could make police brutality quite so funny. There are some really cool shots throughout too, although these are often hindered by some weak editing, which also convolutes a fairly simple plot. Azuma is a necessary evil in a place chock-full of depravity and filth, so much so that his superiors even recognise his extreme methods as tolerable. There isn't really any of the moral turpitude you'd expect, because this violent cop really just doesn't really care, and lucky for everyone else in the station, he landed on their side of the law. It's littered with ruthless violence and black comedy, which arises less from punchlines and more from punches. While its muted, deadpan tone may have been a little much at times, Kitano's contrast between the slow and the chaos was fantastically worked, with the final confrontation perfectly epitomising that juxtaposition.

There seems to be a lot of discourse on whether Close is emotionally compelling or manipulative. Unfortunately, I fall on the side of the latter. It feels like Dhont has manufactured this film to make it impossible for the viewer not to cry, and while that may be a factor in getting your audience to feel emotion, it certainly does not make a film more rewarding. Its heartfelt moments feel a little too engineered to make you feel that way, rather than being earnest, truthful moments of sorrow. It just doesn't take any risks or commit to any particular direction- is it a film about toxic masculinity, queerness, or something else entirely? Having said that, Eden Dambrine absolutely kills it in this role, delivering perhaps a more nuanced performance than the film permits, which deserves all the praise. Although, for a film about loss, he seems to be the only fleshed out character, with Rémi simply serving as a plot device to carry the story forward. Dhont explores Léo's grief as he blames himself for the suicide of Rémi, but then he offers no alternative. Sure, it's devastating, but isn't it a little harsh to offer no solace and just let us, and more importantly, Léo, believe that Rémi did kill himself because of him? It felt like Dhont didn't know what direction to take Close , and I have no doubt people will rate this highly because of the gut-wrenching emotional scenes, but that's just not enough to make for a good film.

film_key: BARDO, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths (2022)
review_clean: I'm not going to lie and say I knew entirely what was going on during Bardo 's 160-minute runtime, but Iñárritu's latest outing proves why he's so well acclaimed. Bardo is a deeply enigmatic (at least until the end) audiovisual manifestation of his own insecurities as a filmmaker, a father, and as a man. It also explores his guilt and neglect towards his own culture, all while being celebrated by another. He channels Fellini and even Malick at times, but mostly he channels himself through the character of Silverio, much like how Fellini channels himself through Guido Anselmi in 8 1/2 , creating a chaotic self-criticism that, alongside Babylon , is probably the biggest swing of the year. There are big risks taken, and some pay off while others most certainly do not. It's a deep dive into the hypocrisy of artistry: one spends their life in search of what gives life meaning that they often forget to live it, and Iñárritu understands that perfectly. The sheer amount of craftsmanship that must have gone into each scene is immense, not only from a visual standpoint but an auditory one too. It truly is an experience, and while it may have only resonated in parts with me, the cinematography and surrealism on display were astounding. But it's the times it takes to breathe that are really the most striking, because, amidst all the noise, it's just a story of a father trying to be better.

Only God Forgives has some cool visuals, but it's severely lacking in the plot department, which is usually fine, but some of the dialogue was a chore to listen to- in fact, I don't think there was one scene where I didn't cringe once at a line. Refn tries to make three different movies in one, and it ends up feeling like some second-rate homage to a better film. Its depiction of women is frankly gross and strange, but I could partly forgive that if it aimed to make any sort of remark on why these characters were presented in this way, but alas, there isn't any such justification. It's a shame this visual flair goes to waste on such a poor story.

Noticeably more restricted than the other of Hitchcock's works I've seen, but that's obviously a symptom of the time. That doesn't make The 39 Steps any less impressive; in fact, it only accentuates what he was able to achieve given the resources available. Robert Donat is amazing as Hannay, though, and is easily the highlight of the film, elevating every scene with Madeleine Carroll with his quick-witted charm.
The music in this was awesome, probably my favourite soundtrack across all the Ghibli films I've watched so far.
I saw the "I'll kill you" foreshadowing coming and it was still brilliant. A phenomenal screenplay and exquisite performances from the whole cast. Truly a timeless classic.

I can't say I was as grabbed by Antonioni's heralded L'Avventura as I would have liked to have been, at least not after the first hour when the story veered away from Anna's disappearance to Sandro and Claudia's dubious affair. It wasn't until I dug a little deeper after finishing the film that I could appreciate what it was trying to say. The film takes an interesting view on love and relationships, showing how fleeting and destructive they can be in the end, but in that one moment drenched in passion, there's nothing else more desirable. Antonioni's shot composition throughout the film is masterful, with most of the visuals being outright perfect in their framing. He uses the distant wide shots and the sparse close-ups as a narrative device to convey the characters' feelings in such a clever way. He paints the men in this film with the same brush: a savage, preying pack only concerned with their own interests, amplified further through Sandro, whose privilege often allows him to capitalise on his lustful instincts unlike his lower status counterparts, who are left only to gawk. While Sandro only ever seems empowered by his privilege, Claudia and, to a clearly greater degree Anna, feel trapped by it. They feel trapped by the societal pressures of how women should act and look, especially ones related to their status, and, from my interpretation, Anna takes her own life because of it. Her shadow looms over the rest of the film, especially at the end, where we see Claudia and Sandro at their lowest. Claudia is uncertain of how to react to Sandro's infidelity because it would be hypocritical for her to be angry, and so we're left with that same uncertainty that we were introduced to at the start. Perhaps that's why I couldn't fully connect with L'Avventura , as its mystery offers no resolutions, and neither do its characters. Or perhaps it's the post-production dubbing that leaves much of Italian cinema feeling less natural and therefore more inaccessible to me. Nevertheless, Antonioni offers respite to the viewer through open-endedness, and satisfies our desires, much like his characters, through a simple run of the fingers through the hair of a shamed lover.

It's probably been said a thousand times before, but what Sam Raimi manages to achieve in The Evil Dead with a relatively low budget is outstanding. The practical effects in this alone are staggering in all of their grotesque forms, but couple that with some great camerawork and campy storytelling, and you've got yourself a classic horror flick. Excited to watch the rest.
I think this took years off my lifespan. Or maybe it added a few extra. I'm not sure at this point.

Masterful dialogue and camerawork, but what makes Sunset Boulevard so spellbinding is the performances from William Holden and Gloria Swanson, particularly the latter. It's just a staggering portrayal of the descent into madness of an actress fading into obscurity, and every second of that journey is mesmeric.

Margot at the Wedding is certainly in competition with The Squid and the Whale for the Noah Baumbach film with the least likeable protagonists. I mean, they're both still incredibly well written and performed, especially between Kidman, Leigh, and Black in this film, but I would be lying to say that either of them was a blast to watch. The characters straddle the line between flawed and entirely insufferable, which I suppose is what makes them more compelling and by extension more human, particularly when combined with Baumbach's snappy dialogue, but nevertheless, this is still probably my least favourite of his work.

Paul Thomas Anderson weaves the rich tapestry of interconnectedness through coincidence as we examine the entangled nature of our relationships and how we impact others. Magnolia blossoms through its ensemble, with nearly every one giving a career best performance, and each of which is left grappling with the vagaries of their fateful tribulations through striking vignettes that build to a climactic conclusion. We're left to ponder whether these coincidences are serendipitous or ill-fated while being thrown around this 3-hour cosmic roundabout that constantly draws parallels between itself and the outside world. Perhaps fate is as totally out of our control as a plague of frogs falling from the sky, or perhaps the onus is on us to shape our own destiny.

Wild Tales is a ridiculous anthological satire that tells six short stories about increasingly outlandish situations. It certainly has its highs and lows, but the awkward turmoil captured by Damián Szifron throughout is excellent and felt very evocative of Ruben Östlund's films. There's a level of catharsis achieved through the cacophony of chaos that you don't find very often, and while some of the stories weren't as compelling as the others, they still held to that riveting notion.

A series of chapters with no end and no beginning. Terrorizers is the shortest of Yang's films I've seen so far, and as such, the storytelling here is notably different. He doesn't have the creative licence that 3 or 4 hours can provide, so he can't flesh out an entire world of characters like in Yi Yi and A Brighter Summer Day . Instead, he leans into the enigmatic nature that this form of filmmaking brings, and creates these characters whose motivations juxtapose one another at every step. The third act of this is total perfection, and while it may have taken a little more for me to get into the first two, Terrorizers still provides this journey that somehow feels both naturalistic and metaphysical.

I'm so conflicted by this. On the one hand, Long Day's Journey Into Night is arguably the most visually impressive film I've ever seen. I know that's quite a claim to make, but it's true. Every frame is utterly stunning. The sparse yet poetic dialogue was also a joy to listen to. On the other hand, I can only say I was actually engaged for about 20 minutes of its 138-minute runtime. For the rest, I have to admit that I was rather bored. It has that Malickian dreaminess to it, but even Malick's films hold your attention with their liberal use of voiceover. Long Day's Journey Into Night is an experience rooted in that which it describes in its title: the journey. On another day, I can see myself rating this lower, but on a different day, I can see myself calling it a masterpiece. For now, I'm somewhere in between.
I've only seen one Gaspar Noé film but this felt very much like a Gaspar Noé film. At least for half of it.

Like Father, Like Son is the second of Kore-eda's works I've seen, and wow, was I impressed. His ability to bring out these nuanced, acutely human emotions in his actors is almost as impactful as the performances themselves. The subtlety with which the film explores relationships between parents and their children, or, as the title suggests, fathers and their sons, is stunning, and I was enamoured with every moment.

Antiporno is loud, brazen, colourful, and unabashedly provocative. Sion Sono takes on the challenge of twisting what first appears to be a soft-core porno into a scathing critique of the adult film industry and, by extension, the culture that protects and even encourages this perspective on women. It's totally self-indulgent in its fourth-wall-breaking nature, but does so in a way that feeds into its over-the-top aesthetic. Within just 76 minutes, Sono manages to push forth a multitude of ideas, from female objectification to the suppression of individuality, all doused in this psychosexual surrealism that is as disorienting as it is engaging. It's easy to get lost in the noise, where I found myself more often than not, but if only for the sheer audacity of what Sono tries to accomplish here, you have to give plaudits.

Days of Being Wild is a story of lost souls- men who are afraid of commitment to a person, a place, an idea. Wong Kar-wai follows these meandering stories in terrific vignettes, sharing many of the same qualities as his later works, although noticeably less refined. It's here that he defines many of his filmmaking techniques that later became trademarks, and while their brilliance does shine in places, they often lose cohesion as a whole within this disjointed story.

Danny Boyle's direction combined with Alex Garland's writing has always proven to be a rather successful collaboration, with 28 Days Later and Sunshine being proof of that. The Beach was the first of their partnerships, and it certainly makes some poignant points about imperialism, even while being a total mess tonally, but it kinda works for me. Though through some further reading, it became apparent that there was controversy surrounding the bulldozing of Ko Phi Phi Le to make it look more like a paradise. I suppose the irony of those actions was lost on those responsible.

"Sometimes, I wish I never came here" Take Out is an intricate portrait of an era, a seamless blend of sociopolitical commentary and deeply personal narrative that is as heart-rending as it is insightful. As with his work in Red Rocket, where he captures the after effects of a post-Trump America, Baker, alongside co-director Shih-Ching Tsou, showcases an uncanny ability to encapsulate an era: this time the post-9/11 society, as experienced by an illegal immigrant toiling in a Chinese takeout. Ming is a man out of place, alienated in America, and painfully distant from his family in China. His day-to-day existence, riddled with debt and discrimination, offers a grim, unvarnished picture of the immigrant experience. He lives in a cage with no true place to call home, all in a sobering reminder of the desperation to pursue just a semblance of the American Dream. One of the remarkable facets of Take Out is its remarkable authenticity. The story is told more through actions, interactions, and settings than verbose dialogue. It feels real because it is real; for the most part, conversations and even the deliveries are carried out exactly as they would in real life, creating a palpable sense of reality for us to be immersed in. Baker and Tsou's tight, intimate camerawork only emphasises this authenticity, while painting a vivid picture of the unforgiving urban landscape, as the echoes of the hustle and bustle of the city reverberate.
Wtf is this cast.

It's interesting being in the unique position to offer a modern perspective on News from Home in a time where you can communicate instantly with someone from any part of the world to another, perhaps even while seeing their face, something that would have been considered impossible at its time of release. We become part of this one-way conversation that Ackerman delightfully narrates against the busy streets of New York City, her words obscured by the commotion of urban noise. It's not only time or distance that dilutes the words on paper, but also one's environment. Much like the news on television, the more we see and hear it, the less meaning it has. People's lives become statistics in a headline. There's only so much that can be communicated through written text, simply because it can never be a full reflection of real life, only the life we want to portray to the reader. Nothing is akin to being there in the moment, and all sorts of feelings of guilt and loneliness can sprout on both sides of the envelope. Our only solace is the hope that these words on paper are enough to sustain a relationship until that fateful day where we finally meet again, deceiving ourselves into believing nothing has changed since we last spoke.
So expertly crafted, and so beautifully heartbreaking.

Much of Flowers of Shanghai left me feeling quite cold, but I suppose that's the point. There's no glamour in these women's occupations, despite how they may appear in their lavish gowns and with handmaidens at their beck and call. They are indoctrinated as children of around 7 or 8 into this lifestyle of monotony, serving as the ironically named 'flower girls' as their innocence is taken away from them by wealthy men that they become bound to. They are trapped with debts they cannot pay, in relationships where infidelity is rife, and hooked on opiates as their only solace from lashings lain upon them by their procuress they call 'auntie' as punishment for underperformance. Hou Hsiao-hsien wonderfully contrasts these gorgeous frames of luxury and class with these themes of entrapment, all romanticised in moments of lust, yet it is never once lewd. Every dimly lit scene from a single lantern casts shadows over its participants, one of truth and one of facade, but it's clear to tell which is which.

Maborosi is Hirokazu Kore-eda's stunning debut, and through liberal usage of wide shots, Kore-eda excels at keeping the emotions at an arms length, and chooses his moments of immersion perfectly. It stands as an atmospheric soliloquy on the ephemeral nature of life, and a testament to those left behind. As it turns out, the empty space that remains takes up more room than you'd think, and it leaves traces that linger, just as potent in their silence as any physical presence ever could be. These traces reverberate in the quiet hallways of our memories, echoing with stories left untold, questions left unanswered. We're left to pick up the pieces of what was; fragments of the past now tinged with melancholia.

It's definitely fun in parts, and the quintessential Quentin dialogue is there too, but it was also probably the most bored I've been watching a Tarantino flick in the moments in between the madness. But man, what a cathartic ending.
Ben Stiller's character is the worst guy ever until he has a line of coke and a Vicodin, so the lesson is... do drugs?
They should've just hopped on a boulder and rode it home like the pioneers used to do.
I wish I could be hypnotised to forget this film.

Really tightly paced indie where the characters actually have some chemistry. Tramps shares a lot of characteristics with the mumblecore sub-genre that I love so much. It's substantial enough to a point that it's convincing and it never overstays its welcome or tries to amp up the stakes when they aren't there.

Honestly think I had way more fun with this one than I did with De Palma's one, which may be controversial. It just has so much campiness and style that feels reminiscent of Bollywood movies, especially with all of the over the top action sequences and frenetic editing.

Probably my least favourite of the 3 so far, but Philip Seymour Hoffman just gives me more and more reasons to think he was just the best ever. What an incredible villain performance that was, and he totally carries this movie.
Might just be the most beautiful film I've ever seen. Then again, I think I say that after every Terrence Malick film I watch.

I'm not American, and yet, growing up, I was surrounded by so much of American culture, from media to music and politics. There was a noticeable difference in the way things within British culture were presented. Even from watching kids television programmes growing up, this difference was apparent. I think it stems from the fact that Americans are told from an early age that they can do anything and that they can be anything. There's even a line in the film where the performer says something like, "One of you kids could be president someday." Stuff like that was always so insane to me because it felt like those people were feeding their youth false promises of stardom and that they should instead be more realistic. It's fine to have dreams, as long as they're within reason, right? Nashville is a microcosm of that dream that lies within the idea of Americana. All these people are from different backgrounds, classes, and statuses, yet they still all believe in the same collective dream. Faith is not based in achievable outcomes. There are no falsities because it's all very real to them. There's no focus on what they can't do, and instead they focus only on their goal. There are no thoughts of what's realistic or not, only this idealised version of themselves that they see in the stars and how they can get there. It's a quality that I both envy and fear. To be able to look at the world and only see opportunity is a remarkable thing, but it's also terrifying. Knowing that the people around you- the ones closest to you- may only be using you as a stepping stone towards that dream is a scary thought. It gets much worse when you realise this mindset extends way beyond that of the working man wanting to escape his monotonous 9-5- it's an ethos that's adopted by all corners of society: from the media, music, politics, and so much more. It's freakishly impressive that Altman was able to capture such a detailed portrait of not only Americana in the 70s, but an image that extends to this very day. One that shows no signs of slowing down either.

Still my favourite of Nolan's work, for now, but that's a lot to do with the fact that I'm just totally fascinated by dreams and the logic behind them. There are glaring issues that become even further prominent on a repeat viewing, but frankly I don't even care, I'm just riding the kick.

Remove Bill Murray and some of the other military subplot and this isn't bad at all. There are some interesting dynamics explored, and the screenwriting isn't nearly as bad as people make it out to be.

It's a rather risky choice to make a film about one of the most influential people in the history of technology and not mention what is largely considered to be his magnum opus of innovation, the iPhone, but Boyle's risk very much pays off here. Instead, Steve Jobs focuses on the man behind the marketing, and the people he strings along on his journey towards legacy. Aaron Sorkin delivers a script possibly sharper than this film's cousin, The Social Network , resulting in moments of performance like a glorious operatic crescendo from Fassbender, Rogen, and Daniels.

"Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity." I don't think I've ever gone back to the cinema to watch a film I had already seen so soon after having seen it the first time until now. Until Oppenheimer . The grand ferocity with which Ludwig Göransson's score elevates each and every element of this film is dumbfounding. The sequence from the test explosion at Los Alamos, to the rally scene, to the meeting with Truman is the very definition of cinematic perfection, and just those 20-30 minutes capture the essence of entire film with such brilliant vision. It's just insane that Truman's comments on Oppenheimer in the film are an almost lessened version of what he said in real life. He very much did call him a "crybaby scientist" as the film depicts (not to his face admittedly) but subsequently when referring to Oppenheimer's comments about the blood on his hands, he said, "Blood on his hands, dammit, he hasn't half as much blood on his hands as I have. You just don't go around bellyaching about it."

I saw the hockey stick coming from the very first moment of the film and it was still cathartic as hell. Also pretty funny that I coincidentally watched this after having seen Cillian Murphy in Oppenheimer twice recently. Just such a strange shift in performances but both still very much enjoyable.
Zemeckis giving me more reasons to think that Back To The Future was a fluke.

I'm so glad I watched this in the cinema when I did because I don't think much could have replicated the mix of adrenaline and euphoria I felt during the ending montage. Seeing it again, I feel like I can double down on the fact that it's definitely a messy ending and many of the characters' storylines aren't resolved in quite the way I would've liked, but regardless, there's not much out there that can make me feel as transported and immersed as Chazelle's work does. The first act will remain one of my favourites ever.

Cameron Crowe's movies are so incredibly kitschy and corny but it just works so well for me. Elizabethtown is pretty messy tonally because I feel like it simultaneously tries too hard to be funny while being absolutely hilarious in moments that feel like Crowe was aiming to be sincere. Nevertheless, between Crowe's trademark indie-pop/rock soundtrack, and Orlando Bloom and Kirsten Dunst's undeniable charm, Elizabethtown proves to be an eagerly fun time.
A 71 year old Michael Mann directs the shit out of this cyber-crime romance espionage thriller with some sublime handheld camerawork and a tightly paced story.

This actually starts off pretty well and I quite enjoyed most of the parts that took place in Florence. However, everything besides that becomes shockingly boring with some technical flaws all over, and simply the lack of tension. It was always going to be a difficult task to follow on from Demme's heralded The Silence of the Lambs , and for the most part Julianne Moore does okay replacing Jodie Foster but it never quite feels the same. Gary Oldman as Mason Verger was a welcome addition though, and his performance excels through the practical effects. Of course, Anthony Hopkins is still spectacular, although seeing much more of him does lessen the impact of his terror, but it's understandable why he wasn't used as sparingly as in this film's predecessor.
Eamon carried.

"I will not be threatened by a walking meat loaf!" "I didn't mean to call you a meat loaf, Jack!" The contrast of some of the best and most terrifyingly grotesque practical effects I've seen with a random hilarious one-liner makes An American Werewolf in London so much fun to watch. The fact that Landis can combine some truly scary sequences with some brilliant dark humour makes this infinitely more entertaining, and it is understandable why this is so beloved.

I'm not sure I understand or will ever understand Miami Vice to its fullest. But I'm not sure I want to either. What Mann has created here is this masterful enigma of mid-noughties zeitgeist, capturing an era of digital decadence from Nokia flip phones to fax machines. It's a time when the majority of crime began to shift into a space that neither criminals nor law enforcement had navigated before: the online world. Through flashes of exposition basking in the nocturnal allure of Miami's skyline, we follow the story, somewhat incongruently, as our protagonists push forth with reassuring confidence. While Blackhat examined the movement into the digital age at a time when the reshaping of the landscape was in full effect, Miami Vice exists in a time just before that- the transitional period where it felt like anything could happen. So our uncertainty with the narrative feels reciprocated through Mann's direction, as he reassures us that it's not something to be understood in its entirety just yet, and so we cruise along for the ride anyway.

film_key: In the Heat of the Night (1967)
review_clean: My first of Sidney Poitier's work and what a powerhouse performance to start with. Can't wait to watch more from him.

In the first 10 minutes of Ali , we see everything about the man we come to know as Muhammad Ali- from a little boy walking to the coloured section of the bus and seeing a newspaper article about the brutalisation of Emmett Till, to one of the most prolific athletes of all time. We see him denounce his so-called 'slave name', Cassius Clay, and go on to preach pacifism through both his religion and conscientious objection. Mann so often explores the lives of extreme professionals in their craft, and so it's interesting here to see how often Ali deviates from a path he sets so clearly for himself. Mann constantly makes the viewer question how a man so devoted and focussed in his belief in both himself and God could be both a pacifist and a boxer, and also loyal to God but not to his wife. For someone so driven by honour, how come he so often falls into hypocrisy? All these questions posed and answered in just 10 minutes of blissful filmmaking. However, it's beyond that where Ali starts to lose steam. Sure, there are parts, particularly the bits that take place in Zaire, that feel like Mann is trying to get at something more profound here, and while Smith's performance is impressive, it never quite reaches the levels required to make a scathing remark on this man of legend. There's so much that remains to be said about this man who essentially wove himself into the fabric of mythos, but by the end, unfortunately, much of it remains unsaid. There are many moments that feel poised to delve into Ali's psyche, but they never end up scratching much deeper than the surface.

Some say that when you die, you see flashes of your life pass before you in a random fashion, as you catch glimpses of the person you were. In many ways, Tarkovsky's Mirror feels like that: like you are cast adrift in a sea of fragmented memories. Through Tarkovsky's lens, past and present become a blurred vision of both his and our experiences. From this disjointed narrative, he holds a mirror to our collective consciousness, as we both look back on not only our lives, but the lives of the people we affected. Mirror is largely known as one of Tarkovsky's most challenging works to understand, and I knew that going into it. But if you try less to understand and more to just feel, it becomes much clearer what Tarkovsky aims to achieve here. And by the time the film fades to black, we feel the catharsis of having looked back at every misstep, every wrongdoing, every success, every opportunity, and every moment of what makes life what it is.

It's an almost insurmountable task- nearly as insurmountable, perhaps, as The Battle of Anthill itself- to definitively declare which of Stanley Kubrick's cinematic masterpieces has left the most indelible mark on culture, both relating to film and not. Paths of Glory is utterly hypnotic, not simply due to its aggressive anti-war sentiments, expert weaving of dark comedy, or Kirk Douglas' commanding performance, but because of how pertinent its themes remain to this day.

Jeff Bridges and Clint Eastwood are an unexpectedly awesome duo in this. My first of Cimino's work, and wow what a strong debut this is. The buddy road trip turned off-kilter heist is done so effectively because there's no need for any personal motive than to just have fun and get rich. It's straightforward but so wonderfully executed at the same time.

Immediately after I watched Ratcatcher , I found myself to be a little conflicted as there were parts of the film I absolutely adored such as the contrast in imagery from the greys and whites of the Glaswegian squalor, to elements and images that felt so elusive and fantastical. But then I felt there were parts that I felt a total disconnect from the rest. It wasn't until I watched two of Lynne Ramsay's interviews, around 20 years apart, that it all clicked for me. She described the film as this sort of "dystopian fairytale". While there are parts that clearly try to emphasise the deprived nature that these people were living in, she makes it clear that it wasn't the intention to confine or label the film as an attempt to capture a portrait of this late 20th century poverty, as it was just what the world was like for her when she grew up. As a kid, you make do with what you have, but you always hold out for that hope of more. It's something that feels like a shared quality with Sean Baker's The Florida Project, especially when James visits the unfinished house and steps through the window into this everlasting wheat field where it feels like time moves in slow-motion (like many of the inspired shots across the film do). Lynne Ramsay, having first started out as a painter then a photographer before venturing into film, so very clearly understands the power of a still image, with prolonged moments without any dialogue conveying so much while saying so little. Small, intimate moments where a character interacts with another, perhaps even without acknowledgment from the other, where nothing needs to be said as you can already feel it. It's a pretty genius move, likely due to financial reasons but nevertheless, to cast both professional and non-professional actors in the roles, as it adds a whole different layer of naturalism that I feel that you wouldn't get otherwise. It feels like these streets, littered with rotting waste and scurrying rats, have actually been lived in because that's exactly true. The dystopia is what allows for the fairytale to exist, as one could not exist without the other.

I read somewhere that making films about death that feel honest and authentic is one of the most difficult things a filmmaker can undertake. After all, how do you direct the absence of something? Hirokazu Kore-eda answers that question through his gentle and warm filmmaking, where it feels like anyone can place themselves into any one scene and watch, like a (butter)fly on a wall, as if a memory was taken from their mind and played out in front of them. There was so much in Still Walking that reminded me of my grandparents, and my parents too for that matter. All the constant bickering about nothing in particular because they were never taught any better way to express that they care for one another. All the care and love that's put into food with these preparation rules-of-thumb that are passed down by the generations before. All these snide comments made behind someones back, or even to their face, that just make you want to crawl up into a ball of shame on their behalf. It's a mix of all these small, seemingly inconsequential details that make Kore-eda's films so incredibly special to me. "They say butterflies that survive the winter come back yellow the following year"

Doesn't quite hold the same emotional depth as some of Lynch's other work like Mulholland Drive or Blue Velvet , but there's something about the balls to the wall approach Lost Highway employs that you really just have to respect. It's so punk-rock beyond just its killer soundtrack, and the sultry audiovisual labyrinth that Lynch loses you in is so bewildering to navigate. While I was impressed by the nightmarish nature of the first act, especially when it came to the sound design, it almost felt like Lynch was trying a bit too hard here, and it ended up feeling like a lesser version of Haneke's Caché. Past that though is where Lost Highway really kicks into second gear, with the looming shadow of horror still ever-present, though now astutely supplemented by Lynch's unconventional humour, which makes the experience all the more compelling. As for performances, Patricia Arquette and Bill Pullman are fantastic, but it's Robert Loggia who steals the show with his over-the-top demeanour and enigmatic motivations.

My first Verhoeven film, and as many so often say, this is most definitely an over-hated gem. The glitz and glamour contrasted with the grime and sleaze of Vegas is portrayed magnificently. The film is visually stunning, and while it does peter out a little towards the end, it's still so well crafted.

There's a level of cultural resonance Kobayashi achieves here that I'm not sure I've ever quite seen before. For a film that's over 60 years old, its scathing remarks on the hypocrisy of political systems are as relevant as ever in the modern day. Couple that with Kobayashi's meticulous eye for composition, which makes every frame of this film, seeped in the viscera of retributive blood or not, pure artistry to behold. Harakiri is not simply a film that stands the tests of time; it's one that grows and evolves along with it.

Before it was revealed that it was the exact concept for the film, I had randomly thought during the start of Slacker that it would be a cool concept for a film to continually follow on from one of the characters in the scene, constantly moving and changing perspectives, and that's exactly what Slacker was. Although in execution rather than theory, this is a much more difficult thing to pull off (especially since my first thought was to stitch the whole thing together to look like it was shot in one take), and I often found myself uninterested in some of the conversations while captivated by another. I suppose that's both the benefit and drawback of having such short interactions with these characters. It's about as slice-of-life as slice-of-life gets- thinly sliced at that, which makes it all the more impressive with how much depth Linklater manages to instil in some of these characters in such a short time. Parts reminded me of those random drunk conversations you'd have during the come-down from a party, just rambling on about existence and our place in the universe, all those words lost to the haze of time and drunken memories.

It's easy to take for granted just how brilliant The Apartment is. It's simple, but it's written so impeccably and the dialogue is so clever that it makes it all worthwhile. I think many people will and have called this overrated (I hate using that word), and I felt that myself a little in the middle, but you then realise by the end just how much Wilder gets right here. It's small-scale and there's not a singular, monumental, iconic shot that's been lauded a classic, but over the whole film, there's not one moment where I thought, "That could have been done better," or "The writing was a little messy there," or "That wasn't edited very well." Just really, really solid direction and execution throughout.

There's so much I absolutely adore about Haneke's style of filmmaking, both here and across his whole filmography. I don't think I'd be preemptive in saying that he's one of my favourite directors. Taking that into account, it pains me not to have rated this higher. There are real shades of masterwork all over Code Unknown; from the way it looks at the immigrant experience alone, you can see the deep empathy Haneke exudes through the camera, a much different disposition than his other films which seem to have the exact opposite quality. Yet he still manages to expertly contrast that with his precise, almost documentarian style filmmaking. Unfortunately, beneath all these brilliant ideas and techniques lies a pretty disjointed narrative, one that makes it difficult to truly grasp all of the emotion that Haneke is vying to portray. Its anthological structure works in parts, but I almost wish that it had dissipated as the film went on, highlighting how wildly different these strangers lives and struggles are, but by the end, noting that perhaps their struggles aren't so different after all.

Sometimes a feeling can be so overwhelmingly powerful that we think the only remedy has to be to invoke the exact opposite- to feel nothing at all. It's not until we set out on this hapless quest do we realise that it's impossible. Even when it feels like we're drowning in a boundless sea of blue, our bodies force themselves to the surface in a desperate attempt to cling to life, when it seems like there's nothing left to live for.

"Some years from now, when I have forgotten you and other romances like this one have recurred through sheer habit, I will remember you as a symbol of love's forgetfulness. This affair will remind me how horrible forgetting is."

There are many gripes to be had over The Last Emperor, my first of which is why this wasn't just in Chinese, particularly due to some of their weird dubbing at the start. However, many of the rest of these gripes are simply offset by the utter grandeur of its design. The set design is immaculate, but what's even more impressive is that so much of this was shot on location. The feeling of historical importance is something that really comes across here, especially when Bertolucci makes sure to measure the scale up to that of an epic; however, its lack of resonance with its characters is something that does fall short of the mark. There's too much focus on these insignificant character moments, especially in the tiresome first act. As such, it's difficult to empathise with the gravity of things going on, which, for a historical epic where the weight of decisions and choices are amped up to the max as we follow characters through what is essentially their entire lives, seems like such a simple misstep. When you look to something like Schrader's Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters , characterisation still takes a backseat to the audiovisual experience, which is second-to-none, and yet we still see so much of what makes and drives this politicised figure. In much the same way, the gorgeous visuals and triumphant score provide a backbone for The Last Emperor, but it suffers from the lack of support that the little moments of emotion can bring amidst all the drama. I suppose it's somewhat ironic of me that I wish Bertolucci spent less time on insignificant moments and more on moments that seemed insignificant.
Feels a bit like Paris, Texas 's depraved cousin.

film_key: Bad Times at the El Royale (2018)
review_clean: I feel like Bad Times at the El Royale is about a draft of the script and some editing down to make it more tightly paced away from being absolutely awesome. The performances are largely fine, although I just can't escape from the fact that it just feels like Drew Goddard thinks he's doing more than he really is.
Expected this to be a bit like Total Recall and it pretty much was. Awesome practical effects to be expected from a Cronenberg film, but also a fun campiness and a bunch of meta elements too.

The last act of this is so fun and wacky, I just wish the rest had been the same. For something that's only 97 minutes, it's not nearly as tightly paced as you'd think, which hinders it slightly, and it could have done with a bit more world building too. The soundtrack was pretty great though, although I wish there was more of it.

You often see these stories about convicts who were falsely imprisoned for crimes they didn't commit, with the bulk of their lives being stolen away for something that wasn't even their fault. It's an inherently broken system of justice, not too dissimilar to the laws dictated within religion. There's a link between this idea and the way Mungiu presents religion in Beyond the Hills . It's something that is bestowed upon someone simply by chance, and in some cases, it can restrict the person's ability to live and act freely as they wish. Within this microcosmic commune, Mungiu deals with this oppressive evangelist approach to religion, but does so in such a way that doesn't feel overly accusatory. It's easy to forget that this is based on a true story at times, because each scene seems so meticulously crafted in such a way as to make this viewpoint come across. It's utterly terrifying just how bleak this is, especially when a place so committed and devout to following their dogmatic teachings of love and compassion is totally blind to the fact that they're doing the exact opposite. It's a very scary thing to see that the institution that is supposed to epitomise the moral standard deviates from it so often, a trait that isn't limited to religion alone. As depressingly sobering as this film can be, it also finds its share of satire amidst its cold backdrop. And I suppose there is humour to be found in my aggressively anti-religious takeaways from this film, even though it really isn't leaning that far towards either side of that spectrum. Circling back to my initial analogy, perhaps Mungiu's perspective here is more akin to criticising the system than the individual, and yet, there's no justice for those who choose not to subscribe to these beliefs.
I think a lot of movies would be better if they had a talking dog voiced by John Turturro.

I couldn't decide whether this was awesome or the dumbest thing I had ever seen during a moment when I had to actively stop myself from unconsciously finding plot holes in this film. However, around the point of the third, I realised that the criticism that Déjà Vu faces is probably the epitome of the 'CinemaSins-ification' of movie watching, and that's frankly the most boring and, for lack of a better word, pretentious way of experiencing a film. That's not to say that Tony Scott's 2006 sci-fi thriller is free from issues besides that; in fact, it's rife with stylisation choices that felt over the top for something that was already so over the top, and it's paced in such a way that it makes the film feel much longer than it is. I've sort of lumped a lot of these similar films in Denzel's catalogue into one heap in my brain, but I thought it was about time that I actually watched one of them and decided for myself whether they're worth the merit they receive, often as so-called 'underrated gems' from the mainstream audience. For now, I'm on the fence.

review_clean: I can imagine your enjoyment of this is directly proportional to the amount of film references that you can understand. Fortunately for me, I got about 75% of them. Need to watch Fitzcarraldo though.

There's a lot I want to say about this film, but I think I'll save it for when I eventually rewatch it or I watch another film in Hamaguchi's filmography that reminds me of this. It sort of showed me that I still have some maturing to do as a film watcher in order to fully grasp why filmmakers decide to depict fundamentally flawed characters in a way such as this. It takes a level of emotional intelligence to move past resentment towards a character so that you can fully understand their motivations, but I don't think I'm quite there yet. Could quite easily be a formative five-star rewatch for me in time.
Connor Roy was interested in exploding buses at a very young age.

It's an unfortunately common thing for people, particularly men from an older generation, to lie and withhold from those closest to them as a means to uphold reputation and save face. As if the way you come across is more important than how you actually are. It's a pretty substantial factor in why men find it so difficult to open up about their emotions, because it then detracts from this idealised version of themselves they were told to protect since they were a boy. It's something that I've tried to work on myself, especially when growing up in an Asian household, it's not something that's typically talked about. But ultimately, feeding this taboo and harbouring feelings not only damages your own mental health, but alters the way those around you perceive their own relationships. By striving to protect this idea of civility and strength, you end up enforcing the opposite. What Ozu does here with masterful static imagery is allow us to see how each moment of empty conversation, which masks any possible intention of care, can be like a dagger to the heart. While living with the truth can sometimes be just as hard as living without it, it's unfair to just assume that ignorance is bliss, because it can stop us from ever truly knowing ourselves, forcing us to be even lonelier than we already were.

Maybe I missed the boat on Rosemary's Baby , but while the performances from Mia Farrow and John Cassavetes do impress, the story is just a little weak. I just didn't feel the tension or at any point believe that Rosemary was insane for what she was thinking. I mean she essentially gets raped by her husband and I'm supposed to believe this is just some stand-up guy? It's like Polanski succeeded in gaslighting Rosemary but not the audience. Then once again by the end, there's no ambiguity or mystery that actually makes it feel all that scary, everything just gets told to you. Perhaps I'll revisit this in time, but I just don't see the makings of a horror classic besides the nightmare sequences maybe.

Alexander Payne, Cameron Crowe and Jason Reitman all make these different movies in the same font and I love them all. It's also pretty cool that this is the movie that Jim Rash (alongside Faxon and Payne) won the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay for. I really like George Clooney in these little family dramas, I wish he was in more of them because he actually has some acting chops but hardly ever showed them off.

Watched this mainly for Lily Gladstone as I'm finally going to see Killers of the Flower Moon on Saturday, and I'm glad to say her segment was probably my favourite. I always have a hard time emotionally connecting to anthology films, as while they can share thematic elements across the stories, they often feel too disconnected for me to fully invest myself in the narrative, and unfortunately that applies here. While I do adore the quaint 16mm cinematography, Certain Women just doesn't add too much more to the stories themselves where it feels like the film is doing more than just telling. The best kinds of quiet storytelling in film fill in the gaps between the sparse dialogue with this almost personification of the landscape; the location itself needs to feel like a character where you can funnel that emotion through, something that's particularly pertinent in Lee Chang Dong's Secret Sunshine , but that just doesn't quite come through here. It's not necessary for anthology films to have some kind of bow to wrap the whole story together with, but Certain Women could have certainly benefited from a slight bit more cohesion to justify just what Reichardt is trying to say here.

End of Watch is a buddy cop action/drama filled to the brim with melodrama and enough copaganda to keep your average "blue lives matter" folks entertained. It's all filmed pretty horribly with David Ayer making the decision to capture most of it handheld, a choice which the main character justifies by saying he's doing a filmmaking course while also being a cop which may be one of the dumbest narrative decisions I've seen. The performances are largely fine, if not hindered by the aforementioned melodrama used to spruce up an otherwise half-baked script, but I enjoyed the chemistry between Gyllenhaal and Peña. I'm starting to think I just really don't get on with David Ayer's work or at least his narrative choices because it feels like he made this film with all the wrong intentions in mind as to what its message is supposed to be. There's no empathy for the victims, and ethnic minorities are all painted with the same brush. It's frankly borderline manipulative, especially nearing the end. If there was more of a criticism regarding these cops lack of care for some of these vulnerable people, attributing it to some sort of larger systemic issue of power as Fuqua touches on in Training Day as this seems to want to emulate, then I'd feel much more sympathetic to its lacklustre direction, but I suppose those things would go hand-in-hand.
It's largely fine, some of the scares are pretty inventive but the grief-stricken widow horror movie trope is starting to get really boring for me.

I would be lying if I said I wasn't curious about Lars von Trier as a filmmaker. His ideology, beyond just that of his patented Dogme 95 filmmaking, always seems to burst the seams of his films, for better or worse. As much as it can get tiring, I really do think his style works best when coupled with his periodically scintillating dark humour, but in the case of Breaking the Waves , that is nowhere to been seen. It's a deeply mean film, and I don't mean that in the way that means all it's characters are evil, but it does feel like we, alongside them, are punished for trying to find joy amidst the despondent atmosphere. The film tries to examine the cost of being selfless in love, be that towards one's partner or to their religion. To give oneself so wholeheartedly to others and for that naïveté to be punished or taken advantage of. It's intensely cynical, and that comes across in the filmmaking too, and while Emily Watson does give a stellar performance, it's held back by the fact that's she's never able to feel true happiness.
The cockatoo scared the shit out of me I can't lie.
Starting Noirvember off with a pretty good one. Let's hope I don't forget about doing this after a week.

Not a massive fan of the amount of narration used in this, but I suppose that's to be expected for a film that's only 68 minutes long. I've also started to notice a lot of these noirs end pretty abruptly, which is something that might take some getting used to. Other than that, I quite enjoyed this, particularly the second half.

Absolutely adore how completely off the rails this went. Duo of Emma Seligman and Rachel Sennott remains undefeated, even though I do largely prefer Shiva Baby , but adding Ayo Edebiri to the mix is only gonna make things better.

No idea what Welles is doing with his accent here, but other than that The Lady from Shanghai is pretty spectacular. I mean, what a thrilling conclusion that was. Stellar camerawork and phenomenal visuals.
