The plot is kind of convoluted and hard to follow, but that's part of what made this so enjoyable to watch, especially when you factor in the decision to end it in a fun house- that's such a clever choice. I know I've not seen many, but this may be my new favourite noir.

film_key: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull (2008)
review_clean: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull feels like Spielberg's stab at an Alien movie, and oftentimes this movie can feel more like a movie from that series than this one. Hell, he even casts John Hurt if the comparisons didn't draw themselves already. As such, it loses much of that adventurer charm that the earlier movies had, and while I actually did rather enjoy the first act of this (yes, even the nuclear blast fridge), as soon as Shia LaBoeuf's character gets introduced, I lost most of my interest. He just has nothing to do the entire film, and simply serves as a constant reminder of this attempt at a successor to Indy that we know from the Dial of Destiny releasing never came to fruition.

Refreshingly modern, but ultimately rather uninteresting as the plot seems to dwindle in circles too much. Panic in the Streets mostly doesn't feel like the conventional film noirs I've been watching, which was a welcome surprise, but left it feeling a little too empty. I think I'll probably enjoy the rest of Kazan's work more.
Brenda Blethyn's performance in this is probably now one of my favourites ever, as is Timothy Spall's. What an emotionally gut-wrenching film.
It'll be interesting to see if I prefer this version or Hitchcock's more. Some really cool shots, but some rather lacklustre performances.
A little too slow for me, but still really enjoyed this, especially those last 10 minutes.
Arguably the greatest credits song of all time.

For a while now, I've held an interest in the American neorealist sub-genre as a sort of precursor to the more modern mumblecore cinema. It provides a station for which filmmakers such as Jarmusch can express the mundanities of everyday life in a way that feels like a reflection of the viewers' feelings when watching it. In Stranger Than Paradise , we feel like a fish out of water in the same way that this Hungarian émigrée does, as between each fading transition between the one-take scenes, we're equally thrown into a new environment, forced to confront the unknown surroundings. It's not a film that particularly aims to highlight the indigent nature of its protagonists, as Jarmusch recognises that that is just part and parcel of life, and instead it focuses on the the ennui of this coming of age story which so often perforates the film's surface in much the same way as Sean Baker and Shih-Ching Tsou's Take Out . It's monotonous and filled with things left unsaid, just like real life, and I suppose that's the reason I find myself gravitating towards this style of films so much because instead of acting as a form of escapism, it serves as more of a reminder that life can often follow a predictable path, where things can seem to feel and look all the same, and while breaking apart from that cycle is difficult, it's also necessary if you actually want to live.

film_key: The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant (1972)
review_clean: "You're with someone in a car or in a room and you want to say something, but you're afraid. Or you'd like to be affectionate but again you're afraid. You're afraid of losing points, of being the weaker one. It's a terrible moment when you can no longer go back and start again."

Sicario: Day of the Soldado was realistically never going to reach the heights of the first after losing both Deakins and Villeneuve- two vital components of what made the first film so great. It's much more on the nose than the first, likely due to Sheridan- one of the few things that was retained from Sicario - wanting to make a substantial enough deviation from the predecessor so that this has its own distinct feel. While it does house some rather exhilarating set pieces, they never seem to accomplish the same impact as before. It's more rigid politically in comparison to the morally grey area that the first film spends much time around, which works in a way that it does feel assured of itself, but the film ends before it can ever reach a real conclusion to these themes. Benicio Del Toro and Josh Brolin remain a powerful duo, but losing the dynamic of the inexperienced rookie in Emily Blunt and lazily trying to recapture that with a one-sided mismatch in Isabel Merced offers little to nothing. It very much feels like the El Camino to Sicario 's Breaking Bad- a subpar and unnecessary epilogue that leaves you with more questions than answers.
That Miles Davis trumpet score was majestic.

Many of the films that were released approaching the turn of the new millennium share this same nihilism about the future that Hype Williams' Belly has. It's like this time capsule of 90s hip-hop culture, with every neon-dipped, low-angled shot reminiscent of all the iconic music videos from Biggie to Missy Elliott that Williams had a hand in, so assuredly capturing the vérité of that hood lifestyle. While you can feel its $3 million budget slowly dwindle away as the film progresses, using the bulk of it to shoot what is probably one of the best opening sequences ever put to film was sincerely no mistake.

"The shooting of On the Silver Globe was halted in the spring of 1977. All the sets and costumes needed to complete the production, which began two years previously, were ready and waiting in Wrocław, Lower Silesia, the Masurian Lakes, and the Caucasus Mountains. All of these sets, costumes and props were destroyed. For many years, the film technicians, wardrobe-dressers and set-builders, stashed whatever they could, in studio recesses and their own homes. I am thinking about them as I finish this film, believing that the small drama of this film and the larger and more noble drama of our lives will continue to interweave into a web of triumphs and failures. My name is Andrzej Żuławski, I directed On the Silver Globe" Only 80% of On the Silver Globe exists today. The rest was either destroyed or never able to be filmed as the Polish government deemed it to be critical of Poland's communist regime. Eventually, shortly prior to the democratisation of Poland, On the Silver Globe was released as a sort of cut down version of what it was originally meant to be, with Żuławski himself narrating of pieces of the lost narrative. In some way, this turbulent backstory only serves to highlight the importance of freedom, a fundamental principle of which Żuławski explores so much in this film. It's this context, this missing 20%, which led to this philosophical odyssey being heralded as one of the greatest sci-fi epics ever put to screen. There exists a certain arrogance in the personification of divine concepts. Mother Nature and Father Time. Is it familiarity we seek, or is it simply putting a face to what we are instinctively led to kill and subsequently worship? As Nietzsche so famously said, "God is dead." If God was a mortal man who lived and died among us, what does that mean for our ideology? Even if we hold no knowledge of the past, is history still doomed to repeat itself? Through all this war, rising from the ashes of a broken society, religion is formed purely out of necessity, not desire; a body to lend our countless unknowings to. But is it truly freedom if it's born out of fear, or is it simply an instinct- an innate craving to just survive.

Watching this again almost ten years on and only now noticing that this is probably Fincher's funniest film. I mean, just the face on Ben Affleck when he says "I know this one!" is hilarious. Also Laray Mayfield needs a raise for some of the best casting ever (and this extends to The Social Network too) because Rosamund Pike, Ben Affleck, and Neil Patrick Harris are such genius decisions for these roles and are 90% of what makes this film so good.

Into the Wild works best when it's simply just a road-trip travel movie about appreciating the small things in life we take for granted, and I definitely have a soft spot for films that make me just want to ditch everything and travel the world. But when Penn delves into this pseudo-intellectualist pastiche of Malick and shoehorns in a ton of religious imagery and symbolism, the film becomes unbelievably grating. There's definitely a good film in here somewhere, mostly in the interactions with the side characters, but you'd need to shave around a lot of that mess for it to begin to rear its head.

Coming off the back of watching True Detective season one, which many consider to be Fukunaga's opus, to watching this feels like a refreshing deviation from what was expected. That's not to say that both projects don't share the same liberal usage of wide shots over a vast field that Fukunaga loves so much, but it's nice to see where he was at before that point. Period dramas can often become overly melodramatic and bland with their antiquated speech and unvarying shot compositions. However, Moira Buffini's script makes the dialogue feel real instead of like a theatre piece, much of those complements carrying over to Mia Wasikowska and Michael Fassbender's performances as well, the former of which I wish was in more starring roles, and Fukunaga's camerawork remains interesting throughout, capturing some gorgeous naturalistic visuals on 35mm.

Absolutely insane to me the level of cinematic maturity and emotional depth of characters in Yang's early work. He really was one of the greatest to ever do it. I have so many thoughts, but I think I'll leave them in my mind as just thoughts, and instead simply reiterate how much I loved this.

"Would you like to know more?" When your satire becomes better than the things you're satirising, you get... well Paul Verhoeven I guess. Starship Troopers is a deceptively scornful critique of American chauvinism and the obsessive hyper-focus on the military as a form of entertainment, with that advertisement even reaching kids, and the mindless violence that spreads as a result. We aren't told how this war with the arachnids starts, except in a passing comment that states the humans invaded their land, but they're presented as gross, stupid creatures to make it easier to stomach the consequences of obliterating their homeland. Verhoeven ingeniously splices in news footage as a representation of propaganda, and even begins what you expect to be a sci-fi action B movie as a high-school flick, with a predominantly white cohort in spite of it being set in Buenos Aires for no apparent reason until you think for a few more seconds. It's so hilariously brilliant how much of this probably would have totally flown over the heads of the people watching this at release.

"But darling, not everyone can create something lasting." It can be a hard concept to grasp that all things must come to an end. Buildings erected centuries ago eventually collapse. Words in a novel fade away. Love between partners ultimately concludes. Through Antonioni's masterful direction, we see the disjointed nature of this couple over a period of a single day, with shadows, reflections, and silhouettes acting as a means of expression for the characters, as they are unable to express themselves. There's a universality to be felt in the message Antonioni aims to convey here; that we must embrace the impermanence of our existence, else feelings will remain unheard, and connections will remain unfulfilled.

Definitely feels like Spielberg-lite, which isn't too surprising seeing as he produced this. Though Super 8 has all the ingredients it needs to be a compelling sci-fi story, it never quite sticks the landing. Some of the characters just feel like they exist only to fulfil certain plot points, and the main group of kids don't have enough of an interesting dynamic together. Still, it's impressive that J.J. Abrams managed to essentially revitalise the appeal for this 80s nostalgia sub-genre, as seen by the massive audience for the subsequent release of Stranger Things .
Will Arnett's Batman carries this movie. I think I'll enjoy The Lego Batman Movie more.

Hardly the worst film of all time as touted by thousands upon thousands of reviewers since the release of The Happening in 2008. Watching this post pandemic, there's definitely this eerie sensibility of barren streets and mass hysteria that Shyamalan manages to get bang on, as well as the feeling of self-preservation in the face of adversity. Sure the dialogue is often horrendous and the acting isn't the best either, but hardly anyone would be able to capture the sense of unease that The Happening has. It manages to push through an environmentalist message, as well as highlight the idiocy of certain media outlets to speculate and downplay the worries of experts. It's a scenario that's frighteningly evocative of recent times. Had this been campier and most of the script been reworked, I don't think as many people would be as taken aback by a minority calling this a masterpiece.
Some of the best production design I've ever seen. Also, Grace Kelly is hot.

I just love a good period piece, and with seasoned Danish director Thomas Vinterberg venturing into his first English language film, photographing the British countryside with such poise and beauty, it'd be a hard task for me to not love Far From The Madding Crowd . Carey Mulligan is stellar as per usual, but as are the supporting cast too, with every pained glance of repressed love communicating so much emotion with so little.

Justine Triet's Palme d'Or winning Anatomy of a Fall is another courtroom drama in a year that is seemingly dominated by the sub-genre in some kind of mini resurgence. Although, unlike its peers, it seems less interested in the result of the case, and more concerned with deconstructing the judicial system, and by extension the media coverage that spans as a result, in how it can misconstrue and depict snippets of our lives as if they were some whole, realised truth. It highlights the danger of conflating opinions with facts, and how the distortion of the truth impacts the relationship between a mother and her son. It's a deceptively straightforward narrative as it asks us to examine the means by which we pick apart people's lives, be that in a courtroom or behind a television screen, rather than any particular outcome. Our feelings as a viewer of whether we think it's a murder or a suicide or merely an undramatic accident specifically tie into every piece of information we learn about this failing marriage; it is as much a dissection of the mystery behind a death than it is of a couple who feel equally as trapped in their relationship as one another, albeit in vastly different ways. We gravitate to either potential verdict, and therefore with the son's painful position, along with either side of this marital battle. Anatomy of a Fall is a film that lends itself to rewatches not only to see which way the evidence turns you, because Triet argues that the outcome is rather inconsequential in the face of the damage that the process brings, but to see how exactly our lives can come across when diminished to the objectivity of facts, and whether it's fair to judge an entire person and their relationships by this depersonalised version of themselves.

Equals bolsters some interesting yet limited production design, but unfortunately that's where the interesting parts of the film end. It never quite feels like its own film with its own message. It's neither gripping enough to be a thriller, nor funny enough to be a decent satire, and you feel like it really needs to commit to either of these directions for it to be successful. Stewart and Hoult do largely well with what they're given to work with (which is precisely zero at the start so you have to commend them for that I suppose). Other than that Equals remains true to its premise in that its painfully dull, with Dustin O'Halloran's shallow piano score playing seemingly incessantly over a compilation of what ends up feeling like stock footage of the leading duo's appendages grazing longingly past one another.

Usually a fan of Danny Boyle's visual flair, but it really doesn't work for me here, particularly the editing and weird stylistic choices. It just feels like it's trying way too hard to not be boring that it actually gets irritating at some point. Other than a surprisingly good performance from Franco and a few moments of impressive sound design, there really isn't enough here to keep me engaged, and 127 Hours would have probably been best suited as a documentary instead.

This probably could have been a pretty good understated drama if it didn't try to bash you over the head with its performances and dialogue constantly. Sometimes less is more, and in the case of Brothers , a lot less was required, even though it just sort of ends without anything to say. Weirdly enough, I think the child actors Bailee Madison and Taylor Geare probably gave the best performances in the film because they're the least in your face.

Some weirdly good production design which makes me think that Mike Judge could have possibly made a half-decent sci-fi flick had this not been bogged down by some of the worst comedy I've ever had the displeasure of watching. I literally only exhaled out of my nostrils once and that was from a throwaway line that said, "Welcome to Costco. I love you.". Awful, awful stuff.

film_key: Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret. (2023)
review_clean: Why hasn't there been more of a push for a Rachel McAdams Best Supporting Actress campaign? But really, why aren't people talking about this more, because it's seriously one of the best films of the year. It's so sweet and honest and terrifically performed all around- Abby Ryder Forston's comedic timing is seriously on point, and you can trace that all the way back to her being 7 years old in Ant Man .
Now I can finally understand all the references.
This really isn't very great, but I have a soft spot for music films and also Elle Fanning can do no wrong in my eyes.

Thereby concludes my film watching for 2023, and my binge of most of Elle Fanning's filmography which I'm sure will carry over into next year. Admittedly, I really haven't seen enough of Francis Ford Coppola's stuff and I desperately need to see more, and whilst much of the acting and line deliveries in Twixt can seem like a bad dub, I can't bring myself to hate this like many do. First and foremost, some of the digital cinematography here is wonderful, especially in those dream sequences. It's clearly made on a lower budget, but talk about making the most of what you've got because this looks great. Secondly, the story behind this is heartbreaking too, with the death of the daughter in the film being a pretty much exact recreation of what happened to Coppola's own son. I recently learnt that it was Ryan O'Neal's son that was driving the boat which led to Gian-Carlo Coppola's death, and with the former also sadly passing away this year, it all just feels like a culmination of all these solemn moments put to film. Above all else, Twixt is an exploration into losing one's faith in the face of tragedy, and as Coppola so delicately described in his heartwarming memoir about O'Neal's passing, "Our families are united in tragedy, which is another expression of love."
Everyone kinda annoyed me besides Troy and Janet.

Undoubtedly filled with a metric ton of melodrama, but still wildly surprising in just how much of Tetris is true. It's filmed pretty blandly, as most of the made-for-streaming films usually are, and could have probably done with being about 15 minutes shorter as there's definite issues with its pacing. While it doesn't rise to the top of the pool amongst the masses of corporate biopics that were released in 2023, Tetris isn't devoid of any personality whatsoever, but you'd think a film about one of the most popular video games of all time would be just a little bit more fun.

How Mann delivers two certifiable masterpieces, both starring Al Pacino, within four years of one another is beyond comprehension. The Insider is for all intents and purposes the pinnacle of investigative journalism in film, with Mann's trademark command over a city skyline now shining the shared quote-unquote spotlight on the blatant felonies committed by Big Tobacco as well as the passive complicity of the media organisations investigating them alike. It questions whether voicing the truth to the masses is a moral responsibility and the scale by which doing nothing actually becomes selfish. Crowe gives what is probably my favourite performance of his career (bar maybe The Nice Guys, but that's a different conversation) not only because it's so understated, but because of the decision to sideline his character for the majority of the third act; at this point we as the viewer assume the role of a member of the American public, hearing only the interview once it goes live, but then moving onto news of the Unabomber within just a few days. "Fame has a fifteen minute half-life, infamy lasts a little longer."

"You remain dead for all eternity, but you're alive only for a brief moment." Lilya 4-Ever reminded me in part of Lynne Ramsay's Ratcatcher except it's bleaker in just about every conceivable way. It's a depiction of poverty in a place where dreams remain as dreams, and any hopes for a better future are shattered by the painful truth of reality. Oksana Akinshina makes this film all the more harrowing to experience because her naivety gives us some semblance of hope that things might just end up the way she thinks they will, even though deep down we, and Volodya for that matter, know better. It feels terrifyingly documentarian because it's a story that's sadly not that original, and the cycles which fuel abandonment and abuse continue to turn to this day.

It's like Oldroyd saw Carol and was like 'I reckon I can do something like that' and then just gives us this absolute nothingburger of a film in Eileen . It feels like it has the ingredients to be compelling, with some strange yet intriguing cross between film noir and Stephen King, but the film never pushes any boundaries or feels at all transgressive. It feels like two halves of two films that were pushed together, and both sides of the story feel incomplete and ultimately anticlimactic.

There's something about the act of observing that holds a special kind of escapism to it. It can be invasive and dangerous sometimes, sure, but seeing something play out while you have no control over the outcome is oddly cathartic. There's no need to struggle to grasp control if it isn't possible for you to have any. I suppose that's why film, and more specifically, movie theatres, are such popular places for finding solace because they're a common ground for people who are trying to relinquish control. They don't communicate with each other in the same way that silent stars of a bygone era don't either; they simply exist in the same dying-scape. What is it about a camera that lingers far too long on an empty space that feels poignant? While our actions in and of themselves may be mundane, there's still importance to the permanence of what we leave behind. It makes certain that even the smallest of our choices hold weight, so that any feeling, including the seemingly endless malaise, isn't unjustified. Tsai Ming-liang creates an almost epitomised version of slow cinema in Goodbye, Dragon Inn, with the film serving as a reflection towards that style, and an homage to the heyday of moviegoing.
Wasn't sure about this until that naked grape-stomping party happened and then I was all in.
Has no right to look this good for 1931.
Visually stellar like most of GDT's work, and I loved the Gothicism even though it feels like he could have used the location a bit more to tell the story.

film_key: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001)
review_clean: It's always an intimidating task to enter the vast world of a fantasy franchise, especially one as revered as this. For such a long time, The Lord of the Rings trilogy has been a major blindspot in my film-watching journey. There's a point in childhood for people born around the same time as me where you either ch ose The Lord of the Rings path or the Harry Potter one, and I chose the latter. It's pretty striking how many similarities there are between each of those stories, though, but with Tolkien's epic releasing some 43 years prior, it's clear to see which inspired which. It feels strange to liken The Fellowship of the Ring to a Werner Herzog film, but much of this did remind me of Aguirre, the Wrath of God . The reason so much of this works for me is that you can feel the environment all these characters are voyaging through because of the on-location filming. Sure, there's green screen work here and there, and some of it has aged poorly, whereas other parts have aged pretty damn well, but it never feels too much to the point where you no longer care about the characters because the stakes don't feel real. As I said before, it's been a long time coming for me to watch these films, and I'm excited to get onto the next.

Can't say I know a ton about F1, but you'd be hard pressed to find someone with even as minimal knowledge as me that hadn't at least heard of the name Niki Lauda. Not usually a massive fan of Ron Howard's work but this was surprisingly good. The opposing motivations of Lauda and Hunt make for the perfect driving force to carry the film forward with. With Michael Mann's Ferrari currently in cinemas which I'm itching to watch, it's pretty interesting to see the flip-side of what I assume that story will explore here.
I think I've had dreams that were better directed than this.

Really don't think the plot-twist is as mind blowing as people made it out to be, but maybe I would have been more surprised had I not known there was a plot-twist at all. Either way, Nicole Kidman is pretty great here, as are each of the child actors.

My first Almodóvar and I loved it- the one thing I went into this expecting was a flourish of colour and I was not disappointed. I thought it made sense to start with the film that I had missed around the 2022 awards season, but there's no doubt I'll be revisiting this once I get through the rest of his films. Penélope Cruz is outstanding here, and I'm surprised she didn't get more buzz around that time either even though she was nominated. Parallel Mothers reminded me a bit of Mike Leigh's Secrets & Lies , not only with its fairly low budget, but with its heart-wrenching story of reconnection. Almodóvar weaves the troubled history of Spain into this thematic core which works ever so well. Can't wait to explore more of his filmography.
Might have to go on a hallmark movie binge or just a Nick Cage one this year because this slapped.

I really loved the first hour of this, but after that point, it seems like A Star is Born simply gets muddled up in its own messaging. Lady Gaga's character's whole aim was to make it on her own in the music business, but why does it feel at every juncture that she only exists for the connection to her husband? And why is it that her venture into a more mainstream pop genre is frowned upon, and she's shown to be only truly happy and fulfilled when she's singing country music? I really don't know what Cooper is trying to say here with that, and I wonder how much the other (3?) versions of this film will compare to this narrative. Nevertheless, the music is pretty terrific here (Shallow in particular) and Bradley Cooper absolutely kills it. It's no wonder he's campaigning so hard for Maestro because he was totally robbed by Rami Malek winning Best Actor in 2019 for the clusterfuck that was Bohemian Rhapsody. I'm less convinced about Lady Gaga, although considering this was still early on in her acting career, and the fact that she's not really as fleshed out as she could have been, I'll give her the benefit of the doubt at least until I've seen House of Gucci and Joker: Folie à Deux later this year.

There's something about cheesy 90s sci-fi that I just love and this is no exception. In a parallel universe, Ethan Hawke is in The Talented Mr. Ripley with Jude Law instead of Matt Damon, and I do wonder what that world would look like.

The kind of film that leaves you by the end wondering, "So what was the point?" As many have pointed out, this is essentially The Social Network but with more burgers, and a heck of a lot less gumption than the Fincher/Sorkin pair provides. It also utterly wastes Laura Dern, which is a sin in and of itself.

"Make no mistake. All of us are racers. We all are certain it will never happen to me. Then my friend is killed. I give up racing forever on Monday. I'm back racing by Sunday. We all know it's our deadly passion. Our terrible joy." There's no question Michael Mann excels when telling a story about a professional in his craft. But Ferrari is a film less concerned about the inner workings of a V12 engine and more about the dynamics of a broken family. When you're racing through life at a blistering speed, the view from the mirror can be a blur, and it's only when the dust settles that everything catches up to you at once. Yet, in spite of all the commotion and noise, you go straight back to work because you know it's the only thing that reignites the fire that you once so readily had burning in your chest.
These French mfs are horny as hell.

Much like how Coppola begins The Godfather with a party, more specifically a wedding, Cimino does the same with The Deer Hunter . These celebrations of life and new beginnings help to emphasise the loss felt when that life is later taken away and when those beginnings are cut short. Walken and De Niro are phenomenal here, and while, of course, there are questions to be had over historical accuracy, I think in some cases, as long as the changes aren't egregious, it doesn't really matter that much. The first hour certainly takes its time, but everything after is just terrific.

Haven't stopped thinking about this since I first saw it. Assuredly one of the very best films of the 21st century, with no boundary between what's real and what's not. Absolute masterwork from Glazer, Levi and Landin. Modern masterpiece.
Someone needs to get Michelle Williams in a rom-com where they live happily ever after.

Thought I had seen this but I was, for some odd reason, confusing it with Fractured with Sam Worthington, which now, reading the description, is ironic for two reasons. One, because I have near zero recollection of the film, and two, is that it probably couldn't be further from You Were Never Really Here . Just from its opening alone, you can tell Lynne Ramsay seriously has the sauce. It's a total deconstruction of the standard revenge flick, subverting expectations at every turn, and seeped in this enigmatic, arthouse allure that keeps it ever so intriguing. It reminds me of a more surrealist version of Fincher's The Killer if the protagonist had been a grimy, trauma-ridden depressive instead of a chronically online perfectionist. As such, it only makes sense to cast Joaquin, as he's always unrelentingly committed to every role, sometimes freakishly so, and that doesn't change here. In that same vein, Jonny Greenwood's thumping score is propulsive, and he never puts forth a half-hearted effort.

That one monologue about how the land was stolen from the indigenous by the colonisers, to then be stolen from the colonisers by the banks and capitalist institutions is such good writing. Sheridan can really bring the heat when he wants to.

film_key: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003)
review_clean: Filled with quite a few plot contrivances and dei ex machina that pissed me off a fair bit, but can't fully bring myself to be that annoyed by this conclusion to the trilogy. Perhaps I'll revisit the extended versions in time to see how they compare with these, but for now I'd say Fellowship of the Ring was my favourite by far.

Mike Leigh's ability to elicit such mind-blowing performances from his cast is second to none, and Another Year is yet another example of that. He shows so much respect and care for his actors, allowing them to sink themselves into these characters that we can all either relate to or aspire to be more like. Lesley Manville is an absolute revelation here, as is the entire cast for that matter, but she really stands out as this person who things have just gone wrong at every turn for. One of my biggest fears is growing into an idle person who has nothing going for them- no hopes, desires, or accomplishments- just a life of sheer monotony. Mike Leigh explores these feelings of isolation through a web of interconnectedness, demonstrating that even if we share the same feelings as others, we still may never feel more alone. I do question the inclusion of Imelda Staunton's character at the beginning of the film (don't get me wrong, it's a phenomenally acted part for such little time), as she neither provides any semblance of hope when you hit rock bottom nor a sense that one is beyond reproach when you end up there. Perhaps it's just a glimpse of what Mary could end up being, or rather a nice touch to show that nobody is too far gone to receive help. Either way, it's a heartbreaking portrayal of regret, something that I'm coming to learn is a common theme across Leigh's films.
I love karaoke scenes in movies.

Hey Disney+, you know can add subtitles instead of just putting '(Talking in Spanish)' ? Missed about 20% of the dialogue and had to figure things out from context because of that. Also, this was way too long anyway; it was at it's best when Dakota was in it.

Sometime ago, after watching and revelling in the two masterpieces that were The Godfather and The Godfather: Part II , I made a mistake that I always try to avoid when going into films, and that was letting public opinion dissuade me from completing the trilogy. Part of me is glad, now, that I decided to wait, as my growth in cinematic maturity tells me I probably would have been swayed by the consensus that The Godfather: Part III was a bad film and a disservice to its predecessors, because frankly, it just isn't. Watching the re-edited CODA cut of the film, closer in vision to what Coppola aimed to create, it makes sense why expectations weren't quite met as expected for many. Firstly, this isn't really a continuation of the themes explored before, and likewise, doesn't carry the same weight of catharsis that one might expect from a conclusion. But more than anything, The Godfather: Part III serves as an epilogue to the saga, with a man desperate to find solace in what he leaves behind, but his sins don't afford him that luxury. While it's clear that there are moments in this film that are severely less refined- some poor acting, shoddy dialogue mostly hampered by ADR, and sparse moments of a made-for-TV aesthetic- there is still an abundance of prestige filmmaking too. Not only that, but Pacino is still fantastic, and Andy Garcia's Vincent Mancini is an absolute welcome addition, besides the awful cousin-love subplot mind you, with his character only furthering the cyclical nature of greed and power. It may have been overshadowed by its legendary counterparts, as well as the release of Scorsese's Goodfellas in the same year (both of which include a minor role for Catherine Scorsese, which I found fun), but that doesn't mean by any means that, at least in its intended form, The Godfather: Part III is an unworthy sequel and conclusion.

Just terrific stuff all round- any film that uses Life's a Bitch to close things up is automatically amazing in my book. In many of these so-called kitchen-sink dramas, they nail their depiction of the day-to-day struggle of living in poverty, but often fail to build up to an ending that shows either a descent towards tragedy or a climb towards hope. Andrea Arnold's Fish Tank is one of the few that does both. Crafted with many of the same pastels as kindred filmmaker Sean Baker makes use of in The Florida Project , but contrastingly lain atop the backdrop of the trademark overcast British sky and its abundant concrete housing projects, Fish Tank set in a time of uncertainty as the dawn of the rapid change that was 2010s fast approaches, driven by powerful performances and a fittingly chaotic mix of pop, R&B, hip-hop, and jungle on the soundtrack. Most of the time, the film can be achingly cynical, but at others, it can be beautifully optimistic.

Decided to watch this after seeing it was 10 years since Philip Seymour Hoffman's passing, and he really was one of the best actors ever. Absolute powerhouse performances all around here from PSH, Meryl Streep, Amy Adams, and Viola Davis. Think the pacing is a little off and this could have done with being a bit longer though.

At the beginning of Peppermint Candy , we see a man climb onto some train tracks, clearly intent on committing suicide. But just before the train connects with Yeong-ho, the camera cuts away, as its passing shadow flashes upon the horrified face of a man he once knew 20 years prior. Through vignettes moving gradually backwards in time connected by reversed footage of a train moving forwards, Lee Chang-dong provides minuscule bits of information that help contextualise how Yeong-ho came to be so nihilistic, and as such, makes a commentary on societal changes throughout South Korea from the 70s through to the late 90s. With Burning and Secret Sunshine being some of my favourite films ever, I don't think there was any doubt that I was going to love this too, even if the backwards storytelling took a while to get used to.

The Marvels was the first Marvel film I hadn't seen in theatres since probably The Avengers in 2012, but I think it's safe to say my interest had been waning for a while, especially after the disasters that were Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania and Thor: Love and Thunder , not to mention a heap of woeful TV shows. However, I'd like to say I was pleasantly surprised, although that may have been helped by my rock-bottom expectations. The first 20 minutes of this are some of the most fun I've had with an MCU project in some time, and while there's still a whole host of problems with characterisation, the way it looks when it's not a CGI frame of space, and the fact that you'd have to watch 2 (arguably 4) TV shows and another film (again arguably more if we're talking about the post-credits scene) to get all the context, I still had fun. Kamala Khan is easily the standout of the film with Iman Vellani's enthusiasm and excitement just piercing the screen, Brie Larson is better here than in Captain Marvel but still she's given not much to work with, and Monica Rambeau is just sort of there. The villain is honestly just a mannequin and could have been anyone, and there were definitely deeper places that could have been gone to considering her motivations, but eventually with a 105-minute runtime, which is considerably less than its counterparts which is very much welcome, there's only so much that could have been explored. P.S. How funny would it have been if there was just a random Nope inspired digestion scene but with the cats.

Safe to say quite a few of the literary references went over my head, but really did enjoy the vibe here, and it's great to see a spin on a vampire story where they're just moody nihilists drowning in their own immortality and subsequent ennui. Jarmusch clearly has a passion for anthropology which shines through most of all here.

"If I were to shout, who would hear me out of the armies of angels?" It seems fitting that many of the Greek stories of legend involve a journey. Theo Angelopoulos creates this all encompassing odyssey of life within Landscape in the Mist , and chooses to centre the narrative on two children who have yet to experience it. It's a quest towards hope when every moment, and every painful loss of innocence, suggests that the goal is nowhere to be found. Yet still, amidst all obstacles, they journey on. It's only when things are shrouded in the mist of uncertainty, and when all hope seems lost, does the answer rear its head, and the destination is reached, though it's not the same place you thought you were heading towards.

After every Adam McKay feature I somewhat begrudgingly watch nowadays, I find that I have to exhaustingly remind myself, "Hey at least The Big Short was pretty great, huh?" Vice is a masturbatory flip book through American politics, with McKay thinking it's enough to simply slideshow his way though social commentary instead of actually embedding it in the narrative. For someone who admittedly knows little about Dick Cheney and the surrounding elusiveness of his tenure, I learned surprisingly little here, and while I do admire McKay's ability to summarise information such that it is digestible, I don't need it to be spoon-fed to me.

Not really a big fan of Tim Burton's work if I'm honest, but I do admittedly have a few big ones left to see, so time will tell if my general disposition towards his work changes. I'm not usually one for the overly endearing films, especially with how much this evoked Forrest Gump in the first half, but I didn't mind this, mostly all because of Billy Crudup though. I just wish there was more about how much of a bad father Edward Bloom was though, and I liked when you could explain the stories as a means for him to romanticise his life, but I don't think the ending particularly helps in that regard in satisfying that explanation, even with the display of slight inconsistency between his stories and real life with the twins.

It was hard for me to not think during Detachment that a director such as Kenneth Lonergan could have made a film ten times more compelling with the material. There's definitely something to be said here about the give-and-take nature of the American schooling system, and, by extension, the education industry as a whole. It's certainly a thankless job, one which I assume is the occupational equivalent of an acquired taste, even if it's not bogged down by a barrage of misery as shown here. Through a jarring direct address, Adrian Brody narrates his way through alleys of nihilism concerning today's youth, questioning whether his attempts at guidance are making any dent of a difference in the way they see the world. There's an interesting didacticism with which this teacher draws from the pain of his own experience to then try to ameliorate that for his students. But much like the educational lifespan of a substitute teacher, these lessons are short lived. Now, this alone would provide enough compelling narrative to work around, but Detachment begins to meander with this underage sex worker saviour plot line that just reads like an incel's fan-fiction, and doesn't really add much thematically to the main story. So with that, coupled with some terribly on the nose character moments, I'm on the fence with the film.

The whistling of birdsong, the patter of raindrops, the rush of city traffic. All these sounds exist in perpetuity within the background of our lives, and yet we only notice their presence when they're not there, or when we're a million miles away. It's only once you're removed from all the noise does the silence feel even more alienating. Tarkovsky's self-proclaimed failed creation Solaris provides a basis for the concepts of memory that he would then go on to master with Mirror , denoting how our past experiences affect our future ones. It explores the loss of humanity as a cost of the pursuit of knowledge, and how, if one aims to strive closer to the divine, the sacrifice is immeasurable.

...And Justice for All is pretty much a mess tonally, and yet it all just works for me. It goes from a sincere and distressing look at how the judicial system fails people on both sides of the law one minute to a wacky sitcom-like bit in the next. For all intents and purposes, it should not work, but with Jewison's stellar directing combined with one of Al Pacino's finest performances, it absolutely does. Perhaps it's a little on the nose to have a defence lawyer be so morally righteous, and it probably would have been better for him to have his own selfish motivations as times to create more of a growth arc. But nevertheless, this is terrific stuff all over.
They didn't even needle drop the song.

Rustin is unequivocally dull, both cinematographically and narratively, which is surprising since the story holds so much weight to it. Colman Domingo is impressive as the leading man, but is left rattling off ultimately inconsequential monologues in a time where consequence was everything. The one black-and-white bus scene was really the only thing that gripped my attention, but the rest left me feeling rather hollow. It's rather ironic that a film also starring Jeffrey Wright can seem like such an apt summary of part of the message that Cord Jefferson explored in American Fiction in the same year about how black stories (and queer stories for that matter) can be restricted to their politics when really they're about so much more.

The 17 minute unbroken long take dialogue between Fassbender and Cunningham is insane. Incredible debut from McQueen. Definitely need to check out the Small Axe anthology film series, and Occupied City whenever that releases.

I recently found myself coming across Haneke's criticism of Spielberg's Schindler's List , saying, in so many words, that it's perverse to aim for entertainment when depicting something so harrowing. After watching The Zone of Interest and how Glazer portrays the casual complicity with which quote-unquote regular people show in situations of unfathomable horror, Haneke's words rang around my head even more, likely more so because of comparisons to The White Ribbon . Not only do I think I should probably revisit Schindler's List , especially after learning more about the misrepresentation of Oskar Schindler in the film, but I also think I should reconsider the way I view violence in media as opposed to real life. Benny's Video examines how to observe violence through the barrier of a screen, but instead of focussing on voyeurism, it rather brilliantly looks at desensitisation, and how one can just as easily mop up spilled blood as spilled milk. We find ourselves empathising with Benny's parents when they're put in an impossible situation, and begin to strategise with them about how they are going to escape it. Without even thinking, we lend ourselves to complicity, once again through the safety of a screen. People are products of their environment, yes, but what Benny's Video so expertly demonstrates is how people can conversely shape the environment that they're in, just so they can see what it's like. Much of the film, including Arno Frisch's chilling performance, laid the foundation for its successor, Funny Games, where Haneke calls out the viewer for the aforementioned complicity, and explores a world of consequences where there is no alternative. For so many, the choice of adapting to your environment isn't really a choice at all. So when we see footage of a pig being slaughtered on a farm, it feels uncomfortable, but when we see what's essentially the same thing in an Egyptian village with a chicken, it feels normal. One feels cold and emotionless; the other feels necessary. Whether viewing footage of war on the news or seeing the same in a film, it's important to make that distinction to avoid blurring the lines on how truly awful real suffering can be.

Sometimes, on this app, I rate films accompanied by a meticulously crafted short essay of justification as to why I felt that way about them. Other times I rate them based on whether they have the sauce. And Michael Clayton has the sauce. Heaps of it in fact.
He's a stronger man than me. I think I would've folded for BDH.

Leagues above Infinity Pool. I can now forgive Andrea Riseborough for her To Leslie campaigning debacle because she's sensational here, as is Christopher Abbott. Dark, eerie, and psychedelic in ways that other elevated horrors only wish they could reach.

Set aside the controversy behind Diana Nyad's claims and achievements, which is enough to criticise the film in its own right, NYAD is still a woefully vapid biopic with enough pointless filler to make your average Oscar-bait feature look like a masterpiece. There's no depth to any of the characters, besides whatever Jodie Foster can muster just on charisma alone, and the creative decisions don't go beyond that of an unimaginative documentary.

Loved how personal this was; you could really feel that all the way throughout. Not usually a massive fan of Kumail Nanjiani and frankly his stand up bits in this still weren't that funny, but nonetheless still really enjoyed this. Might be a new comfort movie of mine.

Whenever I watch a parody movie, I think, "Wow this is awful, why did they ever make this?" But at the same time I weirdly miss that they don't really make them anymore. I mean, this contains just about every negatively connoted '-ism' in the world, but there are a couple jokes and references here and there that kind of land. Maybe there's just such a low bar set for these kinds of movies that this one just doesn't suck as much by comparison, but it does still suck quite a bit.

Certainly smug and without a doubt on the nose, Larraín's El Conde aims this satire about Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet more towards a mockery of the parasitic nature of his fascist rule than to any particular event under it. In much the same way as Ridley Scott navigated the life of his own sleazy, militarist juvenile in Napoleon without any real strive for accuracy, El Conde also reads as a purposefully lightly-researched opinion piece. It's a trait that serves in its favour when conducting these witty, Knives Out style interviews with Pinochet's family, or when it turns to its vampiric horror, but works against it when it tries to do anything more.

"It is the gods who weep. They see us killing each other over and over since time began. They can't save us from ourselves." Definitely drags a little in the midsection, but everything surrounding it is pure mastery. Ran is my first Akira Kurosawa film in colour, and wow, does he make use of it. Probably one of the best-looking films I've ever seen, from stunning battle sequences to idyllic mountains towering over fortresses. Couldn't help but try to laughably draw comparisons to Succession, given that each of them are essentially King Lear adaptations from different eras. It is definitely an interesting conversation to have as to why tragedy draws us in so much, Shakespearean or otherwise, especially when we know that there cannot be any other resolution. Is it holding out hope that we might be wrong, or are these stories just vehicles for us to teach ourselves to appreciate things while they're here? To that end, Ran tells us to not waste time with avarice and greed because that only breeds more of the same, but instead to cherish the things that matter; a sentiment so poignant when you consider the level of artistry achieved by a man who was turning blind, no longer able to experience in the same way the visual medium he had dedicated his life to.

Wanted to love this, but hard to say that it didn't feel a bit disingenuous. Naturally when approaching a subject matter like this, your first thought would to tackle it with a sprinkle of dark humour and the occasional sardonicism. But here, unfortunately, it just does not feel that convincing. Each moment of laughter should either be sharply contrasted with the overarching goal of suicide, or serve as a reminder that life is worth living, but On the Count of Three does neither. Now, you could argue that it chooses this path to deviate from what you'd expect from a film like this, but it's just so painstakingly predictable how this was going to end from the very start. It's a shame really, because I did really enjoy Christopher Abbott and Jerrod Carmichael in their respective roles, but the steps that lead to their mental state just feel too severely underwritten.

Since the beginning of human existence, religion has been used as a vehicle to provide comfort, give peace, but also to control. In line with Marxist belief, it is an opiate of the people, and given the widespread anticipation for the release of a sequel to Denis Villeneuve's sci-fi epic, Dune , one would be hard-pressed to say that the series hasn't garnered a similar level of euphoric cult following, an ideal that aligns with the basis for this successor. There are few films that can be described as generation-defining, but I don't think there can be any doubt about Dune: Part Two wearing that helm. All throughout history, the tenets of hereditary leadership amidst an immense accumulation of power have led to a weaponised charge for superiority and a subsequent control over those you're supposed to inspire. Ideas drip like poison in tyrannical regimes, so much so that even clairvoyants can turn a blind eye. Paths of feigned morality now lead to a Machiavellian climb to power with flagrant disregard for the cost. These ideas are all wrapped in the shell of an exhilarating blockbuster, which, in the same way as Cameron does in Avatar: The Way of Water , takes the time to allow us to bask in the sheer magnitude of its breathtaking worlds. Chalamet proves to be a formidable leading star, with each of his cast mates equally as compelling, and for once, a franchise leaves me wanting more instead of less. Rest assured, I'll be at the front of the swathes of people waiting restlessly for a third instalment, whenever that may be.
"He's my favourite, Goofy" Was totally unaware that Queen Maeve was Irish until now.
Nice to see McQuarrie and Cruise teaming up before they struck gold with the Mission: Impossible films. A pretty decent action flick, a bit too long but still fairly fun.
This just did not want to end.
"It's a good scream. It's a good scream." What a picture!

Must say that I think I much prefer Cronenberg's more obscure work, but this twist on a mob flick is pretty interesting, especially with Viggo Mortensen at the helm. Still have to see A History of Violence and A Dangerous Method to complete their collaborations together, but it's probably one of my favourite career moves for him to go from doing The Lord of the Rings trilogy to these films.
This would be the type of film to give me nightmares as a kid because I never really used to watch out-and-out horrors but my parents deemed it plenty fine for me to watch psychological thrillers.
Ralph Fiennes is insane in this.

I'm always a little conflicted about these films about mental illness that sort of deviate from what things would be like in the real world. On the one hand, it is nice seeing this idealised version of what we expect empathy to look like, and it's comforting to live in this escapism if not just for a little while. But on the other hand, it's just not a reflection of what living, and being around someone, with mental illness is like. And I get that things vary from person to person, and that it's not exactly a necessity to show all the harshness, but it's just something that stops me connecting with this entirely.
Alright dude, what the flip?

Sometimes I Think About Dying doesn't bring anything particularly new to the array of quiet Sundance indies that explore similar themes, and while Severance may lead the way in terms of the liminal, office space surrealist pieces, it still has just enough there to feel relatable and warm. Daisy Ridley gives what's probably her best performance to date even though, utterly unfairly, she hasn't been in all that much since her rise from the Star Wars sequels. The film doesn't quite justify even the 94-minute runtime, and would have been probably best suited to being a short instead. Nevertheless, I hope this serves as the propulsion Ridley needs to get herself in more projects, indie or otherwise, but I'm unsure as to whether the upcoming Rey solo film will boost or hamper that progress.
Did Ethan Coen just out Emma Seligman Emma Seligman? Idk maybe? Probably not.

"I was so sad the day I met you, I can't remember why" Can Olivia Cooke stop being in movies that make me cry? But seriously really love that she finally gets to use her actual voice here. I'm a big of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind , but I think I actually prefer the more restricted, dialled back approach taken here as it just feels so much more real. Not only that though, but it is set in a pandemic just before the actual pandemic happened, and I can only imagine watching this back then would have made it hit even harder.

Some gorgeous imagery and really quite remarkable production design here, especially for the budget, but I can't say that I was all that engaged by the narrative overall besides the love story and I also found the audio to be a bit off. Honestly wish it was just about a man falling in love with a woman through her dreams rather than all the tax audit advertising bits.

Insomnia is the only feature film in Christopher Nolan's filmography that he didn't at least co-write, and you can definitely feel it here and there. It's a solid cop thriller that gets a little jumbled in the middle, but mostly sticks the landing, although a more biting conclusion definitely could have been reached. Al Pacino and Robin Williams are pretty good here though, and propel us through what would otherwise be some pretty half-baked dialogues. Nevertheless, it feels good to finally finish Nolan's filmography, aside from a few short films.

Guarantee if I had watched this when it came out it would be one of my favourites of all time and probably would have had a pretty big impact on my childhood. Still glad I'm finally getting around to watching it now though; can only imagine how exhilarating this would be in theatres.
Whatever you think of Ricky Stanicky , you have to commend John Cena's commitment to the bit.

film_key: Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny (2023)
review_clean: You'd think the most exciting thing for a historian to experience would be to witness first-hand the events that they so diligently study, and while this fifth instalment in the Indiana Jones franchise sees the titular character experience just that, it so pitifully fails at being exciting. On paper, Dial of Destiny had just about everything going for it: Mangold coming off the back of Logan and Ford v Ferrari , Mads Mikkelsen and Boyd Holbrook as the antagonists, and Harrison Ford passionately returning with just about the only character in his filmography he still holds dear. Unfortunately it neither succeeds as a nostalgia-bait homage nor as something new and fresh. For the most part, it's just a nothing film, and while I'm sure watching this on a plane probably didn't help in my immersion, I'm sorely disappointed to say that this is probably my least favourite of the series.

"Don't try to understand it. Feel it." Still have my issues with this, but on vibes alone there's nothing quite like Tenet in Nolan's filmography, and any issues are diminished to nothing after a temporal pincer movement.

"If grief envelops some like a crashing wave, there are some to whom it spreads more slowly, like ink in water." Even more spellbinding than when I first watched it. Utterly insane to me that a film of this quality may only be my 3rd or so favourite Park Chan-wook film. The epitome of a neo-noir in the digital world, be that through means of investigation or just the astounding digital cinematography all throughout. Absolutely has to be one of my favourites of the 21st century now.

My first of Laurent's directorial efforts, and I must say I am fairly excited to see more. While the shades of Rustin Cohle from Pizzolatto's novel that this was based on can be felt all over the grizzly character that Ben Foster embodies, it certainly feels like Galveston is at its best when it's more like The Florida Project than True Detective . That being said, Elle Fanning is spectacular as always, and Laurent's direction shines throughout, especially in a head-turning oner that subverts one's expectations from a bloody shootout, with its aftermath leaves more to chew on than simply bullets. But when undertaking a story such as this in just 91 minutes, you need a little more than just that.

So funny how wildly different Sally Hawkins and Ben Whishaw are here to their usual roles. Daniel Craig is good. Michael Gambon is great. Sad to see where Vaughn has ended up with his last 3 films being pretty much schlock, even though I've yet to see Argylle , but let's hope that the rumours of some sort of Argylle-Kingsman cinematic universe die a fiery death and he returns to making films like this.

As if A Woman Under the Influence wasn't already a long, long overdue watch, this comes along and gives an insightful and articulate breakdown of the film in a breathless dialogue between Jessie Buckley and Jesse Plemons (only just realised while writing this that they both have near enough the same first name).

Not really a massive anime connoisseur outside of Ghibli and a few of the more mainstream series out there, but finally getting around to watching Your Name. has perhaps convinced me to give them more of a go. Absolutely stunning animation that western cinema really can't even get close to, and a cute and heartwarming story to boot.

Feels like a bigger and better version of The 39 Steps , with each of these set pieces being more impressive than the last. Ends a little quick for me, but I'd say I've had that same experience for every Hitchcock film so I think it's best just to get used to it. But nevertheless, this is my favourite so far, by far.

Based on a novella from Russian novelist Nikolai Leskov rather than directly drawing from the original Shakespeare play, Lady Macbeth basks in its slow, sultry darkness, with Florence Pugh encapsulating the familiar manipulative qualities of the eponymous woman in a gradual descent that grows increasingly ominous- a performance indicative of her subsequent deserved propulsion into stardom. There's much to be said in the conversation about the recontextualisation of Shakespeare's characters over time, and none are perhaps as infamously maligned as Lady Macbeth, known here as Katherine Lester. But instead of angling the film in a way that makes us feel any real sympathy for Katherine, Oldroyd instead takes a uniquely dark path with some truly sinister moments, which are compelling but do leave a gap for a little more nuance. In a similar way to which Sofia Coppola explores Marie Antoinette's loss of naivety as she's confined within the four walls of her residence, Oldroyd explores the consequences of regressive confinement. The film essentially serves as a cautionary tale of what society felt at the time would happen if women, particularly outspoken, audacious women such as Katherine, were given the licence to make choices of their own, rather than being satisfied with being reduced to mere property.
Had to do a double take when I heard Chaiyya Chaiyya at the start of this.

"How wonderful it would be if my whole life so far turns out to have been a dream, and suddenly I wake up and I'm someone else entirely." The master of horror Kiyoshi Kurosawa instead points his lens at the horrors of urban malaise in Tokyo Sonata , trading chilling scares for domestic drama. Unlike his countryman Hirokazu Kore-eda, whose films, described by shomin-geki, are the bonafide epitome of the sub-genre, Kurosawa instead focuses on ideas at large, commenting on how gender roles and masculinity can spread like a disease in modern households, equally in western and eastern cultures, crushing any semblance of ambition or hope in favour of pride. In spite of being infused with abundant traces of satire, the film is overwhelmingly bleak for much of its runtime, and where we think we see cracks forming in the familial structure from the weight of financial stress, we instead notice that they've been there all along. The thinly veiled façade is lifted, and we're left with two battling ideas of what could have been and what could be.
Judd Apatow needs to be arrested for his crimes.

Nick Nolte is absolutely outstanding in this. Weirdly enough he reminds me quite a bit of Ethan Hawke, who probably gives my favourite performance across Schrader's filmography in First Reformed, with his mannerisms and speech. But this performance is a close second.

film_key: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010)
review_clean: Sometimes an artist's work can feel so profoundly personal that it can be difficult to connect with. While you can recognise the heart that's put into it, you can never feel any more than a distant spectator. For most of my first Apichatpong Weerasethakul film, I felt that way. There are moments, especially in slow cinema, where you can feel entirely immersed in the experience, transfixed by nothing in particular, but nevertheless immersed. Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives is a film firmly rooted in experience, so while at times you can feel as if you could lose yourself in the stories being told, more often than not they're at an arms length, and there's only so far empathy can take you.

Certainly has the vibes of Linklater without the commitment to pull it off. I mean was there any real reason why this was set in the 80s instead of present day? Nevertheless, Kristen Stewart and Martin Starr are pretty great, and Ryan Reynolds is surprisingly more palatable than usual. Still haven't made my mind up on Jesse Eisenberg as he still seems to play the same guy in every film he's in with varying levels of insufferability, but luckily he's on the somewhat lower end of that spectrum here.

Clearly borrows a lot from Blade Runner , so it's no wonder why I adore the cyberpunk world and all its futuristic aesthetics (funny because this is set just 5 years from now). Unfortunately, it's just a bit too sterile for me, and the reason Ridley Scott's film works so well is the contrast between the harsh and soulless environment to the romance, and that doesn't really exist here.

Very much in the same ballpark as Detachment in so much as it explores the dynamic between a teacher and his students, both equally as troubled in their own ways. A top performance from Ryan Gosling as always, and while Half Nelson often overcommits in the direction of being grounded to the point where it can become a little repetitive, it doesn't do so to the point where it has nothing to say. In fact, it posits some worthwhile points about white saviour narratives, some of which puts films of a similar vein such as Freedom Writers to shame. But it also shows how the give-and-take nature of teaching is not too dissimilar to the give-and-take nature of addiction, and how each can have an influence on young, vulnerable kids' lives.

I'm actually quite surprised at just how funny I found this. Perhaps that makes me a sadist, and while dark humour isn't unheard of in thrillers, I was surprised at just how much there was in a film that ends this cynically, particularly one which Kubrick famously said was the scariest he'd ever seen. Nevertheless, I can concur with just about every point made about The Vanishing , all of which come to the shared conclusion that it excels in that it's just so horrifyingly straightforward. In films like these, there are always twists and turns and subversions used to lead the audience astray from what really happened, just so that the final reveal hits that much harder, but here there's next to none of that. In its stead is a slow unraveling of events, and a chilling portrayal of what an everyday family man could become just out of sheer curiosity.

If the supply of nearly half a million condoms to Olympic Village at Rio 2016 is anything to go by, it's that athletes are supremely horny, especially at the highest level where competition is their lifeblood. When talking about a sport where grunting is essentially paraphernalia, in a film directed by Luca Guadagnino, that sentiment is going to carry through tenfold. Challengers is absolutely invigorating, with the dynamic duo of Reznor and Ross thrusting the narrative forward with pulsating electro-pop synths, crafting what's perhaps their most galvanic score to date, or at the very least since The Social Network . If the discourse surrounding whether or not Zendaya is a movie star (in the traditional sense of the phrase) left you sitting on the fence, or net more aptly, then Challengers will be sure to tip you over the edge. Faist and O'Connor are equally if not more compelling though, in fact the latter gives by far the standout performance of the film, and do terrifically well to embody the sweat-drenched head-over-heels "white boys" as Zendaya's character Tashi so potently puts it. It's a film where advantages aren't just something gained on the court, but a means to outmanoeuvre and sabotage. But Kuritzkes' script is less interested in the match winner, and more focused on the psychosexual point scoring, but that doesn't come at the expense of some thrilling playing sequences, particularly in those last 10 exhilarating minutes.
Malick did it better. Do yourself a favour and watch The Tree of Life instead. Also, I bet that book sold 0 copies.

Between this and ...And Justice For All for Pacino, and this and 12 Angry Men for Lumet, they must have been some of the more progressive people in Hollywood at the time and I love that. The scope Lumet has to make his films poignant to this very day is astounding. On another note, as I'm sure has been pointed out tons of times already, but 1975 was such a killer year for film: Dog Day Afternoon, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Nashville, Jaws, Mirror, Barry Lyndon, and tons more I'm missing I'm sure.

Just imagine if any of the voters for overruling Roe v. Wade in the US back in 2022 watched this film. I would hope that the outcome would have been significantly different. The amount of anxiety and dread Mungiu is able to instil into a narrative that's fairly minimalistic is mind-blowing. With long takes that only ramp up the tension with every second they linger on, and conflicts that are restricted to the periphery as to highlight the effects a problem is causing rather than the problem itself. It's brilliant stuff all around; hats off to the actors for making it feel so real.

Adored the first act of this, but after that I sort of lost interest: character motivations become unclear and the film just ends up meandering a little. I haven't seen many, but I'm yet to see a film that totally blows me away from the French New Wave yet. I suppose I will have to keep watching.

Really gorgeous stuff. I mean, easily one of the best looking digital films out there surely? And the day-for-night cinematography is just nothing short of spectacular. As for the story, it's quite brilliant how First Cow positions you in such a way as to root for its protagonists, particularly when they're the opposite of everything prototypical about Western leads. Yet we root for them nevertheless, even when they're just as opportunistic as all the people they encounter throughout the film. Sure, the capitalist greed stemming from the top of this newborn regime is what breeds this scrounging for survival, but it goes to show that both parties are equally as inclined to take advantage of those with less power than themselves. It's very much the genesis of the modern idea of the American dream, in a similar thematically tangential way as There Will Be Blood is the genesis of American capitalism, and Reichardt leaves it very much up to the viewer of whether they see it in a negative or positive light. There's camaraderie to be found in a shared ambition, but that also leaves room to exploit the naive. The land upon which opportunities are built can both metaphorically and physically feel like a capsule of a foregone time, and so it can be difficult to imagine it as the basis of anything new. It's easy to watch the trees grow, the people move, and the landscape change and think that everything that can be done already has. But within that sentiment lies a poignant statement about the cyclical nature of systemic inequalities that lay seeded in the very same soil that plagues the institutions of the present.
Doesn't try and do too much, plus it's lighthearted fun and easy to watch. Smulders, Pearce, and Corrigan are great.

I'm sure this may have even been labelled progressive for the early 80s, but looking back on Trading Places now, it's hard to say that it hasn't aged poorly. From a slurry of racial stereotypes and outdated language, to actual blackface and to top it off a shot of the twin towers that evoked a notably ironic chuckle from me after I said, "How could this age worse?" before remembering that it was directed by a child murderer. Be that as it may, Eddie Murphy is absolutely stellar here in what is probably his breakthrough role- from innocuous, fourth-wall-breaking looks into the camera, to just some fantastic physical comedy that he later became known for. While it's nice to see the situation flip on its head come its resolution, it's not hard too see where the butt of the majority of the jokes lie, and so including the obligatory 'Landis is awful' comment, I'm just not sure our protagonists actually learn anything by the end of this.
I had a headache before this so imagine how my head is feeling now.

I can't decide whether it's a good thing or not that I'm not at all familiar with the pillars of classic literature that these period pieces are often adaptations of, outside of the names of their esteemed authors. Sometimes you can get lost in trying to make sure a retelling is faithful to the original story that you forget to consider artistic intent. Irrespective of that, I do very much adore how intimately Wuthering Heights is tied to its location- from the fog enveloped moors and perpetual rain, to the boggy mire and native wildlife. Andrea Arnold's liberal use of close-ups and handheld, as well as the 4:3 aspect ratio, keeps us within reach of the characters as well as the landscape, allowing us to feel the emotion even with the surrounding context stripped back. While the film is overlong and the child actors are far more convincing than their aged counterparts, it's this naturalistic approach from Arnold that leaves Wuthering Heights feeling memorable.

It's always interesting watching these metatextual films, because they highlight things in such a way that is a wholly unique experience to anything else. In Right Now, Wrong Then , Hong Sang-soo recognises the power of the medium by which he is telling the story. So in the first half when things are awkward, messy, and ultimately failed, they mirror how most things go in real life. But Hong recognises that the art of cinema is escapism (and brilliantly omits the director's own definition in the second half to allow us to come to this conclusion ourselves), and so manipulates the power of the medium to change things to better fit this reality, quite literally showing things from another angle. It's no longer awkward, at least not to the degree of estrangement, and character's decisions more comfortingly mimic that of a traditional romance narrative; it's bittersweet, but it allows us to resonate with parts of each half that feel pertinent to our own stories.

Dan Stevens is absolutely hilarious in this. Who'd have thought that he was also fluent in German on top of all the other things he's got going for him. It was nice to see a more humorous version of this narrative instead of the Her or Black Mirror 's Be Right Back types . That's not to say I'm Your Man doesn't find it's moments of introspection however, but it does so in a way that doesn't feel melodramatic, and it blends the sci-fi in brilliantly.

Wildly imaginative and wholly unlike anything I've ever seen before, but I'd be lying if I said that this wasn't a slog past the first act or so. Driver is so obviously one of the most talented actors of his generation, furthered only by the projects he chooses to star in, and there's no change to that here. Once you understand what Carax is going for, everything else that follows simply becomes spectacle rather than anything steeped in interesting commentary, and there's only so much you can get out of being wowed by some spectacularly framed musical numbers, unfortunately leaving Annette in the camp of films that I can respect, but not necessarily enjoy.

It seems a given that films that depict themes of sexual abuse, especially those instances including children, are bound to be divisive. Some people see the depiction of such media as endorsement, and naturally it's one of the most difficult subject to get right. With Una , adapted from the play Blackbird by David Harrower who also wrote the screenplay for the film, Andrews aims to show how the toil on the victims can be a far worse punishment than whatever befalls the malefactors, and how growth can be stunted far beyond anything physical. It bravely tackles the idea of reciprocal obsession, albeit in far different ways; how predators become infatuated by their victims and absolve themselves of any wrongdoing by assuring themselves their actions were justified, and conversely how victims become involuntarily inseparable from their predators. It's not an issue that's particularly new, especially within the realms of criminal psychology with things like Stockholm Syndrome, but performances from Rooney Mara, Ben Mendelsohn, and young actress Ruby Stokes, make it convincing. Methods for dealing with trauma are not a one-size-fits-all thing, and so I think there is room for nuance when exploring topics such as these, as long as they're made with the victims in mind.

When films explore themes of repression within religious institutions, especially ones as authoritarian as Orthodox communities, it seems inevitable that they're going to test the consequences of that repression, and that narrative doesn't really change with Disobedience . However, unlike pious sapphic counterparts like Mungiu's Beyond the Hills , it aims to look at things somewhat optimistically, despite its washed-out grey palette. Through both Rachel Weisz's character's free-spirited nature and Rachel McAdams' character's masked melancholy, we see two sides of the same coin; one which chose to leave the source of her torment, and another which chose to build a life from it. Within this, gaps in the narrative rear their heads, as we never truly get to see what drew Weisz's away, nor what compels McAdams' to stay. But that's where a deeply empathetic performance from McAdams, and almost comparatively powerful performances from Weisz and Nivola paper over those cracks. Without being familiar with the source material, I can't quite say whether Lelio was conflicted on where to end the film, but it certainly felt like it could have ended at least 4 times by my count, and the result is a conclusion which feels too on the nose, and could definitely have benefited from some ambiguity.

Amidst all of the discourse surrounding Coppola's latest release Megalopolis that just screened at Cannes to a, safe to say, mixed response, I decided to visit one of his other features that I have been meaning to watch for some time. With gorgeous black and white cinematography, Rumble Fish explores the activities of a handful of teenage hoodlums, each existing in the limbo of foregone gang violence, a time they reminisce about without having ever experienced it.
