Our protagonist, Rusty James, longs for an era of purpose, trapped by his own loneliness- his relationships are shallow, he was abandoned by his mother, his father's a drunk, and he constantly lives in the shadow of the mythos of his brother's name. Much like the colourful killer fish that remain separated only by a sheet of thin glass, each of these wannabe gangsters shake with eagerness to become the new apex predator, not knowing that there's so much more out there than the tank they live in.

Very much holds the same sort of branch to urban monotony as Tokyo Sonata , but this time imbued with the suffocating atmospheric horror that Kurosawa became known for with Cure and Pulse . Unlike these encompassing masterpieces however, the forces of evil aren't personified into a character that the audience can recognise. Instead, it remains invisible, only contextualised by the jarring sound design that underlies so much of Kurosawa's work. With only 45 minutes, he accomplishes what some filmmakers couldn't with 2 hours, and yet, I still wish this was longer, but maybe that's just me being greedy.

I don't even know how you'd even begin to write a script this erudite and articulate. In much the same way as you're not really required to understand all the business jargon that each awfully selfish character spouts in Succession , you don't really need to do the same here to understand the motivations behind or consequences of each terrible characters' actions. Nevertheless, the poetry in the eloquent dialogue is simply mesmeric, as is the way the palace and its surrounding gardens are shot.

The ultimate film about disparity. Disparity in class. Disparity in wealth. Disparity in societal expectations. I have since read the Murakami short story that this was based on (yet to read the Faulkner version), and while the eerie disquietude of it all remains, the division of wealth isn't as apparent- Haemi's counterpart is noted to be poor, but Jongsu's isn't, rather just less so in comparison to Ben's. Of course, with it being a Murakami work, it was based in Japan too, which also leaves an interesting difference with Lee Chang-dong using Trump broadcasts as well as North Korean propaganda to draw parallels between Eastern and Western political culture. It's really interesting to see the differences between an adaptation and its source, especially since I'm so often more familiar with the former. Aside from that, Burning is still an absolute masterpiece, and still one of my favourite films ever. Also found out recently that it was the highest rated film ever by the Jury Grid at Cannes with a 3.8/4, and yet it didn't win the Palme.
So glad Gore Verbinski is finally out of director's jail.

Spectacular. Exhilarating. Mad Max: Fury Road . All words that are synonymous with one another. Not just adrenaline-fuelled, but adrenaline-born; a fiery product of the very gland that stimulates fight or flight. Not only that, but a product of heated happenstance given its infamous behind-the-scenes antics and cursed production. Watching this in preparation for Furiosa , and part of me knows to never align myself with the George Miller doubters, but another part recognises the genius serendipity of Fury Road , a cacophony of brilliance immersed in the dust of post-apocalyptic milieu, and wonders just how Miller could strike gold in this landscape not once, but twice. I suppose time will provide the answer to that question.

Always have a soft spot for films that cast people that actually look like real people. Plus this was surprisingly great; quite literally the perfect thing for a nepo-baby to make with how this privileged kid cosplays as some tortured artist surrounded by fake relationships as if that would give him the precedence to become renowned (in a career where most names don't really escape the circles of extreme connoisseurs anyway, much like with cinema).

Probably enjoyed this more than most because I frankly couldn't care less for American politics and hence some fantastical stretch of the imagination in that respect isn't really going to be that much of a stretch for me. Although, it definitely feels as if people are piling on Civil War as the effective cinematic pariah for this year, and perhaps that wasn't helped by Garland's interviews and A24's promotional material, but it does feel like my assessment of the so-called apoliticism (some are calling it centrism which inherently proves my point that some people don't really have a stance on what this is and are just riding a wave) is different from others'. It feels like, to me, that Garland is saying that there is no such thing as apoliticism in an environment such as this, and seeing things from the quote-unquote objective point of view of a photograph can only lead to desensitisation. Bias is intrinsic to capturing a political landscape, and while it's not a uniquely American means of thinking to demand a stance in the prototypical bipartisan way, the red-pill/blue-pill culture has certainly accentuated that mindset, which is ironic because nowadays they really aren't that different from one another. I'm not saying that Civil War commits where it should, however. The reason why Jesse Plemons' guest appearance in this is so lauded is because it's one of few moments across the film's surprisingly short runtime which dares to attempt at being transgressive. Further, a lot of the dialogue definitely felt like a first draft that was just run with because it was secondary to the atmosphere, which isn't wrong, but it does get frustrating when characters talk in circles. Aside from that, where the film excels is almost solely in its viscera; gunshots actually feel impactful, fire burns hot, and all other sounds of war are terrifying. The whole film acts as this journey for this young journalist to capture "the single most important picture in American history", but there's no real subversion or lesson learned that recontextualises that moment by the time the shutter is closed, and everything just sort of happens exactly how the film makes you expect it would- hell I even called the moment where Cailee Spaeny captures the moment Kirsten Dunst dies. So in the end, it's not really any ideas regarding apolitcism that unearths the issues with Civil War , but the lack of gall to deviate from the path and say something truly scathing, and there's tons of directors who could have likely accomplished that better than Garland.
I feel like if I think about this premise for any more than 10 seconds it gets disturbing.

"The only way to change the world is if you actually try" Part of me respects the unabashed approach to what feels like a passion project, even though it was in actual fact born from the off-the-cuff riffing between Chris Pine and Patty Jenkins on the set of Wonder Woman 1984. But the fact that Pine decided to make his directorial debut an intentional Chinatown pastiche, which also draws from the likes of The Big Lebowski and Under the Silver Lake , narrated by a hipster pool man who writes to Erin Brockovich as a means of self-therapy and hallucinates about lizards, is something worth commending on its own. The fact of the matter is, I'd sooner watch 100 variations of Poolman before I ever laid eyes on an artificially generated film, because no machine could ever muster up something so pitifully bizarre. Next to nothing lands here. There's no tether to the story, the characters are caricatures that have no motivations, and the dialogue is not even half-baked, it's tenth-baked. It's a humourless spoof of the neo-noir genre that aims to- well, actually, I have no idea what this was aiming to do. It's so directionless that I'm not sure I can even call it a directorial debut. I can always respect a big swing, but when the miss is this bad, I'm not sure it warrants any merit.

Reminded me a little of von Trier's Breaking the Waves, but thankfully not quite as relentlessly cynical, although it can border on it at times- for which I was awaiting comeuppance but it doesn't quite manifest in the way that you'd expect. Really stunning capturing of the rural landscapes, and while I did enjoy the magic realism, the sort of divine impassibility of Lazzaro in the second half the film becomes difficult to reconcile with, to the point where it can feel more about the symbolism than the characters themselves. Neverthless, I'm glad I've begun to explore Rohrwacher's films; especially looking forward to La Chimera considering this watch was a recommendation of Josh O'Connor .

Very TV-movie and the dialogue kinda stinks at times, but it does feel sort of like how Primer does for sci-fi but for anthropology instead. Watched this because of TikTok clips and whenever I do that, the films tend to be of around this quality. It's entertaining to a point, but this barely tries to do anything. Plus the music was annoying.

I've got a bad track record for keeping with franchises so I thought I should finally watch this. Pretty damn good. Probably would have been better had I remembered more about the original- some side characters reappearing kinda threw me off as I didn't think this would really be connected outside of Neve Campbell and Courtney Cox reprising. Gets a little too meta at times, although I suppose that's the schtick. Also, I love the little segments where it feels like we're following another protagonist for a while like with the start and with Sarah Michelle Gellar's character (cinephile sober sorority sister is entirely more fun to watch than Neve Campbell I'm sorry).

The parallels to Flowers of Shanghai draw themselves, but I did much prefer how House of Tolerance allows its subjects to feel at least some happiness within their occupations, even if it's solely sprouted from a shared trauma. When making critiques such as these, with lavish gowns contrasting unglamorous lifestyles, it's so common for filmmakers to make their characters relentlessly tortured to really drive home their point, and while there are moments of that here, it's always to build to a greater point. Sexual acts are tolerated with hopes of a better future, even though they recognise that this future is unlikely to ever materialise. It balances psychological and physical entrapment within the palatial walls of this superficially decorated maison, with any semblance of sexualisation underpinned by a solemn reminder, both visually and sonically, of the illusion of choice. Women on display to passing voyeurs like animals in a zoo, kept bound by the notion that they may some day be set free from their gilded cage, and Bonello extends that idea to the modern day.

It's a pretty ingenious move from Payne to subvert Downsizing from what you'd expect its subject matter to bring. If not only from what you derive from the failure of marketing this movie in the right way- although that may have been a bold subversion in and of itself now that I think about it- from the concept alone you'd think that this would be some kind of zany, screwball comedy in the same wheelhouse as Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (replace Matt Damon with Will Ferrell here and that's probably what you get). But instead, Downsizing uses its concept in such a smart way that we almost forget about it altogether. I mean, the aim of any creation such as this is to achieve such a level of ubiquity and seamless transition that you forget that it even exists, and Payne uses this as a narrative device to totally absorb the viewer into this world. That's not to say Payne gets everything right here though. The satire is there to be played with, and while I can appreciate the restraint at times, it's hard not think about what someone like Ruben Östlund would have done in his place, particularly with the ending. The idea of making the downsized community simply a 1:1 microcosm of the wider world is a pretty good first step, but painting Matt Damon's character as a man who loses his purpose to then reject that purpose in favour of a newfound one is a little too safe for me, and doesn't quite comment on the culpability that the inventor of the technology has, and how the resulting measures of their village can be seen as hypocritical. Nevertheless, I still think this is fairly overhated mainly due to people's predetermined notions of what they expected it to be, and while it's not exactly near the top of Payne's filmography, it's hardly the woeful mess many have labeled it as.

Enjoyed how the architecture of the city is shot, but really unsure about the vibe that the filmmaker was going for here. I get the whole millennial ennui thing that it's going for, but we learn so little about the protagonist that he just feels boring. Honestly think that this should've just stuck with the failed romance angle (and then maybe a subsequent romanticising of everything else instead) because everything past about 20 minutes didn't really work for me.

Enjoyed much of the physical comedy but the characters were just too insufferable for me to enjoy the rest. A few tropes in here that really just irritate me more than anything. The chemistry between Cary Grant and Katharine Hepburn was great though.

Aggressively fine. For a film about stunt performers, most of the stunt sequences in this were hardly anything special. Gosling's charisma elevates a script that's otherwise inundated with cringe meta humour and references that just feel like filler for everything else, and makes the chemistry between him and Blunt almost believable.

A little hard to connect with at the start due to the overlapping narratives that are slightly difficult to place to begin with, but as the narrative unfolds and relationships between characters become more apparent, Sibyl really grows stronger. It's messy, but it's an organised mess. Performances all around are pretty great, with Sandra Huller being the standout- no wonder Triet went on to work with her again on Anatomy of a Fall. One thing I'd note is that sex scenes are actually believable and passionate, which is something that a lot of Hollywood movies just can't seem to get right.

Ffs yeah idk why I always fall for these kinds of films but yeah I cried. Chris Evans is great. I haven't seen much of Mckenna Grace's stuff but if she's anything like her potential shown here, she needs to get away from Young Sheldon and Ghostbusters and start doing real things.

I can always respect directors for being singular in their stylistic choices, and between this and Fallen Leaves , it seems as though Aki Kaurismäski has remained in the camp of hopeful cynicism for well over 30 years. There's a naivety in both the prudent, risk-averse and the unflinchingly despairing films that seem to exist in the binary extremes of today, and so it's refreshing to see someone who can exist so comfortably in a less prevalent middle-ground, mixing sardonic comedy with bleak surroundings. Shadows in Paradise kicks off Kaurismäki's so-called Proletariat Trilogy, where he explores the social realism of everyday working class people- although seeing how similar this film is to his latest, I can imagine you could add a few more to that collection. It explores a relationship that blooms against all odds, set on top of a stellar soundtrack (currently trying to find the name of that song at the end) and muted palette, all encapsulated by his trademark nonchalant brevity of his characters' dialogue, which I can only imagine must have inspired Wes Anderson.
Absolutely not.

Doesn't quite come together as it should, with odd pacing and a few scenes above the acting ability of some of the amateur actors. But Invincible is at its best when Tim Roth takes centre stage with a powerful performance which reflects how Nightmare Alley might look at the precipice of Nazi Germany in WW2.

The fact that this both starts and ends with a shot of the American flag irks me, because there isn't enough of a recontextualisation in between that to make the repetition poignant. It's not as solidly anti-war as most of its counterparts, even when it strives to be, and Spielberg's trademark sentimentality (in the same way as Schindler's List which I still need to revisit) irks me more than it moves me. That being said, the opening D-day sequence is an absolute masterwork, and his eye for shot composition is pretty much second to none, at least at this longevity.

When a film has more going on in its periphery than what we actually see in camera, it always seems to grab me in ways that others just can't. Like Someone in Love presents itself as more or less straightforward, but its jarring ending leaves you feeling like you've missed a whole other act that was playing in the background. It's really brilliant writing, with much of it, in true Kiarostami fashion, taking place through dialogue in cars, although now on the neon-illuminated streets of Tokyo rather than the sandy deserts of Iran. This departure is more than simply geographic though, with moments that feel almost antithetical to Taste of Cherry - it feels enigmatic in its message about identity where Taste of Cherry feels didactic, and even with both having seemingly unresolved conclusions, they each fill the gaps in strikingly different ways.

Wholesome, but also not. Vilifies the violence of man in a similar way to The Jungle Book ; interesting that this was released right in the middle of WW2. Emphasises the circle of life really well, and the hand-drawn animation is beautiful.
"I chose you, too" Kore-eda gets me every time.
So fucking dumb and I kinda loved it. Can only imagine me liking this more in time. Need to watch more of Korine's stuff now.

Doesn't quite reach the heights of Rumble Fish, which I was amazed to find out came out in the same year as this, but still gives a pretty good insight into the consequences of toxic masculinity. What a stacked cast too.

Totally spellbinding. A man burdened with the gift of finding lost treasures and yet can't find the one thing his heart desires. We might have a true star on our hands with Josh O'Connor; between this and Challengers, he's made quite the impression on 2024. Where Happy as Lazzaro falters in making its mythological hero fundamentally infallible, La Chimera thrives in making his imperfections the source of his drive, and explores the passion for a craft that stems from a place of grief and loss, culminating in one of the most gorgeous endings I've seen in a while.

Anthologies are a tough nut to crack. Make the through-line between them too obvious and it sort of defeats the purpose. Make them too disconnected and the audience will be left wondering what the point was. Yorgos Lanthimos' fabular triptych serves as a somewhat return to roots for the Greek director, once again collaborating with his fellow countryman Efthymis Filippou to create three stories that explore the perversities of human desire. The film aptly opens with Eurythmics' Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This), with the three tales revolving around a dream that serves as a sort of turning point in each. Much like his earlier work with Dogtooth , Lanthimos marries some dark humour (which may not come across as all that witty to those just now exposed to his work following Poor Things , but are laugh-out-loud hilarious to those more familiar with his work- too bad they're just a little few and far between) with an ambling sense of trepidation. It's his most steady work to date, in that it doesn't move with quite the same narrative drive as the rest of his filmography, and even though it's clearly intentional, it does make the film that much harder to connect to, especially with the changing storylines. From a story about a sinister task, to Possession -esque tale, then a Cronenberg cultist chapter, all subtitled in a similarly cryptic way about a dialogue-less character called 'R.M.F.', Kinds of Kindness is exciting in theory, but it's hard to escape the notion that Lanthimos is purposefully holding back, but he doesn't quite give you enough to figure out why.

After feeling less than satiated by my dose of absurdist comedy following Kinds of Kindness , I decided to look back to other renowned works within the sub-genre. Roy Andersson's Songs From The Second Floor , the opening film in his Living Trilogy, exists in a purgatory of loosely connected satirical vignettes, with all the drab, urban greys feeding into the lifelessness of capitalist dystopia. The rules of a mundane world fold in on themselves, often surreally and through skit-like moments that often linger in the background, with characters sacrificing their own beliefs in pursuit of financial gain.
Shooting a child by an ice cream van is fucking nuts. Love John Carpenter.
Nobody really does satire like Verhoeven. Thought I had seen the remake of this, starting to think I was remembering the Dredd remake with Karl Urban instead. But this is just awesome.

Falls into a fair few of the genre clichés you'd have hoped it would avoid, but The Watchers is still a solid debut from Ishana Shyamalan. The dialogue is painfully overloaded with clunky exposition, but there are definitely some interesting things here from a visual standpoint. Wish it was just a little bit more robust narratively (it even commits the mortal sin of literally telling you its message by the end, if the predictable twist beforehand wasn't bad enough). But it's really not a bad start at all, and with her father backing her up in her corner, I'd say I'm still fairly enthused to see what she comes out with next- hopefully she works a little more on finding her own cinematic voice.
Probably on the better end of this category of film, but like most of them it's aged pretty poorly.
Distortion through obsession. Voyeurism through surveillance. Intimacy through intrusion.

I don't think it's a coincidence that I've found myself gravitating towards stories circling the confrontation of one's mortality. Ikiru , The Thin Red Line , Still Walking; they all seem to evoke such a strong connection between the innately human experiences that the characters and the viewers share, tied together with a profound poeticism that allows us to see things from a hopeful perspective, even if the events that are transpiring aren't typically depicted in a positive light. But therein lies the skill of filmmakers like Angelopoulos, who can turn these looming moments where we have to face the questions of whether our lives were ones spent well, into an encompassing feeling of respite, where we can vow to make the most of the time we have left. "I once asked you "how long will tomorrow last?" and you answered me: Eternity and a day."

Fun as hell, with some really neat visual gags and physical comedy throughout. Tom Cruise as electric as ever, and this acts as a sort of precursor to all his action-star focus from Jack Reacher to 4 (almost 5) Mission: Impossible movies, although I think it could have been even funnier had he leant into the himbo-ness of it all a little more.

Ultimately tries to do far too much and gets a little muddled in its messaging as a result, but there's no doubt that Howl's Moving Castle is instantly iconic for it's gorgeous soundtrack, stunning visuals, and idiosyncratic characters. Unfortunately though, many of the other films in the Ghibli catalogue share those characteristics and have more to offer in the narrative department.

film_key: Me and You and Everyone We Know (2005)
review_clean: I hold a nostalgia for moments of connection before the ubiquity of social media. I was alive, but it's not really a time I experienced as I was only a kid. I almost wish I was born a little earlier so I could have experienced what it was like to develop those relationships with people (not just romantic, but everyday human relationships) without the looming backdrop of the digital world. It's almost a question as to why you would choose to converse with someone over a shared passion, or a shared perspective, if it was infinitely easier and more convenient to do so online. But Me and You and Everyone We Know exists in a time just before that, where miscommunications were simply that, and not more fuel to stoke an imaginary fire. Miranda July fills it with equally heartwarming and hilarious interactions, which all end in a host of heartwarming and hilarious ways, some of which a director like Solondz would take a step further, but I appreciate the restraint here because it works really well.

Aside from the obvious, it's always a difficult time watching rape-revenge movies, and I tend to avoid them for the most part because they always seem to go the same direction. No fault of the writing per se, but there's really only one way you can justify these kinds of stories going without being irredeemably nihilistic. So while The Nightingale naturally doesn't break any new ground when it comes to the narrative, it certainly boasts some powerful moments that make it worthwhile, and evoke their fair share of vicarious anger, intertwining the journeys of two people who have lost everything in immensely different circumstances, but bond over their shared grief. Radek Ładczuk's 4:3 digital cinematography is stellar, capturing the Tasmanian wilderness with such clear affection.

No idea why I decided to rewatch this (I think part of me was unsure I had watched it at all but that soon rang untrue as soon as I recalled the introductory "oven" room scene), but it's actually quite fun. Don't get me wrong the dialogue is god-awful, the characters are annoying stereotypes but it is kinda fascinating to see their different approaches to things. Beyond the first half though, the conceit goes from fun and gimmicky to a little too on the nose- yes, even for a movie based on an uber specific era of escape rooms actually being a thing people go to (which is another confusing thing because why are these people just showing up to an escape room alone). Either way, the production design is pretty cool, and I'm about 80% sure I haven't seen the sequel, so at the very least, this served as a refresher before I see that.

So close to loving this, and perhaps in time I will, but I can't say I was entirely engaged throughout, even with some really striking images. Greenaway explores writing as love, writing as hate, writing as history, writing as sex, and writing as art, often experimentally splicing the frame with contrasting images, using the film as a canvas for his own artistic expression.
Gives that warm and fuzzy feeling that hallmark movies tend to, and that was exactly what I was looking for. Really quite surprised that AnnaSophia Robb wasn't a bigger star after her childhood.

Honestly don't think this gets nearly as silly enough as it should, and ends up feeling more like an Escape Room 1.5 than a sequel. The first act is spent recapping the first movie, and the rest is just regular puzzle solving with characters dying that you never cared about anyway. It totally misses the opportunity to expand on the enigmatic organisation behind these games, and actually ends exactly how it should have begun in the first place. But even after saying all of this, I would still totally watch another one of these, because even though there's no doubt in my mind that it's schlock, it's still just about creative enough to be entertaining.
A little tedious outside of the enthralling pool scenes if I'm honest, but Newman, Scott, and Gleason do just about enough to keep it afloat. Mostly just watched this to watch Scorsese's sequel.
RDJ carries this movie so hard it's insane. Tom Cruise is pretty great too though.

With vignettes that twist and turn and contort the lines between past and present, and reality and fiction, Funeral Parade of Roses serves a seminal piece of transgressive cinema, with a narrative as liberally bound and fluid as its characters' identities, both in front of and behind the camera. Matsumoto plays with this idea of masks, not only as a symbol for gender non-conformity, but also as a tool to explore the transformative power of the medium itself.

Undoubtedly dripping with sweat and style, but unfortunately misses the mark by its conclusion, and ends up having less to say as its plot progresses. The chemistry between O'Brian and Stewart is palpable, and Glass' approach to surrealism is a commendable swing, but it all gets bogged down by a litany of plot contrivances that become too distracting to ignore (both of them leaving to go to the Vegas would have been a much more interesting route to take).

A much better experience to let this wash over you and just feel instead of trying to analyse and understand every piece of symbolism. Found it to be far slower the first time watching like that, but this time it flew by, but no less staggering by any means.

Definitely thought this was going to take a darker route given that the only other Moodyson film I've seen thus far was Lilya 4-Ever , but this was actually quite sweet. Not afraid to make its characters flawed, and actually casts teenagers as teenagers. A little weird how they did the English title though.
I'm ready for the Brad Bird renaissance. Please come back Brad Bird.

"It's like being in a dream" Just a stunning piece of work that I can only see myself loving more and more over time. The way the camera follows the characters almost improvisationally, navigating these tangentially interconnected storylines that play with time in a way that I've never seen a film do before, culminating in what's now one of my favourite ending shots. Such an assured debut from Bi Gan, and between this, Long Day's Journey into Night , and A Short Story , he's easily one of my favourite up and coming auteurs.
Charlotte Rampling has a knack for playing Reverend Mothers it seems.
This is where that one Cillian Murphy meme comes from?!
I've had enough of these little yellow fucks.

Feels just so close to being great without ever actually getting there. Wouldn't say this feels as Lynchian as people are saying besides some minor shades of Inland Empire , although I haven't seen Twin Peaks yet so perhaps I'll reserve judgement on that. Léa Seydoux is terrific as always, and I certainly find myself wanting to see more of Bonello's work as The Beast is absolutely one of the more adventurous films of the year so far.

Finally getting around to watching some more Fellini and this one is a far more straightforward watch than 8 1/2 was. Can't say I wasn't bored a fair bit by a large chunk of the middle but the ending was glorious- Anthony Quinn was really good here, but Masina's character didn't entirely work for me.
The cinematic equivalent of a lullaby, gently exploring the memories and feelings that a still image can evoke.
A deserved Oscar win for Christopher Plummer. Need Mike Mills to make more movies please.

Just a big Where's Wally? of Hollywood actors and meta references that pay off in ways that I absolutely loved. Part noir as an ode to Hitchcock and to Hollywood in general, but also a bit of a 'fuck you' to studio execs. The start with the camera voyeuristically weaving through conversations was perfection. Could be a 5 on rewatch.

Really cool stuff. Need to watch more vampire and monster movies in general because they always seem to be so exciting with their style. Wanted to explore Kathryn Bigelow's earlier work to see how it compared to her war-fixated later films, and I must say this is a lot more fun. Need that Tangerine Dream score injected intravenously.

Wouldn't really agree with the people saying that this hasn't aged well at all. Is it a product of its time? Sure. But to say that it's themes aren't at least somewhat pertinent to this day would be flat out wrong (especially if you look at stuff like the far-right race riots plaguing the UK at the moment). Poitier, Hepburn, and Tracy are all outstanding here, even more so the latter because he died shortly after. Love the moment after he has the small crash with the black man that his prejudices unearth themselves again, as if that's all it took for him to abandon the principles he swears he lives his life by- felt very much like Do The Right Thing in that regard. But also just how it shows the changes in mentality between generations, where some act on things out of necessity whereas others act based on feeling, which is summed up pretty wonderfully in Poitier's response to his father: "You listen to me. You say you don't want to tell me how to live my life. So what do you think you've been doing? You tell me what rights I've got or haven't got, and what I owe to you for what you've done for me. Let me tell you something. I owe you nothing! If you carried that bag a million miles, you did what you're supposed to do! Because you brought me into this world. And from that day you owed me everything you could ever do for me like I will owe my son if I ever have another. But you don't own me! You can't tell me when or where I'm out of line, or try to get me to live my life according to your rules. You don't even know what I am, Dad, you don't know who I am. You don't know how I feel, what I think. And if I tried to explain it the rest of your life you will never understand. You are 30 years older than I am. You and your whole lousy generation believes the way it was for you is the way it's got to be. And not until your whole generation has lain down and died will the dead weight of you be off our backs! You understand, you've got to get off my back!"

Undoubtedly one of my favourite titles of all time now- not only because it refers to an actual deity and all the routes of symbolism that can be derived from that, but because it can be interpreted as a metaphor for the lights which saturated the streets of Taipei, whereas the rebels are the non-conformist youths who feel alienated when clutching to the now relics of that time. Tsai Ming-liang's feature-length debut explores the consequences of that alienation, and how it can manifest itself in different ways depending on who you can share that burden with. Rebels of the Neon God is certainly more propulsive than Tsai's later work, especially with the electronic ambience of its soundtrack accompanying the film.

Vagabond is constructed of tracking shots that its protagonist can hardly stay in frame for. She either passes by entirely, leaving the camera behind, or joins an already established shot. Of course it could signify the nomadic nature of Mona, but since Vagabond is stitched together from accounts of her encounters with various other people, fixed together like testimony, these shots lie on the periphery of that story, and so when the fourth wall is broken by the maid and the camera itself is introduced as a character, these moments become redefined as Mona almost leaving her signature behind on the people that she meets, for better or worse. For most of the runtime, we forget where Mona's journey will ultimately lead her, until Varda cynically reminds us of her unceremonious fate, which we're left to question whether it could have been avoided.

Still quite on the fence on found footage, but Matt Reeves understands that you essentially need an idiot or someone selfish behind the camera to justify its existence, which is essentially the only reason T.J. Miller is palatable here, otherwise he would be incredibly grating. Probably been said a million times, but the post-9/11 hysteria captured here is terrific, and Cloverfield manages to land where The Happening does not. Unfortunately shows the monster a little too much for my liking- I think keeping the fear and uncertainty as the main driving force would have been far more effective, but I understand for marketing reasons that it probably made more sense to do it this way.

Worked for me, in terms of social commentary, far better than Dream Scenario did, and even though we hardly see any development from our narcissistic psychopath of a main character (either improving her outlook or worsening it), it still punches hard when it needs to. Sick of Myself comments on the desperation for young people to seize some sort of cultural relevancy, and the means they're willing to go to get there. Drowning oneself in a web of malicious lies and somehow still having the arrogance to imagine a world where everything is going to turn out alright. I must say I had issues finding any sympathy with either of the two main characters, but Borgli manages to structure the film in such a way that it doesn't feel like you need to, and instead you can sympathise with trying to fit into a hostile world of influencers and pseudo-PC organisations rather than any of the characters in particular.

With Perfect Days , Wim Wenders urges us to seek beauty in the everyday things and people we may encounter, and Koji Yakusho's character finds solace in the monotony of his daily routine. But more importantly than that, Wenders recognises that this outlook requires a certain amount of delusion, because life doesn't work in such a way as to allow for each day to be the same as the last. We can choose to block out any fragments of interference in the periphery, but then nothing we would experience would be real, and all the things we romanticise are fallacy. "KOMOREBI: is the Japanese word for the shimmering of light and shadows that is created by leaves swaying in the wind. It only exists once, at that moment."
Rest easy Gena Rowlands.

The start of Piotr Szulkin's apocalypse tetralogy, which feels reminiscent of works such as Gilliam's Brazil and parts of Tarkovsky, to create this Orwellian nightmare, based on a Jewish legend that has served as a basis for and been adapted into a whole host of science fiction work, most notably Frankenstein . It's hard to follow by design, and as such makes it hard to become tethered to, but pierces through at times with its political commentary and philosophical shell.

Is it weird for me to say this is my favourite Harvey Keitel performance? A little rough around the edges? Sure. But still just great stuff all around. Scorsese at his roots, beginning to show shades of the brilliant characterisation and depth he brought to the mob genre as a whole, but his love for cinema is ever-present right from the very start.
Didn't work for me the first time, didn't work for me this time.

Enjoyed this far more than I was expecting, definitely one of Shyamalan's better outings. Partly a spiritual successor to Signs , evoking Funny Games at times too, as such I wish it got a little more brutal with it, but I get that M. Night's not exactly known for that. But yeah camerawork in this is top-tier, and the way we're just thrown into things really helps ramp up the tension.
Pretty awesome when it's a psychedelic trip, particularly with the practical effects and all the trippy visuals, but a little tedious when it comes to everything else if I'm honest.

With Haneke's debut The Seventh Continent , he challenges the viewer to endure the same monotony as this seemingly regular family experience through drawn-out long-takes of mundane tasks, and through three similar but eerily distinct parts marking the same day of 3 consecutive years, he explores the consequences of alienation, and an attempt at escapism to a place that doesn't exist.

"I think it's kinda sexy that John Malkovich has a portal, y'know, sort of like, it's like, like he has a vagina. It's sort of vaginal, y'know, like he has a, he has a penis AND a vagina. I mean, it's sort of like... Malkovich's... feminine side. I like that." Long overdue watch.
A quirky romance movie with an almost worrisome amount of blood.
Not sure how this is the first time I've noticed Oscar Isaac/Al Pacino similarities but I'm glad I have nonetheless.

Seriously impressive stuff for a debut feature from Molly Manning Walker, and Mia McKenna-Bruce absolutely knocks it out of the park with what's now one of my favourite performances of 2023- reminds me of Florence Pugh a bit actually.

"I feel like hell is coming" Officially the longest film I've ever seen, by some margin too, and I'm actually quite surprised at just how accessible this was. Lav Diaz is so very clearly tethered by memories, both good and bad, from his childhood in the Philippines. As he tests the bounds of the medium by forcing the viewer to become a static observer for each increasingly bleak event, we become encompassed in a place and a time. When one's identity is so strongly tied to a specific place, it can be hard to come to terms with what you become when your environment changes, and when the place that you grew up in becomes unrecognisable. Diaz sets up this looming cataclysm by making this barrio a microcosm for the rest of the country under the kleptocratic Marcos regime, with the residents of this once tight-knit community left to fend for themselves in a sort of fearful limbo . They try to stick to traditions, but those fail them. They try to stick close to those they know, but they become maligned by the threat. Turbulence in the social climate are mirrored by the actual climate- with torrential downpours perpetually drenching the background of the film, forbidding it from escaping to the silence. With some of the most gorgeous black and white cinematography put to screen, Diaz both starkly captures an era, but also lends a sense of timelessness that makes these issues extend their pertinence to this day.
I'm a bitch for investigative journalism films. And those split-diopters wow.

Interesting in its pro-choice allegory, but pretty uninspired in just about everything else. Immaculate clearly borrows heavily from the likes of Rosemary's Baby , and even Ready or Not , with some giallo inspiration in the mix too- but I just wish it had the gall to get a bit more goofy with it. The trimester timecards and the "Goddamn it!" upon her water breaking had led me to believe that Mohan just might get there by the conclusion, and while watching a pregnant nun brutally kill a couple of people is definitely fun, it still doesn't quite drop the act of being just a little too self-serious- something that makes the first two acts of this a slog.

Definitely more accessible than Blue was, but not nearly as thematically rich. Three Colors: White is at its best when it's simply about a man trying to get back on his feet and regain some sort of purpose in his life, but loses me when it keeps circling back to his past. The friendship between Karol and Mikołaj is easily the best part, but it ends up taking a backseat when it should be the emotional crux of the whole film.

film_key: The War of the Worlds: Next Century (1981)
review_clean: A vast improvement on the previous instalment in Szulkin's Apocalypse Tetralogy , from both a filmmaking perspective and a storytelling one. Its surrealist, almost Truman Show- like quality brings a sense of levity to the dread, which is hugely appreciated, especially when tackling a subject as bleak as this. It's similarly Orwellian to Golem (obviously an adaptation of H.G. Wells' novel- funny that I've seen this before seing Spielberg's version), with the government using the media to fuel propaganda to continue to poke and prod at their constituents like caged animals, knowing that they lack the drive to fight back- epitomised by its conclusion where our protagonist futilely grasps for their action. "You accept only this what reinforces you in belief, that passivity is a virtue and a must. Because this is what you want to believe in."

Now completed Lynne Ramsay's feature length filmography, and she has to be one of my favourite directors right now. She shows empathy in such a way where it's never head on, but always feels fulfilling. Samantha Morton is totally captivating as the titular character, and the soundtrack is equally as memorable. Ramsay navigates the story, and Morvern's decisions, in ways which you wouldn't expect them to go, but does so in such a natural and compelling way that feels so unique to her as a filmmaker. Can only see this growing on me in time. Can't wait to see her collaborate with Robert Pattinson.
Decided to start October off with this horror movie.

Very 2000s, perhaps even more so than the first, which sometimes works but a lot of the time didn't- seriously there are more effects on screen than an Indian soap opera. And while the flipped structure is interesting at first, it isn't nearly utilised enough, and the twist ending ends up doing a lot of the heavy lifting here. Also didn't think that the traps were all that great either.

Utterly insane. One of those films where it's futile trying to dissect every aspect to try and decipher what they mean because that's squarely not the point. Leos Carax moulds this amalgam of ideas through vignettes connected only by one man and the limousine driver that guides him to each one. Partly a meta deconstruction of the method that goes into conceptualising a character, and partly a satirical piece on growing tired of the act of performing itself- be that through cinema or through everyday life. An apathetic digitisation that shuts you out like tinted windows, and gradually sucks away any morsel of care you had for the thing that you once loved, and as such the performance is forced to carry on.

Didn't love this to be honest. Gets into things far too quickly without much time for us to ever actually care about any of the characters- if their idiotic decisions, or lack thereof, didn't already sway us in the opposite direction. The music is overbearing, the performances are weak, and having nearly all the exposition done through the radio/TV felt lazy. The only thing that quite struck me was the ending, if only for its unflinching cynicism.

Some really awesome moments in here that, with a bit more solidity in the connective tissue, could've led to a modern horror classic with It Follows . The initial kidnap scene, the first house scene, the pool set piece- all such great ideas that don't quite get the payoff they deserve. Don't get me wrong this is some pretty fantastically directed stuff- hell it's pretty much even been riffed on already with Smile and even Talk to Me - but with a little more depth and consistency to the mythology, it could've extended its timeless nature beyond just its aesthetics. Still, I did really enjoy the twist on the typical horror antagonist.
Cinema in its purest form- just straight experimentation. Insane how modern this looks at times given that it's almost 100 years old.
"Of course it's Pete. Look at him" Probably the most I've laughed at a Coen brothers movie. This is pretty much how I see most of the southern American states.

Plays like a greatest hits of the Alien franchise at times, where the film is at its absolute weakest- the visual references like the hole-in-the-hull or the Engineer from Prometheus are far more compelling nods to the earlier films than a resurrected Ian Holm or a rehashed version of a classic line. But it's such a shame that Álvarez felt the need to incorporate those into the story because Alien: Romulus has more than enough strength to hold its own. The initial space heist, the inventive use of the Facehuggers, the acid laser-maze, the shifting allegiance synthetic- all such awesome and original ideas that work so well as, or as part of, set-pieces. For better or worse, Álvarez is clearly such a big fan of the earlier films, and of the sci-fi/horror landscape in general, that he brings fresh ideas to a story that unfortunately feels a little too diegetic to what came before. Still, this rips.

"Fly like you, not like them." Definitely feels a little rushed at times, making the emotional moments a little harder to connect to, and loses steam with the third act killer robots instead of just focusing solely on the island and the winter- the conflict between the animals coexisting should be the crux rather than the capitalist commentary it tries to go for- but I'd be lying if I said this didn't give me a warm feeling inside. The VA work is pretty spectacular, and the animation is fun, but I just wish it veered away from the generics and embraced its heartfelt core.

Wasn't totally captivated by the first half of this, perhaps due to my own lack of focus too, but the second half was spectacular- particularly in scale, with some parts even feeling like a Kurosawa film. An analysis of faith, creation, and the way that people can manipulate both to fit their own beliefs. Helps now that I know that Andrei Rublev was a real person, which recontextualises much of this for me, particularly the ending. So I may have to rewatch this sometime with that knowledge.

Sean Baker's Red Rocket is probably one of the best films of the decade, if not the 2000s in general. That's not just because of a Simon Rex performance that I will still insist deserved a Best Actor win, but because, like its main character, it knows exactly what it is. Mikey is a piece of shit thrown back into his hometown, now transformed under Trump's presidency. He fucks people (over) and takes what he wants because his experience makes him hardened in such a way that he can't navigate the world any other way. With The Apprentice being released this year and election results on the horizon, it's hard to think that any satirisation or attempts at encapsulating the feeling of Trump's America could be more aptly surmised than in the microcosm that Baker creates with Red Rocket- about a man so abundantly reckless yet so devilishly charming that you can't help but listen to what he has to say. All that is to say that Baker's Palme d'Or-winning Anora, which explores a sex worker in a precarious situation for the umpteenth time, doesn't quite nail the one thing that could take it from brilliant to a masterpiece- the naïveté of our titular character. For a profession that hinges on transactional exchanges, she seems awfully gullible to jump at the chance at legitimising one of these relationships, even if it is for the dreamy son of a Russian oligarch. It's not quite infantilisation, but it's a lack of understanding of accountability- something that pops up in The Florida Project too- and here, it essentially boils down to Anora not seeing the big waving red flags in front of her. Now that can be easily explained by experience, or lack thereof, of course- Mikey is a middle-aged veteran of the industry, whereas Anora is seemingly just getting started- but it causes issues when you feel like the point where she should flip from concerned wife to vengeful victim should happen sooner than it does. Now that that's out of the way, I have to say this is probably far and away the funniest film of 2024 so far. Mikey Madison knocks it out of the park with all her Brooklyn sass, and her back and forth with the three Armenian goons, or rather stooges, is just hilarious. Sometimes the bits linger for a little longer than they should, but they're laugh-out-loud funny every single time. Baker no doubt nods towards Showgirls with Anora 's jarring ending, that turns the laughs to silence, and I feel it will definitely be hit or miss with some. More in the tune of Verhoeven though, I wish we got to see a little more of the glitz and glamour of Vegas, to then later contrast with everything else. I can only imagine how much of a symbolic haven that Las Vegas would be for a young sex worker, and so it's the perfect place to then begin to tear that naivety away and make that closing shot feel all the more affecting.

film_key: The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989)
review_clean: Been on a binge of Greenaway's films this year and something about them just click with me. Michael Gambon is spectacular in this- all his gluttonous, vile moments contrasted with his hilariously sharp dialogue, which is only elevated by his Cockney accent. Brilliant!

Very much this year's Dream Scenario . Stan is terrific, Reinsve brings a snide awfulness that's distinctly lacking in Hollywood cinema, particularly in female roles, and Pearson provides the kicker that it doesn't matter what you look like if your values and character aren't genuine. Gets a little on the nose, especially when it turns into a meta deconstruction of itself, but far and away more affecting in its analysis of body image than The Substance was.

Fun as hell, and it's clear that Hartnett is having a blast. Somewhat wish this had stayed a single-location film just because the concert setting is so compelling, almost like a reverse Die Hard , but I still did enjoy what we got, even if it couldn't quite decide when to conclude. I do admire the direction that Shyamalan's films are taking though, like how Knock at the Cabin was essentially him coming to terms with what it's like to raise a child in this chaotic world, and now with Trap he's exploring the gifts and troubles of fatherhood, all the while shilling his popstar daughter. Love it.

Get what it's going for, but really don't think it works.

Smile 2 strangely upgrades on its predecessor in just about every way- set pieces, directing, and Naomi Scott as the lead, but at the same time this is largely the same movie as the first. There's no new way that this protagonist navigates this quote-unquote illness, and even the shocking monster reveal at the end of the first film is repeated at the end of this one- totally a missed opportunity to expand on that. That being said, this is still a fun time- still a little too reliant on jumpscares, but they're thrilling nevertheless, and about 30 minutes too long, but Finn mixes it up just enough to make this still an enjoyable ride (someone needs to tell him to chill with the upside down shots though).

Been itching to watch another Bergman film following my trip to Sweden, and finally got around to it. Probably the most straightforward film of his I've seen so far, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it doesn't quite hit the depths of Winter Light or Persona. Still, a sweet contemplative piece about mortality, with some interesting dream sequences.

Gorgeous film with a gorgeous ending. Such a powerful performance from Yun Jeong-hie. Lee exploring that poetry isn't something that can be forced or manufactured: inspiration flows as naturally as a river, and comes from the depths of our experiences and memories. It's almost a curse that as we get older we gain more of these experiences and have more stories to tell, but our minds aren't as equipped to tell them. So memories become feelings, and feelings become poetry.

Starting to become a big fan of Miranda July's work between this and Me and You and Everyone We Know- I just wish she made more films! Taps into the indie quirkiness quite unlike anyone I've seen, and underlines heartfelt moments with some brilliantly deadpan humour. Evan Rachel Wood is spectacular here, from her physicality to her mannerisms, as is Gina Rodriguez who I typically find so-so. A real standout is Emile Mosseri's transcendent score though, which I had listened to in parts before this, but listening to it in its origin is special.
This is like crack cocaine for white people.

Coen's had so much sauce from early doors. Such charged filmmaking here, as soon as the chasing begins, this kicks into second gear and stays there till the end. Plus, Nick Cage is just so good in a zany, slapstick role, and fits into the Coen's comedy perfectly.

A hypothesis that the act of simply existing- drifting through life with lethargy and automation- doesn't need to be a bad thing. I must say that I think what I got out of this film was seemingly different from what I'm reading others have. To me, My Dinner with Andre serves as a sort of antithesis to the ideas that The Matrix brought about, in that we need this escapism from our default selves, and it poses the idea that maybe taking the 'blue pill' isn't emblematic of cowardice. It's an embryonic version of what that symbol, and its counterpart, has contorted to mean today, and while My Dinner With Andre 's ideas of human connection and meaningful relationships remain a prominent feature of discourse, particularly in a world so much more imbued with technology than just an electric blanket, I feel as if it's, in actual fact, a sardonic evaluation of pseudo-intellectualism, wherein this rambling discussion between these peers is largely of little consequence in comparison to our insertion of ourselves into it. Much like how the waiters serving the food breaks the immersion of this back-and-forth, our gradual understanding that overanalysing human connection by drawing parallels to theatre, art, or science is perhaps more an exercise in self-aggrandisement than actual existentialism. It's a critique of all those who find the need to romanticise every aspect of their lives in order to feel fulfilled, where instead accepting one's current state of being shouldn't be seen as a failure of imagination or a surrender, but instead comes from a place of real acceptance. Andre Gregory's elaborate stories and Wallace Shawn's skeptical responses are ultimately two sides of the same coin- a carefully constructed dialogue that systematically dismantles both the grandiose spiritual quest for meaning and the defensive mundanity of accepting the hand you're dealt. My Dinner with Andre uses the guise of insightfulness to mask a pointed criticism of intellectual posturing, unravelling this ostensibly improvised performance into the meticulously choreographed artifice that it is.

Likely found this more palatable than my American counterparts who were no doubt inundated with the face of this deplorable man on their television screens for the better part of a decade. It's certainly interesting having a biopic released about a man currently at the peak of his, and likely anyone's, cultural relevancy- so many of these types of films navigate their central character's journey up until their death, or at least until some kind of tragic downfall spurred by a fatal flaw. But with The Apprentice, Abbasi uses this fatal flaw to fuel a parasitic relationship between mentor and mentee- Jeremy Strong's Roy Cohn and Sebastian Stan's Donald Trump. Stan progressively becomes more like the caricature that we're all more familiar with today as the film progresses, leeching his mannerisms, quote-unquote killer instinct, and malevolent worldview. It's a vampiric transformation, of which Stan embodies brilliantly and Strong mirrors even better, where Trump metaphorically consumes Roy Cohn's life essence, supplanting his mentor and leaving him as nothing more than a hollowed-out husk. While the film gets a little distracted in the second half at trying to solidify a basis for his ethos that extends to this day, it's initial focus on a power hungry scion desperate to outgrow his father's legacy is riveting. He then projects this goal onto his newfound surrogate paternal figure in Cohn, now desperate to prove himself only to then supersede him, ultimately revealing the consuming nature of ambition as a kind of rewarded cannibalism, that only leads to a collapse for those who get eaten along the way.

Films that effortlessly capture a place or a time tend to be my favourites. What Béla Tarr and Ágnes Hranitzky do so well with Werckmeister Harmonies isn't unlike what Michael Haneke achieves with The White Ribbon . A lingering bubbling of contempt that occasionally erupts to the surface with some inexplicable tragic event. Nobody knows why these things are happening, just that they are, so they attribute their cause to some arbitrary reason in order to regain some semblance of control in their despondent lives, only to find that in this place, and in this time, they never had any to begin with.
Glad I stayed to the end credits to see "No Jews were harmed in the making of this motion picture."

Doesn't quite match Yojimbo, but still brilliant. Toshiro Mifune is spectacular as always, and bounces off each character with such hilarity. The blocking is immaculate- it's Kurosawa what else would one expect- and it gets surprisingly poignant towards the end, even finally paying off the lack of blood with one violent burst in a way which is both cathartic and meaningful.

Still getting used to the vibe of silent films, but this was probably one of the more narratively straightforward ones I've seen so that helped. Also was my introduction to Naruse's filmography, so thought it best to begin with his earlier work.
Sometimes even my cold, dead heart is warmed.

Great stuff. Need to watch more of Eastwood's directorial efforts as they're certainly a blind spot for me. Love that this was more of a straightforward character study than a twisty-turny courtroom drama that I was expecting. Seems like Hoult's having quite the year- still need to see The Order and Nosferatu when it comes out, and I'm excited to see his Lex Luthor too.

Makes sense that this, or more accurately The Gift , was made as an accompaniment to a piece of music- a spectacular bit of work by Eiko Ishibashi by the way. Evil Does Not Exist serenely guides us through the facets of humanity, and how these fit together amidst the backdrop of nature. I don't think the abrupt ending, which is foreboded by the building disquietude and sudden ending of the aforementioned score throughout the film, is particularly unfounded, as from this growing ambience of thriller and what I could draw from the title Evil Does Not Exist , it was always going to come to some culmination of cynicism- it's just the form that this would take that was in question. For me, the title is saying that evil isn't an inherent trait, and it only occurs as a consequence of circumstance- a deer only attacks when it's gut-shot and feels like it has no other choice. It seems like this would make a good double feature with Perfect Days , with both films carrying this underlying backstory that never quite rises to the surface.
Came for that one underwater shot, stayed for all the rest- seriously one of the most visually impressive films I've seen. Mitchum is spectacular too.

Watching this as prep for Eggers' version, but this was great. The use of shadows was really cool. Can now finally understand the Hash-Slinging Slasher episode of Spongebob fully now. Might watch Herzog's version and maybe Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula too before.

Just as in Wuthering Heights , Robbie Ryan's handheld cinematography here is gorgeously intimate, capturing pockets of nature in such a serene way. Unfortunately that quality doesn't quite permeate into Bird thoroughly enough, with the most compelling moments of sincerity withheld to the periphery, notably Barry Keoghan's character, and Arnold instead tries to balance her trademark depiction of poverty with this bandaged ethereality. It's a departure in the sense that magical realism isn't something that's typical of these kinds of films, but it's almost not enough of one to where this feels like something groundbreaking.

Wasn't feeling it to begin with but as soon as John Wayne gets introduced it kicks it up a notch. Wanted to get more into westerns and thought this a good place to start- we'll see if I keep any sort of consistency in that regard; probably not.

A deplorable mess of a film that'll no doubt sweep awards here and there and earn itself a few Oscar nominations too. It's such a bonkers idea that you think if it fully leant into the camp of it all it might (a big might) just scrounge up enough juice on sheer gall alone to make a decent musical. But as soon as this gets remotely serious, it's frankly abhorrent. A cartel boss who transitions with the help of a criminal defense lawyer- don't even question the logistics there because they don't explain them- and it acts as a quasi-baptism, washing her sins away and allowing her to work for an NGO locating people missing as a result of drug-related crime. If you noticed the irony there, well you're one step ahead of Emilia Pérez . The music numbers are forgettable, poorly staged and lit, and they don't particularly advance the plot whatsoever- something that could be forgivable if they were actually enjoyable in any way. The only saving grace is Zoe Saldaña who you can tell is giving it her all, almost too much really, but the film is too loosely held together to make her attempts worthwhile.
Brando is ludicrously good in this, and everyone else is great too. Loved that the ending mirrors a closing curtain on a play, because so much of this does feel theatrical.
How is this the same guy that made Shame.

Such razor sharp dialogue, and brilliant use of shadows. One of the noirs I can definitely see myself rewatching because the pay off is so good. Only thing that annoyed me was that I thought there were a few holes in the murder plan, but didn't end up bothering me too much.

Wasn't too much a fan of this to begin with as I was mostly just confused, by design of course. But as this went on, I found myself more and more absorbed by this story. Gotta read Philip K. Dick's novel which I'd imagine would grab me even more, as I'm sure some of the gripping monologues in this were directly pulled from the book. Would love to see Linklater do even more of this kind of stuff again; Apollo 8 1/2 was pretty fun too.

Few of these pretty clearly better than others. Twins with Buscemi was good, the Cate Blanchett one where there's 2 Cate Blanchetts, RZA and GZA with Bill Murray (mostly because of RZA saying "You can trust us, Bill Murray" ), and the best one which was the Alfred Molina and Steve Coogan one- so awkward and funny, "I just want you to love me"

A thing that I read that I found interesting- which spurred me on to watching this tonight- was that in both this and In The Mood For Love , Wong Kar-wai said that the first things they shot were the sex scenes, so the actors could grasp some sort of baseline for how the relationship between the characters would be, without the ambiguity of longing or desire clouding the journey. With In The Mood For Love , the sex scene was cut, and with Happy Together , it's the first thing we see. I just thought it was a nice parallel that draws a sort of dichotomy between the two films, with each still holding that trademark feeling of yearning at their core. And Tony Leung is phenomenal in both.
One of those rom-coms where I prefer the dynamic between literally every other character than the main couple. Also appreciated the random Paul Giammati cameo.

Far too self-insert for my liking, and these leads, particularly Culkin's character, are frankly just too unlikable for this to work for me- and they hardly change or learn anything by the end anyway.

Scattered with individually powerful moments, but unfortunately this never quite works for me as a whole. Seeing as this was mostly a recount of a memory, propelled largely by Denis Lavant's introspective voiceover, I would have preferred if it had committed more decisively to being more disjointed and poetic, or more linear and cohesive, but instead it straddles the line between both, which makes it frustrating to connect with. Still though, Agnès Godard's cinematography here is stunning, and Denis' strive to capture a raw form of masculinity is commendable at the very least.
Ok I pull up.
So wonderfully authentic; from the way this is shot, to all the brilliant performances from a mostly first-timer cast. Domingo and Maclin are terrific.

Little torn by this one as it's commendably experimental in it's point-of-view styling- which takes a lot of getting used to if not just for how the dialogue sounds coming from behind the camera- but it just leaves me a little too cold for what's such a tragic story. The documentarian aspects of this are brilliant, and Ross really nails that home in the last 10 minutes, but when looking at Nickel Boys from a strictly narrative perspective, it becomes really hard to latch onto these characters when we only really see portions of what they're going through. Still, a super impressive debut, and landing a Best Picture nomination on your first go is some feat.

The bastardisation of a dream. I'd be hard pressed to describe Brady Corbet's 215-minute fiopic (fake biopic, I'm coining that now) as an epic. Sure, it feels large scale-an immigrant trying to find his feet in big America and taking on this gargantuan project, backed by Daniel Blumberg's underused, yet triumphant trumpet score- but really it's a personal story about artistry, and the ending really drives that home. Frankly, I'm surprised, especially in the epilogue and given the current climate, that there wasn't a more solidly didactic parallel made between the forcible displacement of Jews after WWII and the forcible displacement of Palestinians today. It seems like a natural misstep because much of this becomes less about the immigrant experience and a search for a place to call home, and more about the actual process of creation and what gets left behind. I'm not saying that's a story that shouldn't be told too, but it just ends up feeling less consequential by comparison. Although, there is something quite brilliant in the way Corbet suggests that immigrants are as vital a building block to modern day America as the literal building blocks of concrete László Tóth uses in his work. Guy Pearce's Van Buren, played like a spectacularly evil caricature, represents the capitalistic spoils of a war that decimated Tóth's home, and still his ego refuses him to turn his offer down; at first when he has nothing, and then again once he has everything he first wanted. He gets sold on one dream and loses another.

If the lack of the usual introductory Marvel fanfare was indicative of anything, it's how Captain America: Brave New World is a far cry from the thrill of the MCU's heyday, if that were ever a thing, where even its most loyal fans are cottoning on to the horribly edited action sequences and vacuous dialogue, to the point where the post-credits scene is yet another meaningless non-sequitur. Marvel tries its hand again at political thriller, after most recently the utter bore that was Secret Invasion , and once again falls flat on its face, although this time its cultural parallels are a little too on the nose- notably a hotheaded president and his Israeli right-hand. It all just feels like biding time as set-up for the next two Avengers movies, which just about everyone besides the execs agrees are coming out far too early.
Thought I'd make better use of my Apple TV Plus subscription and watch something other than Severance. Safe to say they need a far better catalogue of movies on there because most of it is trash.

film_key: Manila in the Claws of Light (1975)
review_clean: I often struggle to connect with films that are just so relentlessly depressing. And while Manila in the Claws of Light certainly falls into that, it also presents this dreamlike escape as a representation of what the characters aspire to. Without that, it would simply be bleak realism under the Marcos regime- not too dissimilar to how Lav Diaz explores it in a remote village in From What Is Before- but instead in a bustling city, where its residents are forced to find any way to make a living, without ever truly living.

Great production design, and stellar vocal performances from Erivo and Grande, but god if this doesn't look fuck ugly. So many scenes with such great sets ruined by a cacophony of back lighting and listless camerawork- just imagine if Paul King or someone had directed this instead. Also, this is far too long, like way too long, especially for just a part one, and focuses on mostly all the wrong stuff. Still, liked this more than I thought I would have, mainly due to that main duo.

Not gonna pretend I know much about Bob Dylan or his music, but A Complete Unknown brushes over not only most of his characterisation, but also just about every major American event across the sixties from the Cuban Missile Crisis to the Civil Rights Movement just in case you forgot what period you were watching. The reason Walk the Line worked- at least narratively- was because Johnny Cash's story was so much more tangible, but when faced with something, or rather someone, more nebulous, Mangold finds himself unable to draw a singular throughline that the audience can latch onto, and it'd probably have been best had this been told from Edward Norton's Pete Seeger's perspective instead. Still, if you're looking for something that's essentially a montage of Dylan's music, (I hadn't listened to much of his music at all prior to this, but rest assured I will be now) then you'll probably enjoy yourself.
Yeah... no-one's doing it like this.

How does one follow up to Parasite ? Well director Bong Joon-ho is no stranger to sci-fi creature features- see The Host- so Mickey 17 isn't so much of a departure, especially now that it's his third English language film. It felt very evocative of Starship Troopers , although the heavy-handed satire sometimes verged on being a detriment, mostly because whenever we're focused on Pattinson, it's an absolute romp, and whenever we veer away from him, the film feels less assured. As such, it loses some of its steam in the back half, where it definitely feels like this has been chopped down, but still remains a fun enough time.
Looks great, but it's also totally bizarre that this doesn't really aim to tell any coherent story. Dreamlike in its vibe, but also the fact that it almost put me to sleep.
So good. Definitely something that lends itself to lots of rewatches. Can't wait to watch more of Araki's stuff.
Think I know who Luigi Mangione's next two targets should be.

Spectacular editing and camerawork here- truly a masterclass. Took a little time to figure out what was what considering the blistering pace with which some of the events are explained, but in retrospect, Z is ultimately a straightforward story whose message is brilliantly transferable to similar regimes stretching even to the modern day, and remains emblematic of a culture that seeks to silence rather than empower. "Any similarity to actual events or persons living or dead is not coincidental. It is INTENTIONAL."

Largely a generic reshuffle of themes that have been dealt with before, and far better- see Ex Machina . Sophie Thatcher is good, but ultimately Companion doesn't really think hard enough about what it's trying to say, and ends up making a few points that feel antithetical to what it's trying to accomplish.

Enjoyed this a fair bit. Love all three of the actresses, especially Olsen. Definitely feels like it misses the trick in actually developing the relationship between these sisters (really can't believe they didn't share a joint at any point throughout this) rather than just airing their issues out, and the dad reveal in the final act doesn't quite work for me, but it's wonderfully shot, and purposefully theatrical, which is always appreciated.

Gorgeously shot by Dong Jinsong, who also did Bi Gan's Long Day's Journey Into Night (and is shooting his upcoming film Resurrection too), so it's no surprise really that this looks as good as it does. A bit like Decision to Leave, mostly because of its noir trappings, although notably less romantic and more bleak in its outlook. Diao Yinan crafts a mystery that often feels less about uncovering the truth and more about confronting how deeply it has corroded the people involved. Liao Fan's world-weary cop doesn't chase redemption so much as drunkenly stumble through its absence, and embarks on an infatuation that feels equally as enigmatic as it does desperate. It's certainly a slow burn, but there's something hypnotic about watching the mundane and the horrific quietly bleed into each other in neon-lit nightscapes and snow-covered streets, even though it doesn't quite culminate in a way that feels entirely rewarding.

Can definitely see why some people find this indulgent, but it seems to me that that is squarely by design. The Great Beauty is a film that plays like a journey through memories, with each scene just sort of happening without any explanation as to how we got there. It's a confrontation of mortality in such a way that I haven't felt since I watched Eternity and a Day - a film I largely preferred to this, mind you- where our protagonist is meandering not because they're lost, but because they're searching- perhaps for meaning, perhaps for feeling, or maybe just for the courage to feel again, like they once did.
Shoots for juvenile humour and shock value instead of anything substantial. Would have worker much better if it was just a full version of the opening before the time skip.

A raucous and riotous romp that Ryan Coogler directs the hell out of, propelled by an unrelenting electric guitar score by Göransson. Partly inspired by Bigelow's Near Dark , and partly a kaleidoscopic purview of Black America, played out as a salaciously charged Western-Musical hybrid that pulses with style at every syncopated dancefloor stomp and reverberating gunshot. Coogler weaves genre like gospel, and intertwines folklore with soul, rage, and rapture- crafting a film that swings, albeit sometimes messily, between the sacred and the profane. It loses steam in a rushed third act, mostly because of the poor pacing leading up to that point and a few askew narrative decisions, but it's unmistakably alive.

People pretending Pacino is bad here need a reality check. Sure it's not in his top five (hell, maybe even top 10) performances, but he's so good. Not really what I expected from this if I'm honest; mostly because I was just extrapolating from the title. Classic Hollywood fare, and there's nothing wrong with that every now and again. It's over the top and it's melodramatic, but it's fun.

film_key: Seeking a Friend for the End of the World (2012)
review_clean: Total mess tonally but those last 5 minutes certainly hit.

Not so much the return to form that many were touting this to be; if anything this should be the baseline standard for what these films should be. Mostly surface level explorations of guilt and trauma thinly threaded through the narrative using Pullman's Sentry, which also leads to far too much retrospective exposition- a symptom again of having to reintroduce characters that some viewers have met before and others haven't. Still, Thunderbolts* boasts some of the better action sequences in the MCU since at least Shang Chi, with an opening birds-eye sequence that overshadows anything that comes after. It may inspire hope for following films in the franchise which choose to do their own thing, but it's still painfully redolent of the issues that can arise as byproducts of the format.

In the middle of a first time Mad Men watch, so it was cool to see Hamm and Slattery in some other roles together here. Definitely need more of these short, funny, B-movie, detective movies around- nice spin on the noir genre that somehow feels fresh too.

"Have you ever shuffled faces like cards, hoping to find one that lies somewhere, just over the edge of your memory? The one you've been waiting for?" Looks stunning and feels it too. A story of unrequited love told through the transience of memory. Keep saying this but I need to watch more noirs.

A totally spellbinding film that, if it doesn't grip you with its story- which is likely because it's as bare bones as bare bones gets, and Hou almost commendably makes no effort for The Assassin to be the palatable wuxia film the audience would expect from its title if they weren't already familiar with its director- then it almost certainly grabs your attention with its stunning on-location work. Similarly to Flowers of Shanghai , it pains me to rate this a 3.5 because I just simply cannot connect with this story, as much as I was mesmerised by it.
It's tragic that I saw both the remake and a Rick and Morty parody before I saw this.
Feels like it would have been far better had Tony Scott directed this.
