A fascinating subversion of the revenge tale that makes use of some astonishing camerawork and opts for silence over a soundtrack to culminate in a film that's as broodingly suspenseful as it is restrained.

Absolutely delightful. Not sure if you can quite emulate the dynamic of the real father-daughter duo because it's just so superb here, as are both Ryan and Tatum O'Neal- been said a million times but probably the best child actor performance ever. EDIT- Did not know about Ryan O'Neal being an a terrible father irl. Misfire there from me.
A transcendental fable of love and loss. Beyond words.

Right up my alley- so quirky and clever with its silly, slapstick humour and dream sequences. The colours and the direction are so perfect, and while it slows down in the second half, I almost always had a smile on my face. Need to watch more Étaix.

Fine. Jack O'Connell probably the highlight, but I don't buy most of this- as if the cops would ever let them leave that studio and walk into the streets with a bomb. If you want a better corporate thriller with Clooney, just watch Michael Clayton instead.

Reminded me a bit of Hamaguchi's Evil Does Not Exist. Don't think it entirely knows what its thesis is, nor how to realise it, but if I said that these weren't some of the most jaw-droppingly gorgeous images I've ever seen, I'd be lying.
Viggo Mortensen with probably my favourite performance from a Cronenberg movie? It's up there for sure.

"This film could be called 'The Children of Marx and Coca-Cola.' Understand what you will." Socialism. Capitalism. Revolution. Conformity. Masculine. Feminine. Godard captures a shift in zeitgeist effortlessly here-through references to events, pop-culture, and an evaluation of the psyche of the young generation that were evolving through the culture that shapes them. He gauges a sense for the dissonance between ideals and lived reality, through a fragmented narrative as systematically broken as the characters themselves.

"And you- still a clown?" "Yes, of course." A work of genius. Yoyo doesn't simply employ slapstick- it's built on it, layered with joke upon joke like a Rube Goldberg machine that pays homage to both Fellini and the silent era. Everything is a set-up for the next gag, and Étaix choreographs it all with remarkable precision.
James Spader is so good in this.

Wonderfully shot, and the vengeful 'personification of Death' trope works well in what's essentially an antithesis to a classic Western (still need to see more), but this severely lacks a character to root for, since all of them are either degenerates or victims.

"I just don't want to do it anymore." "Do what?" "Be your friend." "Then I'll be your friend." A perfect representation of male friendships and masculinity and the toxicity that can spawn from both, told using two real life friends. Falk is excellent, Cassavetes is outstanding.

Not exactly innovative, but a real-time, mostly single-location, tightly-paced approach to a saturated sub-genre was probably the best way to go. Doesn't provide anything new with its thesis, but boasts enough sheer viscera and tactile sound design to coast through well enough.
It's almost funny how many times this does the confrontation/narrow escape trope. As a follow up to Near Dark, this is pretty disappointing honestly, especially since it starts off pretty well.

As much as most of us wouldn't want to admit it, the idea of procreation is at least a little bit selfish. The feeling that you want some part of you to succeed and live on once you've died is an inherently egocentric ideal. Jenkins acknowledges this but doesn't condemn it, nor does she condemn any of these characters, which is what makes Private Life so great. Reminiscent of Baumbach with Marriage Story or Mistress America , particularly with the literary, intellectual New York milieu, but different in the sense that it's less concerned with wit or self-laceration, and very rarely succumbs to melodrama. Hahn, Giammati, and Carter as the central trio are all wonderful. Certainly an under-seen gem.
Feels like this took the most boring possible route for a concept this wild.

A woman ambling aimlessly through life, cornered by passivity, and, as a result, gets taken advantage of at every turn, while doing nothing to combat it. Fuel to her own fire of slow self-erasure, drifting through an indifferent world as the camera follows with the same indifference. Barbara Loden is spectacular; shame she never made another film.
Man, I miss Succession.

Feels a little like an overeager overcorrection of the character assassination that was Zack Snyder's interpretation of the Man of Steel (I still have no willingness to watch ZSJL ). James Gunn clearly wants to start his universe off with a bang and looks for inspiration in the past, where his now rivalling studio machine, the MCU, got its start with The Avengers. But where he fails is that he lifts the made-for-TV sheen that Whedon plastered over the 2012 film, and misses with what should have been a sleek and simple clean slate, inundating the audience with character after character, and location after location like a bad comic book. Some may be pleased by this trigger-happy approach, but what we've learnt from a barrage of Marvel misfires is that comic book movies are not comic books, and therefore can't follow the same narrative rules as one. That being said, Corenswet fits the part like a glove, and his chemistry with Brosnahan's Lois Lane is undeniable- although her character is surprisingly unsubstantial to the plot given just how much of the film she's in. But for me, Nick Hoult steals the show as a maniacal Lex Luthor, tackling his motivations with a nailed-on clarity that felt desperately needed. Nevertheless, the heart is there, and that's one place you haven't really been able to fault Gunn over his projects, and I'm cautiously optimistic to see what he has in store.
Feels reminiscent of Lowery's A Ghost Story , and almost certainly more a domestic drama than horror. Just wish it had stuck to that rather than trying to switch it up in the latter half.
Actually enjoyed this far more than I thought I would. Lots of slapstick humour which is always appreciated.

Was never really a big fan of the original Gladiator which is surprising considering how much of a Ridley Scott apologist I can be, but this naturally did little to nothing for me. I don't buy a single one of these character relationships, and all of it just felt like a rehash of a better movie- which is exactly what this is.

Hard-pressed to call this 'deceptively straightforward' when in reality it just feels simply straightforward. Feels less like an analysis of digital malaise as a spiritual successor to Pulse, and more a light commentary on grind culture and the pursuit of escaping the monotony of a 9 to 5. Seems a bit too reverse engineered from that final scene, and while I commend his efforts to tackle modern day issues, this is probably my least favourite of Kurosawa's work thus far.

For the first time in a long time, an actually stylistically assured aesthetic is delivered in the MCU, with retro-futuristic production design that builds a world that feels unique and tactile. It comes as a welcome surprise that Marvel's first family is met with so much adoration out of the gate, although that doesn't last long once they're confronted with an impossible choice. This initial set up in the first act, notably montaging its way through the already well known origin story, is a fantastic (had to get it in there) introduction to what should have set the tone for the rest of the film, but unfortunately it really doesn't. Not only do the aesthetics get laid to waste, particularly in a rather catastrophic third act where the budget seemed to have run dry, but the dynamic between the characters that are a part of this so-called model family is nowhere to be seen. Each one gets their own, albeit shallow, set of motivations, but they never coalesce in the way that they should. It becomes less a realisation of a comic book and more a realisation of a storyboard, wherein everything is so surface level and rushed, including the mythos of two of Marvel's most awesome antagonists in Silver Surfer and Galactus, that it becomes more a pitch meeting for Avengers: Doomsday , with even diehard fans bracing for a cataclysm of cosmic proportions.

One of the most batshit insane blockbusters I think I've seen in recent years. Parts Children of Men , parts Shaun of the Dead, and parts Mortal fucking Kombat . Danny Boyle infuses his 2000s style all over this, with quick cuts and jarring edits that feel just like the original film. Going to be crazy to see where Nia DaCosta takes this next, especially considering that ending which I'm sure will fly over the heads of much of the American audience.

With Weapons , Cregger sets out to elucidate and give credence to the deep-seated fears of the American public. A film set in a small-town suburban school- named as it is- it's hard not to instantly think of school shootings. And while the film doesn't hold your hand like much of modern horror does, this idea, along with an atmosphere of collective trauma and survivor's guilt, is viscerally apparent. He builds suspense to a sharp point and pops the subsequent bubble in a brilliant clash between horror and comedy reminiscent of his first feature, Barbarian, but instead traverses the gory punchline through non-linear, interconnected vignettes of the ensemble, which, granted, each feel like they withhold the catharsis a bit too much with conflicting climactic cutaways, but also bring to the surface a demonstrable culmination of shared guilt and grief.
Where's Ice Cube?

film_key: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998)
review_clean: A trippy road trip that meanders through Vegas with a dizzying concoction of paranoia and anxiety. A deconstruction of the sensationalism behind the War on Drugs, and the rise of disillusionment in pursuit of a contorted American Dream. Depp is great, but del Toro is extraordinary. "I was right in the middle of a fucking reptile zoo, and somebody was giving booze to these goddamn things. Won't be long now before they tear us to shreds.

A clever spin on the jaded, disillusioned cop stereotype, and in fact, a spin on stereotypes from a range of different ethnic and societal groups. Mamet doesn't point any fingers per se, but instead begs questions as to whether any of these communities are as complicit in their own pitfalls as the systems that are meant to be there to protect them. Prescient today absolutely, although Mamet's stance on Zionism has notably changed from the relative neutrality he shows here- there's an ambivalence from how he displays the grooming of a disenfranchised Jewish man who'd sooner say he's a cop than a Jew, to the alienation and lack of assimilation of the Jewish people in America- to a more staunch supporter of the regime.

PTA allergic to making a bad film it seems. I mean, what a debut this is. Not only looks gorgeous, but making a mellow, neo-noir-esque thriller with this cast, just a year after Casino came out- awesome. Feels the most Tarantino of PTAs filmography if that makes sense, but deftly more restrained.

"I think time is rushing by, and I haven't accomplished anything." A gallery of banalities curated in such a painterly way from Andersson, with each stroke of grey and beige journeying us through vignettes about the absurdity of life, as has been a common through line across the films of his I've seen thus far. It's sterile and forlorn, but there's still this overarching feeling of optimism that Andersson is trying to convey to us; an insistence to float above the misery and despair that edges us ever closer to an apocalyptic apathy, and choose to feel instead.

A serviceable whodunnit that will no doubt run riot with all the British mums and dads- wouldn't be surprised to hear of this hitting records of some kind on Netflix UK. Frankly, this should be far more fun than it is; it focuses on all the most boring parts of the mystery, and the so-called club don't really work together as a team at all. Also... Chris Columbus directed this?!

A confrontation between traditionalism and modernism, where the dubious intentions of the intruding crew hold a mirror up to Kiarostami's own practices as a filmmaker. So much of the film hides in shadows- characters and events withheld to the periphery while we focus on the deceptive simplicity of our protagonist, following him as he meanders through the mundanities of this small, secluded Iranian village. It breathes with absence that shapes into this atmosphere of a cinematic afterlife, where the loss of purpose reveals meaning rather than obfuscating it. It is fitting, then, that The Wind Will Carry Us borrows its name from a line of poetry, because the film itself feels so much like the visual manifestation of one.

As seems to be the general consensus, a pretty woeful first act that had me worried that this was going to be composed of all the same gauche, washed-out stylisations of the rest of Apple TV Plus' catalogue, Killers of the Flower Moon notwithstanding. But it really does pick up after that, with Spike's energy transferred into the camera and its movement. He, and perhaps Guadagnino, seem to be the only directors with the gall to remake such cinematic heavyweights, so while this had practically zero chance of coming close to the masterpiece that is Kurosawa's film, you still have to commend the effort. Highest 2 Lowest can feel preachy at times, but that's likely a byproduct of Spike's overcorrection to making this feel as rooted in the modern world as possible (if Apple's constant product placement didn't do that already). The hills of Yokohama are replaced by the skyscrapers of New York City, and Mifune's sybaritic shoemaker Kingo Gondo is switched out for Washington's music magnate David King, who, much like in the original film, finds himself between a rock and a hard place in a case of mistaken identity in a kidnapping. It's quite brilliant that our first confrontation between King and the perpetrator is between the glass of a music studio, not only because it's A$AP Rocky on the other side, but because of the parallels to how High and Low comes to a conclusion, which is mirrored again later on. It's not quite encapsulating nor incisive enough to consider it a worthwhile remake; though I suppose there's no value in weighing art in that way, which is what Spike's thesis seems to be by the end of the film.

film_key: We're All Going to the World's Fair (2021)
review_clean: Ever so slightly bare-bones for me, but if the scale tipped too far the other way I'd be more annoyed, so I guess this is fine. There's definitely a strive to capture specific epochs through Schoenbrun's two films, with this one tackling adolescence and internet challenges like a warped version of Eighth Grade, so while it can feel like a short film's worth of ideas stretched into feature length, but it still vividly evokes early 2010s net-culture, fused with the singular, isolating atmosphere of the pandemic. Sort of the antithesis of a coming-of-age story, where the periphery of the era feels thick with a melancholic nostalgia.

Save for my mistake with Fassbinder's World on a Wire , I haven't logged a TV show on Letterboxd since I started my account at the end of 2021. It's something I decided early and stuck to, a bit like how I decided to write a review for every feature-length and short film I watch (something I've considered abandoning in part on more than multiple occasions). Having said all of that, it seemed apt, especially with David Lynch's passing earlier this year, that Twin Peaks be the thing that becomes an exception to that rule, and I'm logging the pilot here as proxy for the whole first 2 seasons of the show. I doubt I'll fit all my thoughts nor articulate them as properly as I would like to, but I'll try. I really didn't know what to think going into the show. Apart from what I've experienced across Lynch's other work, I really had no reference for what this would be like, which is surprising since I carry little hints or spoilers for just about every popular TV show I haven't yet seen- the downside of having a good memory is that these are near impossible to gaslight myself into forgetting. But I didn't really have that for Twin Peaks , and so I began quite surprised of just how straightforward it seemed at first, having expected Lynch's surrealism right from the jump. But I suppose that's what makes it all that affecting when it does arrive; credit to him and Frost for figuring that out. Not only is that balance met perfectly, but also in conjunction with earnest, heartfelt, funny, thrilling, and mysterious moments across the whole show, an indelible score by Badalamenti, and Kyle MacLachlan, who knocks it out of the park in the lead role. It certainly loses a little steam in parts of Season Two after Laura Palmer's arc sort of concludes- as much as it can with her ghost haunting the narrative and every facet of the town and its people- but it brings it back around with an ending that's just so remarkably bleak (and frustratingly 'incomplete', though I can't imagine how much worse that feeling would have been in the 90s) it's impressive in and of itself. Nothing exists quite like Twin Peaks , only in pastiches and homage that have come after, and I'm quite certain that nothing quite like it will ever exist again. It's a frightening and comforting thought, though I suppose it'll be an exciting feeling to actually be there for when a show comes close to emulating this balance of heart and spirit, if that time ever comes. Now onto Fire Walk With Me and The Return. I'll probably review The Return and then not review another TV show again. I did a few on Serializd but the app kinda sucks so I never actually stayed up to date with any of my TV show watches, nor do I plan to. "I'll see you again in 25 years."

film_key: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me (1992)
review_clean: Equally devastating in its sadness as it is tragically horrific, Fire Walk With Me illuminates what we had only known about the last moments of Laura Palmer's life through secondhand accounts, piecing together the gutting details we previously understood only in part. It constructs monsters and otherworldly spaces, both to externalize and to bear the unbearable weight of suffering. Every connection is transactional, whether forged in love or malice, because even in her most unfathomable pain, even kindness could feel like a burden, and in retreating from these rare gestures of care, Laura was, in her own tragic way, trying to shield those who loved her from what she felt was the inescapable, contagious weight of her suffering. Sheryl Lee is transcendental.

Now finally completed Paul Thomas Anderson's filmography, and as I suspected, not a bad film among the lot. It's scintillatingly impressive how much he keeps you in stride here with a plot that's basically (intentionally so, of course) incomprehensible. One of those ones that you just have to let wash over you than try to grab onto anything in particular. Knockout performances all round, Phoenix and Brolin in particular.

I mean, talk about capturing the zeitgeist. Paul Thomas Anderson is invariably one of the best and most consistent filmmakers working today, well within the discussion of being top of his class of contemporaries, and so when you heard that Warner Brothers was giving him a $150 million stimulus cheque to make his new film, you knew that you just had to be in the cinema to watch it. Opening with barbed wire-encased detention centres holding entire families of people feels already horrifyingly redolent of today's America, until a tacitly placed 16-year time jump shows us that nothing has really changed at all. In One Battle After Another, revolutions are as cyclical as the word itself, and the people that enact them are tired and worn, endlessly striving for a change that never comes. But PTA doesn't leave us in this pit of nihilism, no. Instead, surged forward almost without pause by yet another remarkable score from Jonny Greenwood, he takes us on this wild ride as up and down as the film's wondrous concluding set piece and sets forth an almost rallying war-cry for future generations to remain steadfast and carry the mantle of 'revolutionary' forwards. It's anarchic to the tune of Fight Club , but less a reflection on toxic masculinity and more on the generic delusions of grandeur and circle-jerk inflations of ego of white nationalists. Penn plays a chauvinistic caricature of every right-wing, roid-raged reprobate rolled into one- and it's one of the funniest performances in years. Chase Infiniti is a revelation and a half, and DiCaprio- you almost forget just how good he is until you watch him on screen again, and he's just magnetic, adding another triumph to PTA's repertoire of iconic protagonists- and the first one to get a Fortnite skin! Fingers crossed for Daniel Plainview next: the pickaxe is already on theme.

"Did I put too much sauce on that?" Instant movie star stuff from Aaron Pierre- what a commanding performance. Think this starts super strong, but flails as it comes to an end. Has to stick to its guns a little more and be the Western it's trying to be, as it spends too much time trying to prove what we already know, although at least it does so with a charged pace.

"Why are you crying? These are not your memories." One of those films where whatever you derive from it, whatever message relays itself to you through the frequencies, is precisely what it's about. Proof of the maxim that the filmmaker's intention is among the least important parts of the experience for the viewer.
John Goodman is so good here. It really feels like I haven't seen him in a film in a while, although I just saw that he's going to be in Iñárritu's new film which should be interesting.

How can the path to hell be paved with good intentions, if those intentions are nothing but vanity disguised as virtue? Nuri Bilge Ceylan's Winter Sleep wrestles with this question across the span of over three hours, setting us down in the vast, breathtaking landscapes of Anatolia only to draw us inward, away from freedom and into confinement. The wide horizons that promise release are constantly withheld, replaced instead by rooms thick with words- long, piercing conversations that trap the characters as surely as the snow and stone around them.

A stripped-back thriller with a good breakout performance from Jennifer Lawrence and a great one from John Hawkes. A bit too 'this place and then this place and then this place' for me- you feel with low budget indies like this they should just focus on a handful of locations and then the scenery.

Could see people absolutely hating this- I mean, even I'm not fully convinced Sono isn't some kind of pervert from watching his films. But there's just no way you predict where this ends up from where it starts- and I'm not sure any other director does it quite like him. It's depraved and darkly comedic, and doesn't let up once it gets going.

"Maybe they're always been with us... those things out there. Maybe they love it... seeing us hate each other, watching us kill each other off, feeding on our own cold fuckin' hearts..." Doesn't flow as slickly as some of Carpenter's other work, but seriously who cares with execution like this? Brilliant imagery, pulpy one-liners, and messaging that's still prevalent to this day. And what an awesome fight scene.

Feel like I'm on the other end of the spectrum to most as I greatly preferred this to Asteroid City , and it's likely my favourite Wes Anderson film since The Grand Budapest Hotel. Benicio is always fantastic, and the father-daughter relationship actually gets me invested in this story, compared to the sterility of his last two films. It's still a little too distant for me, but it's certainly the most fun one of Wes' films has felt in a while, and it hardly needs to be said, but it looks sensational.

Assuredly one of the most potent and viscerally effective horror movies of all time. If the first half of intense claustrophobia doesn't get you, then the monsters certainly will; a twist I was aware of, but that certainly didn't make it any less haunting. Also didn't know just how gruesome this got-truly an uncomfortable experience. You'll never catch me doing any cave bullshit like this.

One of Scorsese's bigger films, definitely a little long but much of this is so impressive, especially in the first act, that it almost doesn't matter. Need to see Howard Hughes' films now, naturally.

Watched the extended cut of this. Likely the most cohesive narrative across Malick's films I've seen thus far, not that that was something I ever really needed when I was watching them. Just a gorgeous film on all fronts. A reversal from the discovery of a 'new world' from one perspective, to a contortion of that discovery from another. Questions whether love is an innate product of nature, or a garden we can sow and nurture and tend through the passing of time.

film_key: O-Bi, O-Ba: The End of Civilization (1985)
review_clean: In Szulkin's third vision of apocalypse, the zombified remnants of humanity shuffle through a decaying concrete warren, sustained by a weaponised myth of salvation. Hope itself becomes the virus- a self-replicating fiction that keeps despair at bay, a narrative that spurs a narrative. O-Bi, O-Ba stands as another bleak, fascinating entry in his tetralogy, a grimy, desolate meditation on belief at the end of the world.

About as bland and uninspired past a riveting first act as it gets. Who thought it was a good idea to repeat the climax not once, but two more times without any real change to the context? I prefer my propaganda with a much healthier dose of fun, please, Ms. Bigelow- see Top Gun: Maverick.
Makes you think, "How the hell is this ever going to come together?" at the start, and then proceeds to come together in the most breathtakingly exhilarating way.

The Long Walk feels hopelessly hamstrung by the era of YA novel adaptations from the early 2010s- the likes of The Hunger Games (not surprised to then see that Lawrence had directed the bulk of that series) and The Maze Runner - adopting their same self-serious bleakness without a trace of the cultural bite that such stories need to resonate. It's so packed full of stretches of didactic dialogue about the failings of society that it forgets to actually engage with them in any meaningful way, thematically or cinematically.

"You thought the 19th century was the glorious age of Imperialism? Wait until you see the 21st century." Happy birthday to the master Edward Yang. Certainly gone too soon- can only wonder what films he'd have made if he were still alive today. Been apprehensive to watch another one of his films because it just means I have one less to watch for the first time. Spectacular as always; probably his most accessible work, certainly his funniest. Believe I only have A Confucian Confusion left of his features.

A fly buzzing, a dog barking, a baby crying- the ambient noise of disintegration, channeled through a career-best performance from Jennifer Lawrence, whose fully committed approach to the role is matched only by the singular vision of one of today's most distinctive directors, Lynne Ramsay. Die My Love is messy- purposefully and pridefully so- but messy nonetheless. A wanton spill of internal struggle poured out into the external world. It's not so much a straightforward examination of postpartum depression as it is a fierce amalgam of emotion, madness, and raw, unfettered humanity. It calls to mind A Woman Under the Influence , with that same collision of love and frailty. But where Cassavetes observed from within the trembling walls of a home, Ramsay seems to tear through them. Though both depict the claustrophobia of domesticity, Rasmay's gaze is more primal, suffused with a fevered intensity that feels perpetually on the verge of rupture. But this very fever, this deliberate collapse of form, comes at the cost of the sustained, aching empathy Cassavetes so potently achieved. It is a bold, unrestrained work- of that there is no question- but its rawness is its beauty and its limitation alike.
Probably the most affected I've been by one of Altman's films so far- adore how he moves the camera here. Sissy Spacek is tremendous.

Antonioni's eye for composition is masterful, but this largely didn't work for me. A vague look at the insular disconnect of the bourgeoisie, with allusions to the ills capitalism that never feel explored because we focus on a romance that I never really bought. A lot of people seem to love the ending of this, but that seemed to be a summary of everything I didn't like about the film. In actual fact, I thought the inverse: the opening was one of the best I've ever seen-loved the visual storytelling and the isolated mood it sets up, but it never really maintains it.

film_key: If I Had Legs I'd Kick You (2025)
review_clean: For all intents and purposes, If I Had Legs I'd Kick You (and yes, I'm still hung up on this year's aversion to commas- Die My Love being another offender) is a horror movie. Like Lynne Ramsay's film, it makes use of jarring audiovisual flourishes to plunge us into the mind of a mother on the brink, hemming us in with suffocating close-ups and anxiety-inducing psychedelia, similarly all anchored by a superb lead performance- Best Actress race this year will be a good one. But despite this, the film ultimately feels a bit gimmicky- and, frankly, a little safe. Making Rose Byrne's character a therapist is narratively too convenient; the hole-in-the-ceiling metaphor is too on the nose; and the barrage of trippy sounds and visuals- particularly the 'not seeing the daughter until the end' part- ends up feeling like a shortcut rather than an earned way of making us feel those same emotions organically.

And what if I said this was Berger's best film yet? Admittedly, not a high bar, but I think this one's getting the vitriol that should have been directed at Conclave and All Quiet on the Western Front. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, and should be unquestionably more fun than it is- how this isn't chock full of sight gags and physical comedy I have no idea, because Colin Farrell is certainly capable of it- but it looks great, and the story of a sweaty, degenerate gambler taking on Macau is pretty interesting, especially when it's under 2 hours long. I do seem to have a certain affinity towards films of this ilk ( Uncut Gems, Win It All etc.), so perhaps it shouldn't be a surprise that this worked for me, and I kinda do want to visit Macau now. Maybe I should gamble my life savings.
Pretty charming. Channing Tatum's charisma makes this work and Kirsten Dunst is always great. Derek Cianfrance may be the most consistently 7/10 guy going.

"In life, far from the motherland. In death, returning to the motherland. Both life and death are governed by destiny." Difficult in the sense that this is so antithetical to the typical historical drama in that it does nothing to educate you of the tragedies of post-colonial Taiwan, and instead shows everything solely through secondary effects-fragments of conversation, sudden disappearances, rumours, or the moments left hanging at the end of scenes. Having now read about the historical context-the 228 Massacre, and the 38 years of authoritarian rule under martial law, including the prohibition against even speaking about these events-the film's approach becomes far more legible. Hou Hsiao-hsien using the device of Tony Leung's deaf and mute character as a symbol of this censorship is brilliant, especially when Taiwan became such a melting pot of different languages that even people who could talk couldn't find the words to communicate. A City of Sadness exists in a time where even writing messages on paper could be seen as a minor act of rebellion. It's a historical film that refuses to historicise, a political film that speaks in the only way it knows how after being silenced for so long, and Hou shows how people lived inside the aftermath.
Very glad I missed the majority of Twitter discourse about this one.

film_key: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring (2003)
review_clean: Obviously gorgeous location work but this resolutely did not work for me. A faux-profound message and a parabolic narrative that I ended up finding rather obnoxious. Probably silly to say, but had this been made like 50 years earlier, I probably would have enjoyed it a lot more.
Mike Leigh just gets it man: so very real, acerbic, and hilarious. Marianne Jean-Baptiste is phenomenal- should have been a shoo-in for the Oscar- best performance of 2024, perhaps the decade.
Josh O'Connor's a fucking star.

It's no coincidence that both this and One Battle After Another depict a flailing disillusionment with authority. In Bugonia, that loss of faith curdles into an exasperated cynicism, gesturing at systems of power it no longer believes in but can't quite escape. It points its satire upwards but recognises that the consequences are always borne by those at the bottom, and so unlike Paul Thomas Anderson's film that hopefully footnotes the idea that life is a cyclical fight against the powers that be, Lanthimos takes an approach more in line with him and his films, and lets the closing sequences quietly portend a bleaker, more absurdist view of human struggle, in a way that recalls the deadpan melancholy of Roy Andersson instead.

Seen people saying that Baumbach is far too young to be doing a career retrospective, especially one so very 'love of cinema', and I'm not sure I entirely disagree. If the obscured quote from Sylvia Plath that opens the film is indicative of anything, it's that Jay Kelly doesn't exactly know what its message is. There's far too much 'throw enough shit at the wall and see what sticks' here for something that's essentially a trite version of The Great Beauty , and Baumbach shockingly tries to nail down line after line of profound dialogue, which was a trait that seemed to come so naturally in his earlier work.

Unlikely to convert any non-believers, and James Cameron remains utterly unapologetic about his shortcomings. Still, those of us who have placed our faith equally in both Eywa and him know exactly what we're in for. Fire and Ash delivers another immersive return to Pandora, where cinematic virtuosity once again outpaces narrative invention, and spectacle is asked to do the heavy lifting- and lift it does. Cameron no longer has the advantage of time in his arsenal to reinvent the medium as he once did, and with technological gains necessarily more incremental, he pivots toward his most honed gift, an unerring instinct for blockbuster mechanics, to craft an experience that's as heightened as heightened gets.

Just some of the best dialogue you're ever likely to hear. I mean, there's having your finger on the pulse, and there's having your finger simultaneously on the pulse of every successive decade, stretching from the 70s to now. Sensational. Would make an incredible double feature with Videodrome.

film_key: Now You See Me: Now You Don't (2025)
review_clean: Like a shitty version of the Escape Room movies mixed with a shitty version of the Mission: Impossible movies. Genuinely think this could have been written in an afternoon.
Pretty cute, largely due to Elizabeth Olsen being endlessly watchable. An eternity in any reality seems like torture to me though.
Merry Christmas!

Pretty much the same masturbatory, 'refusal to be the butt of the joke' stuff from Allen, and yet this is still terrific. It's always an impressive feat when you can immediately recognise the bits and bobs of inspiration that other films have pulled from another, and that happens multiple times here. And I always love films that make a place feel like a character.

film_key: A Matter of Life and Death (1946)
review_clean: Gets a tad tangential with the courtroom debates on England vs America, but it's still one of the most impressive technical feats I've ever seen. My first of Powell & Pressburger, excited to watch more.
This may be the worst offender since Wicked for soiling its enchanting production design with lifeless camerawork and a woefully sluggish narrative. A slog, frankly.

A pretty decent espionage thriller that works best when Ahmed is the taciturn and enigmatic "man behind the curtain" rather than the muscle, yet remains sharp and tightly edited enough to be an enjoyable watch. Best served with cheese, wine, and various cold meats, which my mum and I indulged in. Happy New Year all!

Runs along the same lines as Uncut Gems and Good Time , naturally, but what I've found myself ruminating on is what separates Marty Mauser from the grimy, Machiavellian protagonists of those films. While Robert Pattinson's Connie Nikas and Adam Sandler's Howard Ratner absolutely feel as though they could be plucked from any street corner in New York, neither character is technically real. Here, Josh Safdie makes a conscious decision to ground Marty Supreme -albeit very loosely- in the life of an actual table tennis player, a figure so obscure that, frankly, none of us had ever heard of him before. That grounding proves crucial. Combined with the film's Pyrrhic ending, the closing needledrop of Tears for Fears' " Everybody Wants to Rule the World, " and the foreshadowing of Gwyneth Paltrow's fading movie star, Safdie constructs a portrait of ambition that is unmistakably American in texture. Each of these elements gestures toward a different facet of the American Dream: success as spectacle, notoriety as validation, and legacy as something both promised and perpetually out of reach. Yet these symbols are not the be-all and end-all of what Safdie is attempting. In the film's closing moments, the focus narrows to something far more intimate, as we are confronted with a crying Timothée Chalamet, separated by a pane of glass from a child whose birth he was absent for. Where Good Time and Uncut Gems leave the viewer to reckon with the chaotic fallout of their protagonists' lives only after their deaths, Marty Supreme shifts that burden. The onus is shared between the audience and Marty himself, inviting us to draw our own conclusions: whether the third time truly is the charm, whether Marty will finally abandon his incessant pursuit of notoriety in favour of something real, or whether he will remain perpetually stuck behind the glass- grieving a life he knows he will never live.
Man I wish Kenneth Lonergan directed more movies.

Pairing ex-Disney stars with two pointed Britney Spears songs- likely the pop world's most famous case of lost agency- is a masterstroke from Korine. A hedonistic, phosphorescent reverie that plays everything straight and narrow, only to distort and deconstruct the meaning of every maximalist abandon of inhibition, fetishising drugs, partying and violence until they're all reduced to a common denominator of sex, and with that, the shared reverie turns into a pipe dream. "I am starting to think this is the most spiritual place I've ever been."

It's perhaps inevitable that some viewers will find Hamnet inauthentic, just as many, including myself, did with Zhao's Best Picture-winning Nomadland . But where Nomadland often keeps its audience at arm's length through its reliance on expansive wide shots, Hamnet does the opposite and draws us in close. There's no attempt to disguise the film's intentions when Zhao opens with an epigraph taken from Stephen Greenblatt's 2004 essay, The Death of Hamnet and the Making of Hamlet . With that framing made explicit from the outset, complaints that the film manipulates its audience into feeling grief- or obliges them to cry- feel misplaced. Rather than questioning the film's authenticity, I find myself questioning the authenticity of those preconceptions. Many people grow up with an aversion to Shakespeare, not because of the work itself, but because they are forced to study it at a time when it can feel boring, incomprehensible, and stripped of any sense of pleasure or discovery. In turn, Shakespeare becomes this almost mythologised figure, elevated beyond reach, detached from the emotional clarity and humanity of the work we continue to engage with today. So when Maggie O'Farrell and Zhao recontextualise this through a semi-fictional account that tackles something as universal as grief and filters it through the lived experiences of William Shakespeare and his wife Agnes (Anne), it turns this mythologised figure into someone we can empathise with, and his work into something we can comprehend and feel. Even before the familiar notes of On the Nature of Daylight signal the close, Hamnet evokes Arrival throughout. Both films grapple with the grief of losing a child, but where Arrival fractures time to explore memory and inevitability, Hamnet bridges centuries, collapsing the distance between contemporary audiences and lives lived hundreds of years ago. It confronts a lingering question that I saw on Twitter a little while back: did people in the past experience emotion as we do? Jessie Buckley's towering and transportive performance answers that question with absolute clarity, rendering grief as tangible as our own.
Pretty damn explicit and kitsch about all its emotional moments but cute nonetheless. I could see a 90s version of this with Nick Cage instead and it's probably better.

Accomplished Malick imitators are few and far between, and while Clint Bentley makes Train Dreams feel transportive and novelistic in a wholly tactile way, it just doesn't nail the ineffable quality that lifts Malick's images from an aesthetic to a feeling, and doesn't commit in any sense to the dramaturgic weight that could make a story like this resonate. Slow cinema for people who don't actually want to watch slow cinema.

Feels equally, if not more, constrained by the burden of being 'one third of a whole' as the first film in the new trilogy did, and though Nia DaCosta had her work cut out for her, especially as an American filmmaker stepping into this franchise, she still manages to pull together a wickedly brilliant middle chapter. 28 Years Later was one of my surprise favourites of 2025, and while The Bone Temple is certainly tonal shift, both thematically and stylistically, slowing things down from the kinetic dread of Danny Boyle's sequel, it feels like the first time in a while we're reminded of the metaphor that the rage virus is meant to represent. It becomes a brutal examination of the philosophy, 'if there is so much evil in the world, and neither God nor Satan exists, who do we blame for our suffering?' In confronting that question, with all its gruesome implications, The Bone Temple suggests the most enduring source of evil has always been human nature itself.

One of my biggest blindspots, and man the way this turns from a prototypical chauvinistic, brazen madness to a primal, mythical hypnosis after Brando gets introduced is staggering. Those dissolves too, wow! Martin Sheen's voiceover is obviously iconic, and Brando is Brando, and half the time I'm wondering how the hell they pulled some of this off before remembering that it's one of the most iconic examples of a nightmare production- feels reminiscent of Sorcerer in more ways than one.

Shot with such vibrant colours and playful costume design that only further emphasise Solondz' pointed dark humour, which works far better here than it did for me with Happiness, mainly because we're just focusing on the one character. I do think there needed to be some comeuppance or notable change in her circumstances towards the end, though I suppose the cynicism of the 'nothing ever changes' conclusion works too. So depressing when you hear about Solondz struggling to finance his films- his latest one having to cancel production in 2024 because of lack of funding, and it would have starred Elizabeth Olsen and Charles Melton too!

What spectacular camerawork here, wow! And Kramer's decision to include actual Holocaust footage is certainly jarring, intentionally so, of course. Stellar performances all round too- Montgomery Clift's part a personal highlight.

A little long and not as immediately resonant as Park's other work, but even with these faults he's doing it better than almost anyone else in the game. Darkly comedic, reminiscent of Tokyo Sonata in that it's a confident satire of the typical, nuclear family, urban lifestyle that gradually decays and collapses from cracks that were already there.

Love the whole gritty, handheld, follow-through-the-streets feel this has. Probably the best of Refn's work I've watched so far. Wish Mads was in it more but Kim Bodnia was a great lead nonetheless. Need to watch the others asap.

Affecting in parts, for sure, but it never quite gels for me as a whole. Despite some terrific performances, I never fully buy into the world Dolan is trying to create. Off-kilter and uneasy by design, particularly with the 1:1 aspect ratio and establishing diegetic premise, but I hardly ever felt truly challenged or provoked by any of it. All felt a little too obvious and tongue in cheek for me.

Nothing quite like watching one of the greatest films of all time to get you out of a slump. Would have been up there even if it had ended when the intermission hit; undoubtedly there once the rest of it unfolds.

Feels like the mid-budget sappy drama is a bit of a lost art nowadays, aside from maybe The Holdovers but that was mainly pastiche. Anyway, this was a pretty good one. Nothing revolutionary, but what a great cast, even some of the minor characters.

I've only seen Trier's two most recent films, including this one, but it almost frustrates me how close I am to the pendulum swinging either way with me connecting with them or not. What I mean to say is that The Worst Person in the World didn't fully grab me emotionally until around the last act, and now Sentimental Value holds a similar kind of understated restraint that leaves me a little too uninvested by the end. These characters are experiencing these big, complex emotions, but it feels like I'm just outside the room every time, a voyeur to the atmosphere rather than a participant. There's a dryness to the sentiment that seems similarly shared by the dryness of a lot of European wit, and it can be easy for either to pass you by if you're not unquestionably present. That being said, Trier's latest film is still full of a lot of heart, that's for sure. The meta layer of filmmaking acting as this therapising bridge between a repressed self and an actualised self is a brilliant tool that he makes use of very well, especially in the concluding scene. Stellan is spectacular, as he so often is, and Renate is excellent too. Frankly, I thought this could have been longer, though maybe that is because I was searching for a little more to chew on. Though, just put enough beautiful women in a film, and I'm bound to enjoy it.

Beautiful and cryptic. Really got under my skin. Lulls you into a trance with vibrant colours and a gentle monotony only to jolt you with jarring sound design and an incongruous narrative. Feels reductive to just call this folk horror because it exists in a limbo of uncanniness that feels as equally comforting as it does unsettling.

Don't love how this is shot, but the way Zahler depicts his violence as banal and ruthless is quite something. Could see this being a much rougher watch if not for the delightful performance from Richard Jenkins.

film_key: Before the Devil Knows You're Dead (2007)
review_clean: Undeniably full of some of the snags of 2000s digital filmmaking, but with actors this good and a script that feels inventive even though it's practically the umpteenth spin on the Murphy's Law downward spiral, it still remains a deft thriller, directed by an 82 year old Lumet.

A little less challenging than I was expecting, but I suppose the rudimentary nature of the narrative could be seen as both a positive and a negative. Certainly a film steeped in personal experience, obviously given Panahi's past, and I'm glad to expand my repertoire of Iranian cinema past just Kiarostami.

An awesome technical achievement, but it genuinely feels like this film is running on autopilot 90% of the time. I mean, there's a barebones script and then there's this; at least Top Gun : Maverick struck the balance right between thrills and sentimentality. I will probably watch F1 2 or whatever gymnastics they'll have to navigate to figure out a name for it- though I fear that it'll follow the same path as a lot of sports movie sequels where it'll struggle to up the ante in any tangible way.

Didn't realise I had missed a monologuing Ethan Hawke until now. A taut, single-location dissertation on the vulnerability of putting art out there for anyone that will listen, set against the easier temptation of putting things out there simply because people are listening.

Appreciate the subversion of The Secret Agent being a slow burn given what people would expect from its title. Strangely enough evokes The Zone of Interest for me in that it captures a place and a time, buried and caked in layers of history and death until it becomes someplace else entirely. Wagner Moura is terrific throughout, as is Tânia Maria in her short time on screen. Some may find this meandering, and I don't really blame them, as the film ultimately leans into a kind of deliberate bathos, rejecting the satisfaction of the narrative it seems to be setting up for itself, but I can't say I was bored for a moment of it. P.S. Randomly thought I had recognised one of the rooms in this film as the same as one in a Brazilian short film I had watched a while back called Green Vinyl, and it turns out the same guy directed this! Not even sure if it's the same location or not, but still have to commend myself. Some catch.

A Sorcerer- esque road trip misadventure in search of a utopian rave in the middle of the Moroccan desert sounds unbelievably cool in theory, but unfortunately with Sirāt, it's totally drab in execution. A narrative that's so hard to take seriously that you almost have to assume that Laxe is shooting for dark comedy- though if so, it's terribly unfunny.

It's fine. Very schmaltzy and I was ready for it to end about 3 times before it did. Kate Hudson and Hugh Jackman are good enough, though I couldn't help but keep thinking of the TikToks poking fun at Jackman's vibrato every time he sings, even though it's less egregious here.

Apichatpong Weerasethakul, one of the pillars of slow cinema, has on many occasions spoken of his comfort with viewers falling asleep to the lulling, hypnotic nature of his films, saying, "I am fine when people say that they fall asleep in my movies. They wake up and can patch things together in their own way," and has even gone so far as to express a desire to "have a cinema specifically for sleeping." With Bi Gan's new feature Resurrection , he decides to skip the middleman, fashioning a film that all but invites unconsciousness by exploring the connective power of dreams. As such, the narrative unfolds with a oneiric fluidity, where characters, places, and moments shift seamlessly, hinting at a faint longing for what slips away, before we are drawn wholly into its current, until we wake to patch together the fragments like shots in a reel of film.

No doubt the snarky contrarians will love to hate on this, particularly because it coincidentally finds itself on the arbitrary list of highest-rated films on this platform, as many coveted releases do before their inevitable fall-off. But as a fan of Weir's novel, I couldn't help but be won over by the feel-good charms of Project Hail Mary . It's certainly a little more MCU-style quippy and a little less of a microcosmic science lesson-probably my favourite characteristic of the book, and it's a shame that it's not as present here. There's also a noticeably lighter weight to the gravity of the decisions and sacrifices made, yet it remains delightful on the whole, much down to Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace-a name close enough that you can't help but think Weir had him in mind while writing his protagonist.
All three of Olivia Cooke, Anya Taylor-Joy, and Anton Yelchin are so good in this. We need Olivia Cooke in more things please.

Having watched both this and Sharp Objects recently, though she's in the latter only briefly, I'm still of the belief that Sydney Sweeney can very much act; it's just that her current path is seemingly a lot more lucrative, which is a sad sight to see.

Feels like when people say "They don't make movies like this anymore," they're usually talking about grand epics when they should really be talking about small, domestic dramas like The Ice Storm. A film that could veer into so many avenues of excessive melodrama, but it never really does; instead it toes the line with sprinkles of dark humour that lesser films would go all out on. Almost feels like the closest thing to a Hollywood Haneke film, albeit vastly less dark and cold-ironic considering its name.

Probably works a little better in a vacuum if you haven't seen the show, and although it's been a few years for me, Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man still falls into the exact same schtick that had already become old post-season 2. It's shot competently enough, but frankly, why did this need to be made? Other than the fact that it is painfully obvious that this is setting up for the spin-off sequel series, it just doesn't justify its existence as a worthwhile continuation. The show became a pretty vapid parody of itself in the last couple of seasons, coasting off Tommy's PTSD and depression as if that's a compelling crux after seeing it for multiple seasons prior, and the film is more of the same. Many well-regarded shows develop cult-like fanbases, and no subsection is quite as insufferable as those who assume the identity of Tommy Shelby as a sort of anti-woke, jingoistic symbol. Usually these audiences are drawn through a fundamental misunderstanding of the material that they're canonising, but I'm really, probably belatedly, beginning to think that Peaky Blinders does nothing to dissuade people that the messages they're taking away and the symbols they're creating are false.

"The dreams of others are extremely dangerous... Never get caught in someone else's dream." For such a major event that impacted the lives of so many people, there's still a noticeable lack of art that captures the rather singular feeling of the global pandemic. You'd expect this feeling to be a little more quantifiable, but perhaps it's the oxymoron of being forcibly separated from the rest of the world but still having access to it that makes this feeling so unknowable. Therefore, through Coma, Bonello forgoes the task of trying to articulate his own experience, and instead opens himself up to the empathy of depicting his teenage daughter's. It's a beautiful ode that tries to capture the complexity of the world being taken away from you just as you've gotten to know it, told through skits with dolls, enigmatic YouTube tutorials, and nightmarish simulations of a purgatorial forest prison. Reminds me a little of We're All Going to the World's Fair in that I'm not sure it all entirely works together, especially for the amount it tries to do in under 90 minutes, but it's nothing if not affecting.
Soderbergh is a savant for this type of sleek filmmaking and he doesn't miss here.

Almost as if Benny Safdie recognised that there's so many clichéd routes that fighting, and particularly wrestling films, take with issues of substance abuse and pushing oneself too hard that he glosses over them for the most part, but in doing so leaves a film that feels like mostly empty space. If Dwayne Johnson really wanted to legitimise himself as a quote-unquote actor, why choose a role so in his wheelhouse?
Think it misses the boat on where it focuses its messaging, especially with the dad character, but McAvoy is great. Should probably see how this holds up in comparison to the original.

Watched this half on a plane and half at home, which may have hindered the experience a little bit, but have to say I'm very much impressed. Always a little sceptical when actors try their hand at directing, especially one as early in his career as Dickinson is, but this is compelling stuff for a debut, with Frank Dillane giving one of the years best performances.

Love Christina Ricci. My first Gallo, and I'm kinda surprised he didn't make more films than he did, even though he is largely known as an arrogant creep-but it's not like that's stopped many others from thriving in the film industry.
What are they putting in these French courtroom dramas?!

It almost adds to the beauty of the film- the sense that parts of our parents will always remain unknowable- with the fact that Erice considered this to be an unfinished half of a story. A coming to terms with information absorbed in childhood, only contextualised once you grow up and look back on it. Scenes fading in and out through light like memories. Gorgeous.

I do find myself wondering how cinema audiences in the US have reacted to The Drama compared to here in the UK, because in my screening much of the film was met with laughter, whereas I can easily imagine some of those same moments landing quite differently for American viewers. That said, the film feels somewhat lacking in the cultural bite that Borgli brought to Sick of Myself , though it's undeniably clever in how the narrative hinges on the fallout from an act that was never even committed, and in the way it both begins and ends as a parody of a romantic comedy. Don't think there's much that could convince me not to marry Zendaya, though.

I remember, sometime after the release of Roland Emmerich's 2009 film 2012 , I was at a family member's house for some gathering, and we had decided one evening to watch the film. A post-film discussion ensued, debating on whether the world would actually end in 2012, or whether it was just a paranoid rehash of the Y2K hysteria that I had just missed having been born in 2001. The conversation continued, some devil's advocates fruitlessly defending the corner of the world actually ending in 2012, no doubt to frighten the then 8 or 9 year old me, and some trying to determine that if the world wasn't to end in apocalyptic inferno in 2012, then when was the Earth, and all of us in the room with it, to meet its untimely demise? It was during this conversation that, briefly and unheard by the rest of the room, my grandma brought up that she thought that the world wasn't going to end in 2012, but 2016. It was a short comment that I paid no real mind to as part of the larger back and forth, especially since I don't think anybody else but me heard it, but looking back a few years on, the comment weirdly struck a chord with me, because my grandma passed away in 2016. So, in a way, the world didn't end then as she said it would, but I guess, in some quietly macabre way, her world did. In Loveless , in a similar vein to Haneke's Caché , the background sound is often populated by mutterings of political news or related commentary through radio. It's one of those implicit period pieces that doesn't quite state what year it is, and so you infer through diegetic cues like the technology used or the aforementioned radio talk when it's actually set. Talk of Russia's presidential election (where Putin came into power again), conflict with Ukraine, and a mention of a growing sentiment of the world coming to an end, signalled by the inexplicable conclusion of the Mayan calendar, lets you eventually place the film as being set sometime in 2012. From this, I was reminded of the earlier anecdote, and empathised with this child, stuck beneath the dying embers of a loveless marriage, and thought that it was like his world was coming to an end too. A solitary apocalypse borne of the cold, cultural stoicism that meant that nobody was listening, that reduces him to being one of many, while the rest of the world- and the rest of the household- try and try to move on with their lives.

There's maybe a nugget of worthwhile stuff in here but it's buried deep beneath layers upon layers of vanity and failed attempts at relevant humour. Seriously how does someone so intertwined with comedy have their finger so far off the pulse when it comes to directing it? A little highlight with Marty, and strangely enough Ivy Volk, who provided my only chuckle of the film. I was going to call Outcome this year's Poolman , but at least that wasn't as insufferable in its ironic self-pitying.

A film very clearly made by an editor, and quite unlike anything I've seen before. Perhaps almost lends itself to the drowsy state I watched this in, and probably the closest comparison to Resurrection that I saw earlier this year. Though, I'm not sure I totally loved the humour, aside from a couple gags, and the fast-paced anthology really made it hard to become invested in any of it; more interesting as an art piece as homage to early cinema than anything else.

An ardent satire built upon a circus of slapstick bureaucracy that leaves you as lost as its juggled protagonists. Trapped in a labyrinthine concrete jungle of choreographed routine that renders the beauty of the old world just out of reach, and instead embraces the chaos of modernity with a fatalistic acceptance.
Laura Linney auditioning for Wendy from Ozark at the end there.

Almost no-one plays the balancing act of sincerity and comedy as well as Cronenberg, and here he's expressing his burning contempt for the incestuous, nepotistic inauthenticity of Hollywood- and Los Angeles in general- with a biting, sardonic edge. A constellation of stars connected by the same depravity and cycle of reciprocal sycophancy. Plus, Julianne Moore and Mia Wasikowska in the same movie- I was pretty much guaranteed to like it.

Been a little while since I last watched a Kurosawa film, but I have to say I think this has been my least favourite so far. Mifune is terrific as ever, and this is no doubt a feast visually, but all the other characters (and I'm going to call them by their original names because I couldn't tell you what they were here) like Duncan, Lady Macbeth, Banquo, and Macduff all feel a bit glossed over. As such, a lot of the emotional power of the play is lost, and even though the revision of the ending is a thrilling watch, I think it kind of highlights why the film didn't totally work for me, because that final confrontation between Macduff and Macbeth feels like an exclusion that is ultimately of no consequence.

You kind of have to take these war flicks at face value, else it's really hard to derive any sort of insight when you're constantly thinking about how each dramatic moment or line of dialogue is a building block of propaganda- though it's almost funny how little of the chaos is chalked up to military incompetence here. Still, Scott's direction of every set piece is top notch throughout, and even though the American accents are all over the place, the ensemble largely do a good job of existing amidst the carnage. At points, the film feels so excessively dismissive towards its Somali populace, to the extent that it can almost read like a British filmmaker's wry, possibly tongue-in-cheek critique of American patriotism, especially in the closing title card, which notes that over 1000 Somalis were killed, before listing, by name, each of the 19 American soldiers who died, in the same block of text. But maybe I'm reading into it too much.

A little too didactic in the first half, but forgivable in the sense that it lays the groundwork for all that is paid off in the second. Sensational stuff from Zahler. A gritty, no-holds-barred thriller laced with moral provocation that explores the limits at which one's ideals are tested when squeezed under the pressure of money or circumstance. A fastidiously measured examination of how far one can be pushed until they compromise everything that they stand for- or are at least supposed to stand for.

Doesn't delve too deeply into the criminal underworld it portrays, instead leaning into a darkly comedic tone that works more often than not. Still, the film is at its strongest when Bob Hoskins anchors its tragic, doomed romance, with his tender vulnerability beneath a hard-shelled exterior.

A little too silly for my liking, but I suppose that's Raimi's schtick. A pretty fun delve into what would happen if we turned the third act of Triangle of Sadness into a full feature. McAdams and O'Brian are both great, particularly the former who's just an underrated (comic) actress in general.

Bana was probably my favourite part of Black Hawk Down, which I also watched recently, but he's on a totally different level here- stellar stuff from him. Been a little hesitant to delve into Dominik's stuff after watching Blonde a few years back, but I've of course heard about how revered The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford is, and watching this has shot that up my list.

The characters don't get the same amount of fleshing out as something like Dazed and Confused, mostly because this zooms through a whole school year in 90 minutes while the former explores only one night, but this is still great stuff, and I'm always a bit of a sucker for this sub-genre. It gives me a nostalgia for a time and place I never actually experienced, and Crowe kind of has it that feeling on lock. The flashes of Nicholas Cage had me wondering if it was actually him or not until I saw him down as Nicholas Coppola in the credits; turns out this was his feature debut!

Couldn't help but think of Lav Diaz saying that he thought of the idea of casting Gael García Bernal as Magellan during sex. In any case, this is stunning. A lingering critique of the reverence for history's mythologised men; be that of an explorer canonised for his conquests or a resistance fighter elevated through nationalist folklore. Diaz interrogates the machinery of historical memory itself, exposing how such figures are shaped, distorted, and sanctified by the narratives that survive them, with the forced imposition of religion extending this same process- colonial violence legitimised as doctrine.

With a film like this where dialogue is so forefront, it becomes very easily apparent when conversations feel contrived or inauthentic, especially when you have inexperienced actors delivering it. While parts of Clerks feel earnest in their means of showing that you have to take action to change your circumstance, the rest just feels like a means to an end, with a few gags thrown in to paper the cracks. You can give enough grace when you see the low budget as well as the fact this is a directorial debut, and I get that the constructed vibe can be a stylistic choice, but the only thing I ever really buy are Jeff Anderson's antics as a way to deal with workplace ennui.

First act rips and the action sequences have some real momentum to them in spite of looking pretty ugly and feeling a little over-choreographed at times. Hard to say that I couldn't foresee exactly where each character would end up within the first few moments of meeting them, but it still builds to a fairly emotional climax nevertheless.

I flip-flop between which of Malick's films is my favourite a fair amount, but it's safe to say the one I find myself thinking about the most is unequivocally Badlands - and that may just answer that question for me.

Possibly my favourite of Allen's work thus far, largely because there's not really a self-insert character here, save maybe some bathetic voiceover; rather Bardem's charming Catalonian is more a representation of who he'd want to be, which is a notably less egregious sin because who wouldn't have that desire? Needless to say, as soon as Penelope Cruz' character is introduced, she takes command of each scene she's in and the rest of the film floats on her energy.

I'm not not a fan of Raimi's prototypical pulpy style, but A Simple Plan works best precisely because of its restraint. As a straight moral tragedy, it feels as cold and inevitable as the snow that envelops its landscape, and just as entrapping. Paxton and Thornton are exceptional together, and every shift in their dynamic lands exactly as it should.

Man, keeping the anonymity of the truck driver the whole way is just not something you would get in a movie nowadays. I'm not as hot on a lot of Spielberg's stuff as many people, and even though this still runs a little long for my liking, it is still a killer debut. A Hitchcockian twist on the old Western standoff that doubles as a critique of masculine pride and the hollowness of its vindication. I was wondering the whole way through whether the in-your-face, bold-lettered 'FLAMMABLE' on the back of the truck was going to be a red herring or not, and turns out it was!

"Our movie was never able to catch up to reality. Reality is sometimes more powerful than movies." Been meaning to check out more of Obayashi's work for a long while, and this was just wonderful. Given the hopelessness that sets in midway through-and knowing it was based on a true story-I wasn't sure where it was going to land, and though it could have easily become overwhelmed by sentimentality, Obayashi ultimately steers it in a way that feels wholly fulfilling. Masako Motai's performance in particular holds the emotional weight of the film with such care.

Comes from the Black Mirror school of high-concept storytelling, where the premise is so strong that it can almost survive on that alone. Backrooms exists almost entirely as an exercise in translating its one idea to the screen, and though it does so remarkably well-particularly in the found-footage segments, which begs the question of why the entire film isn't shot that way-everything surrounding it dissipates into the same liminal void it seeks to evoke. There's something to be said about its attempt to capture the agonising drudgery of office life, with its endless beige corridors and the electrical buzz of fluorescent lighting, in a similar vein to Severance , and the geography of its labyrinthine structure is particularly impressive. This lands especially well amid a growing cultural distaste for the commute-to-cubicle routine in the age of remote work, and Chiwetel Ejiofor's failed architect is a good vehicle for that feeling. But it's his conveniently positioned counterpart-a therapist with unresolved childhood trauma that remains unresolved by the film's end-that offers no real foil and exists primarily as a conduit for exposition, a crutch that seems all too increasingly common in contemporary cinema. And therefore, what we're left with is a film that renders its own mystique too concrete by the end, collapsing its horror into an inert space that feels largely incomplete, though perhaps that's just opening the door on expanding on the lore of the Backrooms even further-even if, ultimately, the more that is explained, the less intriguing the idea becomes.

film_key: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown (1988)
review_clean: Very fun! Love the colours, the deadpan delivery of all the absurd lines of dialogue, and the fact that it's all told through only a small handful of wonderfully designed locations. Thought this would be more of an ensemble given the title, but still very entertaining nonetheless. Need to see more of Almodóvar's work for sure.

Doesn't decide at all what tone it's going for and it's almost all the better for it. Definitely overlong, and a little overcomplicated, but Hackman's great as always. Love that we see shades of action star Tom Cruise before that became a fully fledged thing; doubly strange that it's in a legal thriller.

Collectively such wonderful performances across the board here. Ambiguous on purpose, sometimes in service of the narrative, though I feel like a better film would have aimed to either side with the malicious pragmatism of a protagonist like in Red Rooms , or with something more empathetic: as there's not really a moment in the film that I believe that this woman could be this couple's missing daughter, and therefore there's never really a moment that I can bask in the same hope that each of them feels. I can appreciate the strive for subtlety, but sometimes I need a little bit more to chew on.

Breathes with the same energy as something like Barbarian insofar as it's an exploration of a very current sort of horror, and Barker's film finds it in the spaces people become trapped inside, though here the labyrinth isn't architectural so much as emotional. The four walls of a suburban nightmare are exchanged for the suffocating confines of an unreciprocated relationship, allowing Barker to interrogate the resentments that metastasise into incel ideology and misogyny-fuelled violence. His internet-native sensibilities prove invaluable in that regard, evident not only in the simplicity of a premise whose monkey's paw familiarity runs the risk of feeling tropey, but which is elevated by his instinctive grasp of the digital spaces from which these grievances emerge, embedding them into the film's DNA with enough confidence that even naming his awkward protagonist Bear feels like a knowing wink towards the viral "man or bear" discourse, and the film wastes no time in telling you which side it's on.

Few debuts leave me this eager to see what comes next from a filmmaker. Even having already seen Godland which feels notably more accessible, Winter Brothers feels somehow more assured; a stunning visual and auditory achievement.

Could easily feel kitsch and gimmicky as Midnight in Paris did, but Farrow and Daniels' wonderful performances keep the sentimentality feeling like a warming homage rather than on the nose. Loved that ending.
Bet they thought they were dead clever with that double meaning of a mountain's apex and an apex predator.
Obviously filled with racist tropes that toe the line of being character flaws until they don't. Still one of the most naturalistically gorgeous looking films I've seen.
This and Liar Liar were basically the same film in my mind and I'm finally checking one of them off. Nice to see John Michael Higgins playing what's pretty much his exact character from Community .
Man, Nick Cage is so good.

Occasionally superficial, in the sense that it tries to probe something deeper but never quite gets there, yet nevertheless very funny. Certainly a rebound for Olivia Wilde after Don't Worry Darling, though I'm not sure there was ever cause for such a dramatic loss of faith in her directorial ability. If anything, the behind-the-scenes drama that sprang from her previous film seemed to stoke the fire here, prompting a much more incisive exploration of domesticity and sex.

Thought I'd do some preparation for The Odyssey tomorrow and watch one of the Anne Hathaway films I hadn't seen, and I gotta say, it might be recency bias, but I think this might be my favourite performance of hers. Reminded me slightly of Margot At The Wedding, though maybe my brain is drawing comparisons where there aren't any just because of the marriage connection. In any case, it just felt so authentic, especially when it's in and around the chaos of wedding ceremonies and all the planning that goes into them, and there's not really much I didn't buy into.

There was a whole host of speculation following the release of Christopher Nolan's previous film, Oppenheimer , especially after what was considered to be a long awaited Best Picture and Best Director win at the Oscars, about what could possibly follow on from what many considered to be his opus. In retrospect, the epigraph that opens that film lay covertly as a sign for what was to come: "Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity." Nolan's exploration of the American Prometheus could only logically be followed by his exploration of a more traditional kind of mythology. Though, his venture to adapt a story that became the foundational archetype by which all succeeding narratives of epic journeys against insurmountable odds followed, including one of his own films in Interstellar , may have been a Scylla and Charybdis in and of itself. Unlike so much of his current catalogue, with an ostensibly complex narrative and a layer of simplicity underneath, the simplicity of The Odyssey is very much a defining feature, and it's the complexity, instead, that lies beneath the surface. And I think it's with that inversion of his formula that Nolan struggles. The film's conclusion, at least, is clear: to defy the gods is to defy your own nature, and to defy your nature is a recipe for disaster; the irony being that Nolan has defied his here too, and it doesn't quite pay off as it should, and, in spite of all the IMAX spectacle, the limitations of the format have never felt more apparent than they do here.

So good! Love the way it plays with the idea of transactional relationships between people as well as the transactional relationship between people and capitalism, and there's no better place to encapsulate the coldness of that feeling than New York. Voight and Hoffman are both terrific-their chemistry as a duo makes this feel slightly reminiscent of films like Mikey and Nicky and Thunderbolt and Lightfoot- and Schlesinger nails the aesthetic with such effortlessness.

Meta stuff in film always reads as a gamble to me. The second a movie acknowledges itself you lose the thing you came for; the barrier of immersion and escapism between the filmmaker and the audience is gone, leaving the film in this vulnerable state of suddenly becoming unreal. Blue Heron pulls something along those lines at around the halfway mark and I spent a little while unconvinced. The social worker group discussion is too on the nose and I could feel the film wanting me to understand something it had already made me feel beforehand. But then, by proxy, Romvari assumes a role in her own film, and her own memories, and instead of it being a document of what happened, it becomes a confrontation that she's standing inside of. It's a film I've seen versions of before, but the story is so particular to her that it leaves room for you to project your own memories and emotions onto it, and that's where it's most affecting.

Largely business as usual as far as your typical MCU fare goes, though I have to say one facet that disappointed me in particular was just a total lack of velocity with these action sequences. Shang-Chi had some of my favourite stunt choreography across these films but Cretton didn't seem to carry that flow here-it's like they begin to build towards something but then cut away before it actually gets anywhere exciting. Still seems as though James Cameron is the only guy to really get what a kinetic action sequence should look like in a blockbuster. Nevertheless, having grown up with the Raimi films and sharing the aspirations of every young boy my age to grow up to be Spider-Man, I still have a lot of room in my heart for this character, and there is some of that heart in the way that these characters interact in the smaller, more intimate moments, but it's lost as soon as things get bigger; it's like they're terrified to make a grounded, self-contained Spider-Man story.

Aged awfully and a lot of this is terribly unfunny, but unfortunately it really does kinda feel like an accurate portrayal of working in a restaurant, even though I've luckily never had to work in hospitality, and it did make me laugh a couple times. Plus, the credits song went a little hard.
Starts a little messy trying to figure out who's on who's side until it gets to a point where is basically doesn't matter. So stylish and fun!

Somehow I was surprised at the level of gratuity and perversion here, but I suppose I should have known better. Still, about as singular as cinematic vision gets, and I can't say that it won't be sitting in my mind for some time. Always bewilders me when I remember that Jodorowsky is still alive.

I seem to have somewhat of a predilection towards these intimate character-dramas about alienation, and I was quite surprised to see that this was Zwigoff's last feature. It does reinforce the protagonist's viewpoint a little too much at times, where instead of him being equally the target of all the art school satirising, he's more the mouthpiece, and I think that misses the point a little. Still, when we focus on some of the side characters like Malkovich and Broadbent, it's a largely fun time.

PSH terrific as always, but I don't think this elevates itself to a level that biopics must in order to really stand out and become memorable. I was kinda surprised that Miller hadn't worked on anything post Foxcatcher, although after finishing the film I read that he's been spending his time making AI generated art for gallery exhibitions, so there's that. Though he's been simultaneously been making a documentary about AI and the shift in the technological space, so I suppose I'll reserve the rest of the judgement until I see the sentiment of that.
